#3495. No, We Aren’t All Eating 'Too Much' Protein

If you’ll permit me a rant—I promise to make it fact-filled and interesting—I am sick of the articles that seem to pop up every few months claiming that we are all eating “too much” protein. They convey an inaccurate picture of how the body uses protein, and they demonize perfectly healthy meals that happen to be high in protein. It’s time to set the record straight.

It is true that most of us eat more than the RDA (recommended daily allowance) of protein, but that's a good thing—the RDA is meant as a minimum. It's true that protein-boosted foods are trendy, and that they're not necessarily great dietary choices in the big picture. It's also true that you can eat a healthy diet with little to no meat, but meat is not synonymous with protein. Let's look at what we actually know about the role of protein in a healthy diet, and how to tell if you're eating too much or too little.

As a refresher, protein is one of the three calorie-containing macronutrients (fats, carbs, protein) that make up most of the food we eat. Proteins are made of amino acids, and these amino acids are required for the growth, repair, and functioning of our bodies.

We can get protein from a variety of sources. Meats are particularly protein-dense; a chicken breast contains about 35 grams of protein. Other animal products, like milk and eggs, are also rich in protein. Plant-based foods tend to have less protein than animal products, but it’s not hard to meet or exceed protein requirements even on a vegan diet. Beans, grains, and soy products like tofu contain significant amounts of protein, for example.

If you’d like a cheat sheet on how much protein you’re supposed to eat based on your activity level, you can find one here. And that’s a good place to start dissecting this “too much protein” myth, because before we can declare an amount of protein to be “too much,” we need to understand how much is “enough.”

The government communicates targets for different nutrients to encourage us all to eat a healthy, balanced diet. These targets are the basis for the “% daily value” labels on the back of packaged foods, and for the nutrient makeup of school lunches. The RDA, or recommended daily allowance, is defined as “the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirement of nearly all (97 to 98 percent) healthy individuals in a group.”

In other words, if 100% of us were to eat the RDA of protein, at least 97% of us would be getting enough protein—we'd be meeting the minimum to be healthy. That's right, this number is a minimum to avoid malnutrition, not a maximum, and not a recommendation for optimal health.

By the way, if you're wondering how that number is determined? For protein, it is based on nitrogen balance. Humans break down proteins, as part of our body’s daily function, and we excrete nitrogen as a result. If you eat enough protein (which contains nitrogen), the amount of nitrogen you excrete will be the same as, or more than, the amount you eat. In other words, if you aren’t breaking your own body proteins down (in excess of what you eat), then whatever you’re eating must be, in some sense, enough.

In this way of thinking, the RDA is the minimum to stay healthy. More is fine; less would mean that you may not be getting enough. For some nutrients, there is also an UL, or upper limit, telling you that more than a certain amount is too much. Upper limits are calculated for vitamins and minerals; there is no upper limit defined for protein.

Therefore, there is no official definition for “too much” protein. If somebody eats more than the RDA, they’re not eating too much; they’re just eating more than the minimum. You’re supposed to eat more than the minimum.

The RDA for protein is set at 46 grams per day for a 125-pound woman, and at 56 grams per day for a 154-pound man. (The USDA chose those as their examples.) That’s based on an RDA of 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram bodyweight, which works out to 0.36 grams per pound. So a 200-pound person would need 72 grams of protein per day.

This USDA report found that most adult men average roughly 90 to 100 grams of protein per day, although men aged 70 and up only get about 80 grams of protein per day. Women tend to average around 70 grams per day, with those aged 70 and up averaging 62 grams.

Above the RDA? Yes. Too much? I don’t see any way of arguing that. And before you say that we’re getting almost double the recommendation, let's check the math. Those RDA numbers are for 125- and 154-pound people. On the other hand, the averages for what we eat are based on actual people, not ideals. The average American man is 200 pounds, and the average American woman is 171 pounds. So, to compare the numbers:

The average woman is 171 pounds, so her RDA would be 62 grams per day. (Women, on average, eat 70 grams of protein per day.)

The average man is 200 pounds, so his RDA would be 72 grams per day. (Men, on average, eat 90 to 100 grams of protein per day.)

Again, there’s no need to stick to the minimum; going 8 grams over, or even 28 grams over, is fine. It’s probably better to go over than to just scrape by, and many of us arguably don’t get enough. Let me explain.

Let’s start with older adults. Not only does protein intake tend to decrease with age, older adults are vulnerable to issues that stem from a loss of muscle mass. People tend to lose 3-5% of their muscle mass per decade starting at age 30, but strength training and protein intake can support maintaining our muscle, and thus likely prevent or reduce that decline.

The Dietary Guidelines include a note that “About 50 percent of women and 30 percent of men 71 and older fall short of protein foods recommendations.” Meanwhile, a study found that older adults who don’t meet the recommendations are “more likely to be limited when stooping, crouching, or kneeling, standing or sitting for long periods, walking up 10 steps, preparing meals, and walking for a quarter mile.”

So even if it’s true that the average adult gets more protein than recommended, there are clearly a lot of elderly folks who don’t. These are the same people who have more issues functioning in everyday life. This may be a chicken-and-egg situation—was the functional decline a cause or an effect of the change in their diet?—but this sure does not seem to be a group of people who should be eating less protein.

There’s another large group of people who benefit from more, not less, protein: people who are pregnant or lactating. Instead of 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight (62 grams for a 171-pound person), the RDA for people who are pregnant or lactating is 0.5 grams/pound (so, 86 grams of protein per day).

When you’re pregnant, you also have higher caloric needs, so the increased total amount of food makes it easier to get the higher protein amount. Still, it makes more sense to spend your energy on making sure you’re getting enough protein, rather than worrying about getting too much.

You knew we were heading in this direction (I say between reps of barbell squats, wiping protein shake off my lips): People who exercise should get more protein than just the RDA.

While the fear-mongering “too much protein” articles sometimes mention that bodybuilders or elite athletes need their protein, they tend to hand-wave this away as a special concern that doesn’t apply to normal people. But I think it’s worth a closer look—and honestly, this situation applies to a lot more people than just a few athletes.

Officially, there isn’t an RDA for athletes; people who exercise can stave off malnutrition with the same 0.36 grams per pound as everyone else. But that doesn’t mean that the RDA is the best target to aim for.

The International Association of Athletics Federations, which governs track and field competitions, recommends that most athletes who are maintaining or gaining weight eat 0.59 to 0.77 grams of protein per pound of bodyweight per day. That’s 101 to 131 grams for the average 171-pound woman, and 118 to 154 grams for a 200-pound man.

A group of organizations, including the American College of Sports Medicine, largely agrees, recommending a range from 0.54 to 0.9 grams per pound for all athletes whose weight is stable or gaining. That includes people who do endurance training like distance running, as well as strength athletes whose exercise involves mainly lifting weights. Those ranges would go as high as 153 grams for our 171-pound woman, and 180 grams for our 200-pound man.

You don’t need to be an Olympian to consider yourself an “athlete” in this sense. If you’re training for a half marathon, you’re doing plenty of distance running, and should fuel accordingly. And if you’re “just” lifting weights in the gym, but taking it seriously enough that you’re training regularly and working hard, you should consider eating in these ranges as well.

Dieting to lose weight is not only a popular American pastime, it’s also arguably good for at least some people's health. If you’ve been on a diet recently, or if you’re planning to go on one, you aren’t a person who should settle for the RDA either.

Research shows that protein intake (and strength training—they go together!) is important to maintain muscle mass when we’re losing weight. After all, you’re aiming for fat loss, not trying to get your muscles to waste away. Muscle loss is especially a concern with weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, but any dieter should be aware of this issue.

For example, this study found that diets ranging from 0.48 to 0.72 grams of protein per kg of body weight (that’s 82 to 123 grams for our 171-pound woman, 96 to 144 for our 200-pound man) resulted in less weight regain after the diet, and helped people to maintain muscle mass and feel more full while they were dieting.

And if you’re losing weight and exercising? The IAAF recommends that athletes who are “undertaking high-quality weight loss” need at least 0.72 grams per pound of bodyweight, and possibly as much as 1.09 grams per pound. That would be 186 grams for a 171-pound athlete, or 218 grams for a 200-pound athlete. Most people won’t need to go that high, and it’s unclear whether athletes need to go that high. But I’m including these numbers so you see how high the ranges actually go.

Ultimately, weight loss is widely understood to be more effective and have healthier results with higher protein intakes rather than lower ones. When people focus on just eating less, without thinking about what their diet actually consists of, it’s easy to forget about protein. But the evidence suggests that you should increase protein when you’re decreasing overall calories.

The idea that protein causes weight gain is a common talking point in those articles about “too much” protein, and it’s sort of true—but it also doesn’t mean what you think it means.

When you eat more food than your body needs, your body can store it as fat. That’s true no matter what the excess is made of—protein, carbs, fat, or even alcohol. The protein you eat gets used for many different things in your body. You can build it into muscle tissue, use it for growth and repair of different kinds of cells, and so on. You can also use it for energy—basically, burning it for the calories.

So if you were eating a perfectly balanced diet, and then decided to add an extra 100 grams of protein per day, then sure, a lot of that protein would be used for energy, and since we’d have excess energy, it would get stored as fat.

But if you ate more protein, but that protein replaced other foods in your diet, then there would be no excess calories to store. Nobody is saying you should chug a couple of protein shakes on top of your regular diet. They’re saying (I’m saying) that you should plan your meals and snacks to include more protein.

For example, if your regular lunch is a turkey-and-cheese sandwich with a side of chips, you could improve the protein content of your diet by adding more turkey to the sandwich and replacing the chips with an apple. Same total calories, but more protein. As long as your total calories for the day aren’t in excess of your needs, the “extra” protein won’t get stored as fat.

In general, high protein diets don’t have any serious health consequences. There’s a major exception, though: in some medical conditions, you may be told to limit your protein intake to protect your health.

For example, people with chronic kidney disease are often advised to use the RDA (0.36 grams per pound of body weight) as a maximum rather than a minimum. Your kidneys play a role in processing protein for excretion, so a lowered protein intake reduces the amount of work that a damaged kidney has to do. That said, once a person with chronic kidney disease begins dialysis, they may be advised to increase their protein intake for better health now that their body has help to handle the higher levels.

People with certain other disorders, like phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, may also be advised to eat a low-protein diet. Obviously, if you have one of these conditions, you should be getting your dietary advice from your medical team (ask for a referral to a dietitian!) rather than from general articles on the internet.

Besides those known medical issues, the occasional findings about eating “too much” protein tend to fit into the “X is good for you/X is bad for you” ricochet news cycle. They’re not holistic assessments of protein in general on health in general, but rather specific research questions that are still being figured out.

For example, this 2017 study found that a high-protein (and high-fiber) diet seemed to slightly worsen one measure of insulin resistance, but it also improved metabolic health and body composition. The researchers concluded that the subjects’ body chemistry was probably just responding appropriately to the changed nutrient content of their diet. A few years later, a study of high-BMI women with insulin resistance saw improvements to their insulin resistance on a high-protein diet.

Or to take another example, a study in 2024 found a link between high-protein diets and atherosclerosis. But if you look at what the researchers were actually studying, they were looking at how leucine (one amino acid found in protein) affects the mTOR biochemical pathway in certain types of white blood cells. By the way, that mTOR pathway is involved in a lot more body processes than atherosclerosis, and does a lot of good things too.

So are these results interesting, and worth further study? Definitely. Worth changing protein recommendations? Only if this effect turns out (1) to actually lead to worse health outcomes, and (2) to outweigh the known benefits of higher protein. The body of evidence doesn’t yet support lowering protein recommendations, nor adding an upper limit.

So if protein is good for us, and most of us can’t really get “too much,” why are so many people arguing that we’re overdoing it? I think part of the reason is just misunderstanding (the writers don’t tend to have a background in nutrition and especially not in sports nutrition), but more often, I think they’re talking about a different issue entirely.

Often the “too much protein” stuff is just a way of talking about the environmental effects of meat consumption or dairy farming. People making this argument are trying to pry the double cheeseburgers out of our hands and reassure us that we’ll be okay. I don’t think an attack on protein is an appropriate way to make that point, since plant-based proteins exist and are a fine alternative. But I understand where they’re coming from.

Ultimately, if you’re trying to make the argument that we’re eating “too much” protein for our health, you really can’t do that without some evidence that we’re eating so much protein that it’s harming our health on a widespread level. And that evidence just doesn’t exist.

#3493. The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Review: Haymitch's Prequel Delivers

Suzanne Collins, the woman behind the young adult dystopian phenomenon known as the Hunger Games franchise, seems like she's pretty calculated with her prequels. I mean this as a good thing. Instead of pumping out endless content and prequels that don't really serve the original narrative (ahem, the apparently permanently unfinished Fantastic Beasts franchise), Collins sticks to stories that help us understand key characters and stories from the first three novels ("The Hunger Games" and its sequels "Catching Fire" and "Mockingjay").

This was true of the 2023 big-screen prequel "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," which casts Tom Blyth as future Panem president Coriolanus Snow and explains how and why he grew into the villain faced by Jennifer Lawrence's Katniss in the original films (where he's played by Donald Sutherland). This is, thankfully, also true of the Haymitch Abernathy prequel "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," based on the 2025 novel "Sunrise on the Reaping."

Haymitch — a role originated by Woody Harrelson and played spectacularly by "We Were Liars" and "East of Eden" alum Joseph Zada in this new film — is sixteen during the Second Quarter Quell, a sort of demented "special edition" of the titular Games that take place every 25 years. For the 50th Games, the all-powerful Capitol in charge of Panem reaps double the number of tributes from each of the totalitarian nation's 12 districts, meaning that 48 kids will enter the arena and only one will survive. Frankly, this premise is immediately intriguing, but director Francis Lawrence and screenwriters Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie ensure that, beyond the shock value, this story remains human, emotional, and gripping from beginning to end. Much of that is also thanks to Zada, who delivers an unforgettable performance.

Playing an established franchise character — especially one originated by an incredibly famous and acclaimed actor — must be a tough undertaking, and I'll get back to the highlights and lowlights of that exact situation before long. First, though, I want to soundly and unrestrainedly praise Joseph Zada, an actor with a massive responsibility in this film. Without a good Haymitch, "Sunrise on the Reaping" fails.

Thankfully, Zada is more than up to the task, and the movie's extremely speedy — but not overly so — pacing means that he has to go through a massive emotional journey in a relatively short amount of time. Zada sells every second as Haymitch, whether he's promising his District 12 girlfriend Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak) that he'll see her after the reaping to breaking down crying just before he enters an arena filled with, presumably, 47 kids who hope to kill him.

Zada is great, but much like Haymitch, he doesn't do it alone. Because, again, "Sunrise on the Reaping" moves at such a quick clip — to be fair, it packs 400 pages into about 2 hours and 40 minutes — he's the character we bond with the most, and the character Haymitch himself bonds with the most is arguably Maysilee Donner, his fellow District 12 tribute played by Mckenna Grace. Despite being enemies back home, where Maysilee is a sort of petty schoolyard bully, the two become unlikely allies who end up making it to the end of the Games together, and Grace brings a steeliness to her role that eventually falls away to reveal an understandably scared young girl. It certainly helps that Francis Lawrence and his team built an astounding world for his performers.

Joseph Zada and Mckenna Grace, the standouts among the tributes — with respect to Ben Wang, Molly McCann, and Iona Bell, the first of whom plays District 12 tribute Wyatt Callow and the rest of whom play Louella and "Lou Lou" McCoy, they, uh, aren't in the movie as much for reasons you can probably ascertain — deliver exceptional performances, but respect must be paid to Francis Lawrence's overall vision and the stunning world-building that he and his creative team deliver in "Sunrise on the Reaping."

When I spoke to Lawrence about the film and other dystopian teen movies he's directed (or is set to direct), he said, "I think the dystopian aspect of these worlds, a lot of it, for me, is about the world-building." This love of the game is evident, because "Sunrise on the Reaping" looks and feels phenomenal.

If you're familiar with the Hunger Games franchise, you know that we've gotten to see two very different eras of Panem, which come with understandably different technical developments. In "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," everything is relatively primitive; beginning in "The Hunger Games," the tech is much more advanced after several decades. "Sunrise on the Reaping" falling pretty squarely in the middle here is particularly cool because of the small details of the world; one such example that I really appreciated is the tributes being lifted into the arena on small platforms as opposed to the tubes we see Katniss and other tributes enter years later. Without spoilers, the technical logistics of the arena play an outsized role in "Sunrise on the Reaping," and the world feels rich, full, and disturbingly real in the best way.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is chock-a-block full of characters you'll remember from previous installments like "The Hunger Games: Catching Fire" and both parts of "The Hunger Games: Mockingjay," and the results are ... a bit mixed. (It was confirmed, long before the film's release, that Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson would reprise their roles as Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark; how exactly that transpires will remain a secret until you sit down and see the movie.) I'm going to mention the breakneck pacing again here, and it's not a bad thing, but it does mean that a lot of characters are introduced and summarily disappear; this is also true of Billy Porter's larger-than-life Capitol stylist Magno Stift, though his legal wife and nemesis Drusilla Sickle, a plastic surgery nightmare gamely played by a vamping Glenn Close, gets much more play.

I wish we'd seen more of Elle Fanning's take on Effie Trinket, a character originally played by Elizabeth Banks, but she's reliably great in her scenes; Kieran Culkin plays a pre-Stanley Tucci version of Caesar Flickerman and is bombastic, over-the-top, and undeniably sharp and dynamic. Jesse Plemons does great work, as always, stepping into Philip Seymour Hoffman's shoes as the taciturn turncoat Plutarch Heavensbee, echoing Hoffman's performance while making it his own.

The best and worst performers behind recurring characters, though, are Ralph Fiennes and Kelvin Harrison Jr. Fiennes manages to bridge the gap between Tom Blyth and Donald Sutherland as Panem's president Coriolanus Snow, but Harrison Jr. is, I am sorry to say, doing a sort of "Saturday Night Live" impression of his predecessor Jeffrey Wright. I appreciate the ask here is big, but sadly, not every actor rises fully to the challenge.

If I have one big "nit to pick" in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," it's a problem that affects a lot of adaptations: it over-explains a lot. Because the book is told from Haymitch's point of view, we learn a lot as he infers and gleans; the movie has to painstakingly say all of that. Still, it's a minor quibble.

Before the release of "Sunrise on the Reaping," I saw and heard chatter, anecdotally, that this movie would surpass "The Hunger Games: Catching Fire" in sheer quality. Respectfully, I have to disagree. Not only is "Catching Fire" the best Hunger Games movie by a long shot and just a really great and well-made movie in its own right — Francis Lawrence, thank you again for that incredible aspect ratio change as we enter the arena, and thanks to your cinematographer Jo Willems as well — but "Catching Fire" doesn't have to explain its narrative as intensely as "Sunrise on the Reaping" does. Still, this is simply a quirk of adaptation, and "Catching Fire" being able to narratively coast off of its predecessor is an unfair advantage.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" might not beat "Catching Fire," but it is a truly excellent addition to the Hunger Games film franchise — and it's one of the most thrilling action movies of the year. As this universe continues to expand (that is, if Suzanne Collins decides to write future books), if we keep Lawrence at the helm and keep casting top-notch actors, Hunger Games fans will remain in excellent hands.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" opens in theaters on November 20, 2026.

The Marvel Cinematic Universe is constantly putting out new projects and most hotly anticipated upcoming Marvel movie is definitely Avengers: Doomsday. Fans who spent years watching the Marvel movies in order are hyped to see this crossover event, which will feature Robert Downey Jr.'s return to the MCU. Kevin Feige recently spoke about his original plans for Kang and Doctor Doom, and fans are not exactly buying his comments.

What we know about Avengers: Doomsday is limited, but from the outside it seems like the title character was brought in after Jonathan Majors was fired as Kang by the studio. Although in the Doomsday edition of Empire Magazine (via Twitter) Feige painted another picture, saying:

It probably would still have been called ‘The Kang Dynasty’, but it would have been a set-up for Doom, midway through that movie.

Well, my mind is blown. For years it seemed like the MCU was setting up Kang to be the shared universe's next big bad, thanks to his roles in Loki and Ant-Man and The Wasp: Quantumania (both of which are streaming with a Disney+ subscription). Although according to Feige, the next Avengers movie was always going to pivot the focus over to RDJ's Doctor Doom. That definitely would have been a plot twist, but the Marvel fandom doesn't necessarily think that Feige is telling the truth.

The Kang actor was notably fired after Jonathan Majors was found guilty on third-degree assault and harassment in the trial against his ex. Fans assumed this is why the character was written off, with Doctor Doom instead brought in as the antagonist of the next Avengers movie, formerly titled The Kang Dynasty. Kevin Feige's comment paint a very different picture, but fans aren't necessarily buying what he's selling. Some Twitter responses to the above comment include:

Well, that was honest. Marvel fans are known for being passionate about the shared universe, and they didn't hold back their thoughts about Kevin Feige's Kang comments. Folks online seem to think that the's not telling the truth about the original plans for the next Avengers movie. We'll just have to see what they think when Doomsday arrives in theaters next month.

All will be revealed when Avengers: Doomsday its release on December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list. No one is expecting Kang to show up, but we'll have to see if he gets referenced at all throughout the movie's mysterious runtime.

#3491. Five Race-Day Smartwatch Hacks Every Marathon Runner Should Know

I love my Garmin Forerunner 970, but the fact is, most runners don't need all the features it has to offer. In fact, for most road races, you can get by with whatever smartwatch you already own—as long as you know how to use it. If you've got a marathon or half-marathon coming up, these five tricks will only take a few minutes to set up, and they can save you from one of many of the small-but-avoidable disasters that can derail a good race.

Nothing spikes pre-race anxiety like standing in a corral of hundreds of people watching your watch fail to latch onto a signal. Tall buildings, crowded starts, and a sea of other devices make the first minute of GPS unreliable, which can leave your opening mileage pace wildly off.

The fix is simple: start the GPS search early. Step outside, into the open, as soon as you've dropped your bag, and select your run activity at least 10 to 15 minutes before the starting gun. If your watch supports multi-band or dual-frequency GPS, turn it on in the activity settings, since it's noticeably better in dense downtown starts. Then, don't press start until the gun goes off (or you cross the line, if you want chip-accurate pacing).

Bonus tip: If you're in a start corral with a long wait, you can lock the signal and then pause the activity screen. Just remember to hit start when you actually take off.

Multiple data screens are great for training, but overwhelming during a race. Too many numbers invite overthinking, and seeing the "wrong" number at mile two can lead you into a very stressful mile ten.

My recommendation is to build a dedicated race screen with three to four fields at most:

Lap pace or average lap pace (not instant pace, which jumps around constantly with GPS)

Distance or lap distance, so you know where you are relative to the mile markers

Heart rate, especially in the early miles when adrenaline tempts you to go out too fast

Elapsed time, for splits against your goal

Keep it clean and stripped down, and avoid the temptation to add cadence, power, vertical oscillation, and everything else. You can always review those stats during your cool-down.

A text from your boss at mile 14 is nobody's idea of a good time. Before race day, switch your watch to Do Not Disturb or Airplane mode, or turn on a dedicated activity mode that blocks notifications. This also saves battery, which matters if your marathon is going to take you four-plus hours.

After blocking the outside world, you can set race-specific alerts, like a high heart-rate alert to keep you honest in the first half. I also know runners who set a recurring time or distance alert for fueling—say, every 30 to 40 minutes, or every 5 miles—so remembering to down a gel or a sports drink doesn't depend on your fading brain.

Here's one thing I learn the hard way, every time: Your watch will almost always say you've run farther than the race course says you have. Race courses are measured along the shortest possible route, but along the way, you'll weave around people, take wide turns, and generally add extra distance. I've run marathons where my watch reads closer to 26.6 miles (nearly an extra half mile), so my "on pace" watch is actually behind my chip time.

The hack: Ignore the watch's auto-lap and press the lap button manually at each mile marker (or at every kilometer marker, if that's what the course uses). This gives you pace data aligned to the official course, not the satellite's best guess. It also gives you a quick mental check against your plan. If you've set up your watch for it, display average lap pace, then glance at it a few hundred meters after each marker to see how you're tracking. And don't panic if your watch beeps for a mile before you pass the marker—trust the course and your lap presses, and do your best to ignore the mismatched distance adding up.

Rain, sweat, high-fives, and a hasty cup grab at an aid station can all trigger accidental taps on a touchscreen watch. Few things are worse than discovering at mile 18 that you accidentally paused, ended, or switched screens on your activity. So before the race, turn on your watch's screen lock, so a stray touch doesn't do anything.

If your watch has a configurable wake gesture, consider turning it off to save battery, and set the backlight to a short timeout. While we're talking watch-wearing protocol, remember to wear it snugly, one finger-width above your wrist bone, for a better heart-rate reading as you sweat. Finally, if your watch has one, use the post-race auto-save reminder. (Otherwise, do your best to hit stop after you cross the finish line.)

Again, you don't need the most premium running-specific watch ahead of race day. If you have time, test these hacks on a long run, so that you're not wasting any precious mental energy during the big day.

#3489. Marvel Boss Officially Reveals Why Avengers Switched from Kang to Doctor Doom

Avengers: Doomsday is a month away and will find the Avengers, the New Avengers, and X-Men from the Fox films facing off against Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom. Originally, the fifth Avengers film was titled The Kang Dynasty and would have starred Jonathan Majors as Kang, who appeared in Loki and Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania. Marvel fired him in December 2023 after he was convicted on assault and harassment charges, and retooled The Kang Dynasty into the Doctor Doom-centric Doomsday.

However, according to Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige, the Marvel Cinematic Universe always would have pivoted to Doom replacing Kang as the next Avengers-level threat, regardless of Majors' legal issues and firing.

Speaking with Empire Magazine, Feige revealed the plan to pivot away from Kang began around the release of the third Ant-Man film in early 2023. "Quantumania was not received the way we would have liked," Feige said (via IGN). "There are many elements of that that we're proud of, the Kang performance being one of them. But we were changing [The Kang Dynasty] even at that point. It would still have been called The Kang Dynasty, but it would have been a set-up for Doom, midway through that movie."

Majors' Kang the Conqueror variant was the villain of Quantumania after Kang first appeared as He Who Remains in Loki season 1. Much like how Josh Brolin's Thanos appeared throughout the MCU before going toe-to-toe with the Avengers in Avengers: Infinity War and Endgame, Kang was being established as an overarching antagonist before The Kang Dynasty. In contrast to them, Doom has been haphazardly established in the MCU via post-credits scenes in 2025's The Fantastic Four: First Steps and the recent re-release of Endgame. Setting up Doom in a film titled The Kang Dynasty would have been a bold move.

From the public's point of view, it certainly seemed like Marvel retooled the Avengers films in response to Majors' convictions. However, according to Feige, that wasn't exactly the case. "We didn't want to rush into any rash decisions in terms of employment. People think there was a cause-and-effect with Jonathan's issues, and that certainly accelerated some things. But the Doom of it all was well underway before that."

Marvel is known for deception and trickery, so you're well within your rights to doubt Feige's comments here. However, as next year's Avengers: Secret Wars hasn't had a title change, it makes sense that the plan all along was for Doctor Doom to supersede Kang as the main villain. After all, Secret Wars shares its name with Jonathan Hickman and Esad Ribić's 2010s comic series of the same name. That event featured Doom as God Emperor reigning over a realm patched together from fragments of various Marvel universes and continuities. As Doomsday is all about universes colliding and resulting in Incursions, it seems very likely 2027's Secret Wars film will adapt the comic of the same name.

You won't have to wait long to see Doom, the Avengers, and more on the big screen. Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters on Dec. 18.

#3487. First Reactions To Brad Pitt's Cliff Booth Movie Have Critics United

It's not every day that we get a continuation of one of Quentin Tarantino's most acclaimed movies. Heck, it's not every day we even get a new script at all from the movie-loving auteur. Ever since he debuted "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" in 2019, Tarantino hasn't directed a single feature film — likely a consequence of his self-imposed (and rather silly) rule to limit himself to only directing 10 total movies. But whatever the case may be, he was clearly interested in diving deeper into this alternate-history world with "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," only this time, he handed over the reins of his script to David Fincher.

Could this unlikely collaboration between Fincher and Tarantino, two very different artists, yield fruit? It sure seems like it has, based on early reactions from the film's Los Angeles premiere. It seems like the entire movie industry has been waiting for this moment, despite the unusual nature of this sequel. Set in 1977, eight years after the events of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," the sequel focuses solely on Brad Pitt's past-his-prime stuntman Cliff Booth long after his harrowing encounter with the Manson family. Gone are his free-wheeling days playing backup to Leonardo DiCaprio's Rick Dalton, replaced by the reality of having to find a new way forward in a much different world. As the film's colorful synopsis puts it, "the fairytale is over."

But not for us! "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" held its premiere screening last night, and social media is positively abuzz with hype from those in attendance. For those looking for a handy roundup of all the first reactions, you've come to the right place.

Is it really possible that we have yet another "Best movie of 2026" contender on our hands this late in the year? If anyone could pull that off, well, we suppose it'd be the dream team of David Fincher and Quentin Tarantino. Starring Brad Pitt, Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Carla Gugino, Matt Groove, JB Tadena, the great Peter Weller, and many more, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" has plenty of star power going for it. But dare we even hope that Tarantino managed to make lightning strike twice, revisiting this deeply nostalgic world for a second time and somehow living up to the hype?

That seems to be the main takeaway from the critics, journalists, and other lucky fans at the Los Angeles premiere. We'll start with Variety awards pundit Clayton Davis, who described the picture as "a wild, hilarious hangout movie" featuring Pitt's "best performance" since his last time in the role as Cliff Booth. He added, "The cinematography is gorgeous. If the 2019 film was a love letter to L.A., this one is a full-on sonnet [..] Fincher and Tarantino haven't been this much fun in years."

As if that wasn't high praise enough, critic Courtney Howard echoed those sentiments and called the sequel "a pure riot. David Fincher's play at a nostalgic bygone era Quentin Tarantino loves works like gangbusters. Takes time to form, but plays like a LA film noir hangout picture." Meanwhile, Germain Lussier of io9 came out swinging and proclaimed this "my favorite movie of the year and it's not even close. Hilarious, exciting, romantic, you'll never guess what happens next and probably not believe it then anyway. Couldn't love it more if I tried."

Of course, as with any significant Hollywood premiere, some of the more interesting reactions are the ones that go against the grain. While most responses are united in singing the praises of "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," a select handful note that they may need some time with this movie to fully soak it in. In a world of extremes, reactions that run towards the middle ground are certainly refreshing, at least.

Longtime critic and entertainment journalist Todd Gilchrist suggested that he was still undecided on whether David Fincher and Quentin Tarantino's unique sensibilities are fully a match made in heaven. "I quite liked 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,' but as with all Tarantino projects, I need to see it (at least) twice to properly digest it. I'm not yet convinced QT's shambling, novelistic approach and Fincher's precision are exactly compatible." Erik Anderson of Awards Watch went even further, highlighting that, "Despite some fun and energetic sequences, I found 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth' to be tonally a bit messy [...] It seemed to want a 70s noir style but should have leaned in more."

As always, each viewer's mileage may vary. Luckily, fans won't have to wait much longer. "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" will receive an exclusive two-week window in IMAX theaters starting on November 25, 2026. It will then come to Netflix on December 23, 2026.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

Once a cleaning run wraps up, most of the upkeep happens at the dock, which washes and dries the mop pads and empties dust into a bag rated for up to 65 days. That said, its onboard water tank is relatively small at 2.3 fluid ounces, potentially requiring extra trips to the dock during larger mopping jobs. There's also no dedicated cleaning solution tank, meaning you'll have to add approved cleaning additives manually to the fresh water. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.

#3484. 5 Actresses Who Would Be Perfect James Bond Girls Opposite Robert Pattinson

Who should play the next Bond Girl? We have a few ideas.

It's finally been confirmed that Robert Pattinson will be playing James Bond in the next canonical feature film about Ian Fleming's stalwart British spy. Back in February 2025, Amazon gained creative control of the character, and while we expressed some consternation over the deal, that didn't stop film fans everywhere from speculating what a James Bond movie might look like in the 2020s. Fast-forward to 2026, and there were several finalists for the role of the new Bond himself, among them Nicholas Hoult, Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O'Connor, and the ultimate winner, i.e. Pattinson.

Now, of course, we can play further speculation games. With 007 in place, fans will now have a marvelous time pondering who might be playing other notable James Bond supporting figures like Ms. Moneypenny, M, Q, Blofeld, Felix Leiter, etc.

And, as is a long (and perhaps sexist) tradition in James Bond lore, he must always be paired with a "Bond Girl" or two in every movie. Bond will inevitably meet and seduce an attractive woman, and the woman will typically prove to be an invaluable ally, a secret enemy, or a doomed innocent who is killed to move the action forward. Some models and actors have even elevated their "Bond Girl" roles into fascinating new characters.

I'd have loved to see O'Connor play a gender-flipped version of a Bond Girl, as we haven't yet had any "Bond Boys," and their time has definitely come. Pattinson could easily seduce men and women equally, and depicting O'Connor in bed with Pattinson would be a fantastic "second place" prize for the actor.

Who should play a Bond Girl opposite Pattinson? We think the following performers would do well.

Florence Pugh may be the most obvious choice for the next James Bond movie. Pugh already has spy-movie-adjacent experience playing Black Widow Yelena in several films and TV shows in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, including 2026's ultra-hit "Spider-Man: Brand New Day," so she could likely slip into the role of a slinky espionage expert with ease. Indeed, she kind of played a Bond Girl-like role in "Brand New Day," anyway, appearing nude in a hot tub as Yelena and offering some vital exposition to the movie's hero. But it doesn't take too much imagination to envision Pugh slithering through a casino or fancy-dress ball, wearing an expensive, Met Gala-worthy gown, snarling at Bond and talking to him with power and confidence.

Pugh is a forceful and talented actor, and it seems to me that she would be able to bite into a Bond Girl role with enthusiasm. Robert Pattinson is also quite versatile and, in the right roles, intense and zany. I suspect that Pugh would be able to match Pattinson's hidden livewire energy, allowing the two to crackle. Additionally, Pugh has previously worked with Denis Villeneuve, the director of the next Bond flick, having played Princess Irulan in Villeneuve's "Dune: Part Two" and the upcoming "Dune: Part Three."

So, the question now arises: would Pugh's Bond Girl be a helpful ally, a doomed innocent, or a secret enemy? Every instinct in my body dictates that she'd end up being the third type, holding a gun on 007 while they both wear nothing but a bedsheet.

Katy O'Brian's breakout role was playing the itinerant queer bodybuilder Jackie in Rose Glass' amazing 2024 crime flick "Love Lies Bleeding," which I thought was one of the best movies of its year. What's more, it's clear from her performance in that film that O'Brian is destined to be a star. She possesses a forceful energy and a lot of screen presence, able to balance the intensity from her co-star, Kristen Stewart.

Some might also recognize O'Brian for her supporting role as Jentorra in 2023's overpriced Marvel actioner "Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania." The actor has since appeared in the blockbuster films "Twisters" and "Mission: Impossible — The Final Reckoning" and had a supporting role on the "Star Wars" TV series "The Mandalorian," so she's clearly comfortable with giant productions and would not feel out-of-place in a James Bond movie.

O'Brian has experience in a wide variety of other films, too, having played the lead in the drag queen-themed 2025 zombie movie "Queens of the Dead" and appeared in the biopic "Christy" opposite Sydney Sweeney. Most recently, she appeared in Edgar Wright's "The Running Man" adaptation.

I can picture a scene wherein 007 travels to a bar somewhere and trades barbs with O'Brian, whose biceps are bigger than his. They can then admire the other women in the joint together, sharing a drink and a seeming flirtation, along with some secret information. Then, once something goes wrong and bad guys begin extracting weapons, Pattinson and O'Brian could stand back-to-back and kick a little butt. She has a black belt in hapkido, after all.

Danai Gurira's first major screen credit came in 2004 when she appeared in an episode of "Law & Order: Criminal Intent." From there, she continued to plug away at her career, appearing in episodes of shows like "Life on Mars," "Lie to Me," and "Treme." However, her real big break came when she began appearing on the hit zombie series "The Walking Dead" as Michonne, a character who's become so recognizable that her likeness has shown up in non-"Walking Dead" video games like 2026's "World War Z."

Her career only continued to swing upward when she co-starred in the 2018 MCU blockbuster "Black Panther" as Okoye, the leader of the Wakandan royal guard. And none of this even scrapes her amazing theater career, with Gurira having authored several plays and scored a Pulitzer nomination for her play "In the Continuum."

When James Bond steps into a room, he usually fills it with his charisma and poise. The women he meets, then, should be able to match one of those qualities, and Gurira could do that in abundance. And here's the thing: She's capable of playing either a poised spy contact in a gown or a rough-and-tumble underground figure with equal skill. No doubt, she could swish across a ballroom, dancing with 007 as Strauss plays on the soundtrack, or she could welcome 007 into a dingy basement to flirt while she smokes a cigarette, only to start swinging her baseball bat at the rival spies who would inevitably infiltrate the area.

Most folks wouldn't recognize Arden Cho's face, but they would definitely recognize her voice, as she played the lead character Rumi in Netflix's super-hit animated film "KPop Demon Hunters." But even if that movie somehow passed you by, Cho has been racking up screen credits for decades, appearing in TV shows like "CSI: NY" and in low-rent movies like "Mega Python vs. Gatoroid." Her most prominent live-action TV roles include her turns as Kira on the "Teen Wolf" series, Emily on "Chicago Med," and Ingrid in "Partner Track."

Cho is also a pop star in her own right, having released her first single back in 2011, a song titled "I'm Just a Girl." (A quick note: Despite the actor being a fantastic singer, Rumi's singing voice in "KPop Demon Hunters" was provided by singer EJAE.) Cho is a professional model as well, having worked on campaigns for Nike and Apple, so she would be wholly comfortable in dazzling gowns and sporting high-end makeup. Her profile is certainly rising thanks to the popularity of "KPop Demon Hunters," and she is slated to appear in the upcoming K-Pop-themed feature film "Perfect Girl."

It's hard to say what kind of chemistry Cho would have with Robert Pattinson, although she certainly seems more down-to-earth and relatable. Pattinson, meanwhile, comes across as relatively aloof. As such, one can envision Cho playing a smoky, clever figure who's able to crack wise with 007 without him being quick enough to notice.

Hunter Schafer's filmography isn't terribly large, but her profile in popular culture is enormous. She rose to fame playing the role of Jules in the HBO series "Euphoria," and her movies and TV shows since have all been either fascinating art pictures or high-profile franchise entertainments. Case in point: Schafer appeared as Tigris in "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" in 2023 and played the lead role in the zany Dan Stevens horror film "Cuckoo" in 2024. That same year, she also had a small role in Yorgos Lanthimos' "Kinds of Kindness," which is maybe the most Yorgos Lanthimos movie that ever Lanthimosed. Then, in 2026, she briefly appeared in David Lowery's sapphic pop diva drama "Mother Mary" and will soon appear in the sci-fi series "Blade Runner 2099."

Schafer is dazzling on screen, bringing both sophistication and naivete to her roles, often simultaneously. She looks like an elven princess, and it's almost a pity she was not cast as Princess Zelda in the upcoming "The Legend of Zelda" movie (with the role instead going to Bo Bragason).

I don't know if Schafer has any fight or stunt training, but one can easily imagine her in a lovely dress dancing with, and kissing, James Bond. No doubt, she could serve as a gentle counterpoint to a relatively gruff Bond, and she would only be the second trans actor to appear in a James Bond movie after Caroline Cossey in "For Your Eyes Only." Schafer, however, could — and should — play a much larger role. I can see her kicking glutes and smirking while doing it.

The 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 ahead of Amazon’s Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date. As for the TV itself, it’s a 2026 model that sits below the U7SG (also on sale for $1,297.99, from $1,999.99) in Hisense's lineup as the brand's entry point into Mini LED, pairing a 4K panel and local dimming with a matte, anti-reflective coating meant to cut down on glare, notes this PCMag review.

For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night. It also does a good job cleaning up lower-quality content, which is useful for older cable broadcasts or compressed YouTube videos—and its Fire TV interface makes it easy to jump between those kinds of content and the major streaming services without needing a separate streaming device.

The U6 Pro also brings plenty to the table for gaming, with HDMI 2.1, VRR, ALLM, and a 144Hz refresh rate that PC gamers can push to 240Hz at a lower 1080p resolution. That said, the panel’s slow response time and poor motion performance can reportedly make fast-moving scenes look noticeably blurry. #3482. Robert Pattinson Wasn't The First Choice For James Bond — But The Original Favorite Dropped Out

Not to give Amazon any free ideas, but the behind-the-scenes drama swirling around the biggest casting call of the year sounds like it could've been a reality TV series in its own right. The fateful search for who would don their most finely-tailored suit and their trusty Walther PPK came to an abrupt end this week, as Robert Pattinson was officially announced as our newest James Bond. But amid all the hoopla and hype, details have already begun trickling in concerning how this high-stakes round of musical chairs came to a close.

As it turns out, Pattinson may have won the highly-coveted role ... but he wasn't the first choice. To be fair, that seems evident enough from the fact that neither his name nor Nicholas Hoult's appeared in most reports identifying the finalists until late in this lengthy process. The intrigue goes much deeper than that, however.

There's a lot more that goes into casting decisions for James Bond than simply who looks best in a suit. The role is notorious for singlehandedly changing the lives of each and every performer practically overnight, especially in light of the usual Bond tradition of picking (relative) unknowns for the title role. There's life before Bond and life after Bond — and not everybody is cut out for all the fame and pressure and (occasionally) backlash that inevitably come with it.

It'll always be to Josh O'Connor's enduring credit that, according to this Puck report, he recognized these factors ahead of time and decided that it simply wasn't worth it for him. For the rest of us mere mortals, it may be tempting to look at nothing but the popularity and wealth and prestige associated with playing England's most defining fictional spy. If so, well, look no further than the toll this clearly took on our previous Bond. Not only did Daniel Craig have to overcome some seriously nasty comments about his physical appearance in the early going, but certain provocative comments late in his run also revealed the arduous nature of these big-budget productions and the many, many off-screen responsibilities associated with it.

Still, as excited as we are to see Robert Pattinson as Bond (and as someone who survived the "Twilight" phenomenon, he may be uniquely prepared for this in a way nobody else ever has), we'll always wonder what O'Connor could've done with the part. Villeneuve obviously saw that potential himself, and the "Dune" filmmaker is certainly no slouch when it comes to casting. Whatever comes next, we'll be seated for O'Connor's next big performance.

#3481. The 8 Greatest Harrison Ford Thrillers, Ranked

Harrison Ford is one of the greatest actors living today, with a career spanning more than five decades and a filmography filled with some of Hollywood's biggest movies. From playing iconic characters like Han Solo and Indiana Jones to smaller, supporting roles, Ford is always a reliable presence in every movie he's in. A significant part of his filmography is also made up of thriller films, which he also excels in.

Here, we take a look at Ford's best thriller films. The Oscar nominee has starred in a wide variety of thrillers, ranging from gripping political dramas to psychological mysteries. No matter the film, he has a remarkable ability to keep audiences invested in every twist and turn. Some of these films have become classics of the genre, while others are considerably underrated. Regardless, they all show why Ford remains one of Hollywood's most dependable actors.

In What Lies Beneath, Claire (Michelle Pfeiffer) begins experiencing increasingly disturbing occurrences in her lakeside home after her daughter leaves for college. Her husband, Dr. Norman Spencer (Harrison Ford), dismisses her concerns as stress, but as Claire becomes more determined to investigate the presence, she begins uncovering secrets about her husband and their seemingly perfect marriage.

Robert Zemeckis famously made this movie as the production of Cast Away was paused. It's an intense, suspenseful thriller anchored by strong performances from its stars. Pfeiffer carries much of the film through her portrayal of someone struggling to distinguish reality from paranoia. For his part, Ford plays against type, swapping his hero persona for someone who seems dependable at first but becomes suspicious. Zemeckis takes advantage of the secluded location, while also delivering inspired shots. With its twists and genuinely creepy sequences, What Lies Beneath is a thoroughly engaging horror thriller that many have forgotten.

Patriot Games follows CIA analyst Jack Ryan (Harrison Ford), who finds himself caught in the middle of an assassination attack carried out by members of the Irish Republican Army. Jack manages to save the target but kills one of the attackers in the process. Now, Sean Miller (Sean Bean) is determined to avenge the death of his brother and starts to threaten Jack and his family.

Taking over the role from Alec Baldwin, Ford was actually not what author Tom Clancy had in mind. Clancy also had initial issues with the script, but all of his concerns were dismissed after he saw an initial cut of the film. While Ford was older than the Jack Ryan in the books, he was an effective actor to play the analyst. Ford brings a wonderful combination of determination and physical toughness to the character, while also showing the softer and more vulnerable side as a father and husband. The film does a fantastic job maintaining the tension, balancing international political intrigue with a much more intimate, character-driven story.

In Clear and Present Danger, Jack Ryan (Ford) is appointed acting deputy director of intelligence after a close friend of the President is murdered by a Colombian drug cartel. However, as he investigates the case, Jack finds out that America has been conducting an illegal mission that manipulates national security and puts innocent lives in danger.

After the solid reception for Patriot Games, Ford and director Phillip Noyce teamed up once again for another adaptation. Clear and Present Danger is an excellent political thriller that shows Jack Ryan's expertise very well. Ford expands the character with more nuance, showing clearly his moral convictions in the face of danger. It's often lauded as one of the best Jack Ryan films because it understands that the character is not a conventional action hero, something the current adaptations misunderstand. On top of the action and gripping political storyline, the film also features Willem Dafoe as Ryan's ally John Clark in a highlight sequence. It is one of the best thrillers of the 1990s.

Witness follows Detective John Book (Ford), who is assigned to protect a young Amish boy, Samuel (Lukas Haas) and her mother, Rachel (Kelly McGillis), after Samuel witnesses the murder of a police officer. Book also becomes a target after he finds out that the murder is connected to members of his department. Wounded, he seeks refuge in the Amish community and has to adapt to an unfamiliar way of life.

Directed by acclaimed director Peter Weir, the film leans more toward drama than thriller, but it's still brilliant overall. The crime story is combined with an intimate and respectful exploration of this unique community. Together with McGillis of Top Gun fame, Ford has an electric chemistry that anchors the film. Witness also excels in its quieter moments, including the famous barn-raising sequence, which reinforces the themes of culture and belonging. The film also holds the distinction of being the only Harrison Ford role that was nominated for an Oscar. It is a beautifully crafted slow thriller that demands your attention and emotion, something that Hollywood rarely makes today.

Presumed Innocent follows Rusty Sabich (Ford), a prosecutor whose professional and personal life falls apart when his colleague and former lover, Carolyn (Greta Scacchi), is brutally murdered. Despite his involvement in the investigation, Rusty soon becomes the prime suspect as evidence points to him. His situation becomes even more complicated when his professional rival takes charge of the prosecution and faces off against him.

This courtroom drama is an exceptional thriller with a central mystery that does not let up until its final moments. Alan J. Pakula, famous for his Paranoia trilogy, excels at making distrust drive the tension. Ford is particularly brilliant as Rusty, with a restrained performance that allows the audience to constantly question his character's motivations and reliability. It has an underrated, solid supporting cast that includes Bonnie Bedelia and Brian Dennehy. The film was followed by a miniseries spin-off, a TV sequel starring Bill Pullman, and a miniseries remake starring Jake Gyllenhaal, which proves that the original story is timeless.

Set in a dystopian Los Angeles, Blade Runner follows Blade Runner officer Rick Deckard (Ford), whose job is to track down and eliminate replicants. When a group of advanced replicants led by Roy Batty (Rutger Hauer) escapes from an off-world colony and returns to Earth, Deckard is assigned to hunt them down. Along the way, Deckard meets Rachael (Sean Young), a replicant who believes she is human, and begins developing feelings for her.

Blade Runner is one of the most influential science fiction films ever made, and it also happens to be a brilliant thriller. Ridley Scott combines the atmosphere of classic film noir with a fascinating sci-fi story. In one of his most iconic roles, Ford is perfect as the weary and cynical Deckard, joined by an unforgettable Rutger Hauer as Roy Batty, whose final confrontation with Deckard is one of the most emotionally powerful moments in cinema. The film maintains its sense of mystery throughout, rewarding patient audiences with its revelations and deeper themes. With its moody cinematography, extraordinary production design and a haunting score by Vangelis, Blade Runner has become a universally beloved cult classic.

The titular Air Force One is hijacked by a group of Russian terrorists led by Ivan Korshunov (Gary Oldman). US President James Marshall (Ford) refuses to abandon his passengers and attempts to fight back against the terrorists from within. With his wife, daughter, and some people from his administration held hostage, Marshall must find a way to regain control of the plane while communicating with Vice President Kathryn Bennett (Glenn Close), who is handling the crisis from the White House.

Air Force One is one of the more outrageous versions of Die Hard. Instead of centering the film on an everyman like John McClane, the film focuses on arguably the most powerful person in the world who is rendered powerless in his own turf. Wolfgang Petersen, who's no stranger to films taking place in a confined setting, having directed Das Boot, delivers a tightly paced thriller that's also action-packed. Ford is the perfect actor to play this unconventional hero, and Oldman is entertaining and intimidating as Korshunov. It can be ridiculous at times, but that's exactly what makes this film a runaway success and a classic.

In The Fugitive, Dr. Richard Kimble (Ford) returns home to discover his wife has been murdered and he quickly becomes the prime suspect. Despite insisting that a one-armed man committed the crime, Kimble is convicted and sentenced to death. However, he manages to escape and goes on the run to prove his innocence. Hot on his trail is Deputy U.S. Marshal Samuel Gerard (Tommy Lee Jones), who will not let him get away easily.

Based on a TV series from 1967, The Fugitive is often considered one of the best-crafted thrillers ever. It is thoroughly entertaining to see Ford and Jones in an intense game of cat and mouse. The former showcases the best of his talents as Richard Kimble, an everyman who is smart and determined, making him relatable to the audience. Andrew Davis directed a film that's action-packed, with great and meticulous production, set in Chicago, utilizing real locations and real events, like the parade where Gerard chases Kimble. From its spectacular train crash sequence to its gripping finale, The Fugitive is one of those thrillers that are just perfect from beginning to end.

#3480. Apple Sports adds UFC events with real-time stats and results

Apple continues to expand the appeal of its free Sports app, which focuses on delivering real-time sports scores and stats, across many different sports.

Today, Apple is adding UFC into the mix, so MMA fans can track the fights live through the unified Apple Sports experience.

Apple Sports will provide coverage of every bout across the full fight card, with live stats like total strike counts, takedowns, knockdowns and more.

Apple Sports features animated background artwork to differentiate different games and matches in the detail view, and UFC is no different with a custom backdrop that evokes the ambience of being under the lights of the Octagon. The details card also includes new visualization to illustrate the number of recorded strikes by target.

You can keep up with the action inside the app, or tap the clock icon to start a Live Activity and get score updates delivered directly to your iPhone’s lock screen.

Apple Sports now comes preinstalled when setting up a new iPhone from scratch. If you don’t already have it, you can get it as a free download from the App Store.

The Sports app is still only available on iPhone right now though; Apple has still not announced plans to do an iPad and Mac native version. You can have the Sports Live Activities from your iPhone show up on Apple Watch and Mac, however.

#3479. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.
