#3478. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

#3477. Google announces Gemini 4 Hydrogen with ‘significant leaps’ in speed, intelligence

After this week’s Carbon availability, Google today unveiled Gemini 4 Hydrogen instead of keeping the “Flash” branding. This model is billed as bringing “cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.”

Compared to Gemini 3.8 Flash (which launched in September), Hydrogen is billed as a “major standalone upgrade” with “significant leaps in both speed and intelligence.” It offers native 1 million-token input and up to 1 million output tokens. Specifically:

“Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class.”

In the Gemini app, Hydrogen is better at following and sticking to your tone, format, and rules, while offering clear tables and visual breakdowns. As such, “email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try.” Additionally, Hydrogen “more frequently calls the right tools (i.e., Connected Apps) and skills for the job.”

In the model picker, 4 Hydrogen is billed as providing “Everyday help.”

Free users in the Gemini app get access to Hydrogen via the “[Auto] model selection when it’s the appropriate model for the prompt.”

Google says Hydrogen significantly upgrades Search (AI Mode) by better understanding your intent:

…you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.

Responses get more visual and will feature a wider range of relevant links. Hydrogen is the default model for AI Mode and is used for “your hardest questions” in AI Overviews.

This was a nice surprise when I opened the app an hour or two ago. It seems to be noticeably better, too.

In Google Antigravity, 4 Hydrogen has an “Extra” thinking tier alongside Low, Medium, and High. Then there’s Orchestrator: “Carbon that may offload routine steps to Hydrogen. Same Carbon-level quality, fewer tokens used.”

To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session.

For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.

For developers, Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

#3476. A Classic Justice League Hero Is Officially Replacing Darkseid In Two Months

DC reveals which unexpected character becomes Darkseid's replacement as the Justice League's next biggest villain. Darkseid wasn't originally devised as a Justice League villain, but his immense power and his obsession with destruction has made him one of the biggest threats to the DC Universe and therefore a recurring JLA antagonist. Besides, the ruler of Apokolips is a multiversal constant, present across all the DC multiverse as a permanent apocalypse looming over every reality. Even when Earth’s greatest heroes destroy his physical body, Darkseid still exists somewhere out there.

Several cosmic tyrants rival or even surpass Darkseid in destructive power, but they ultimately pose smaller threats to the DC Universe. Beings like the Anti-Monitor, Perpetua, Nekron, Barbatos, Mandrakk, and the Empty Hand have each come close to unmaking reality itself, while Brainiac and Lex Luthor match or exceed Darkseid’s intellect on Earth. However, most of these villains usually pop up once every decade for a crossover event before vanishing back into dormancy, while earthly geniuses like Luthor lack Darkseid’s divine army of Parademons. Darkseid strikes repeatedly across generations, constantly corrupting worlds, hunting the Anti-Life Equation, and even reshaping entire timelines like the Absolute Universe.

No other character embodies the total eradication of free will like Darkseid does, but some DC figures make remarkable attempts.

Justice League Unlimited #27 presents one of the most dramatic heel turns in JLA history. On the cover, Michael Holt sits triumphantly on a throne shaped like an upside-down Omega symbol while a shrunken Atom perches on his shoulder. Having previously lost his cherished sense of "fair play" to Charon in the underworld and watched the Atom grow increasingly disillusioned with the League’s villain-amnesty policies, Michael Holt finds an unlikely partner who shares his frustration with the status quo. The solicitation for Justice League Unlimited #27 confirms his new antagonistic role, teasing, "ONCE A MAN, NOW A NEW GOD. MR. TERRIFIC ASCENDS!"

ONCE A MAN, NOW A NEW GOD. MR. TERRIFIC ASCENDS! Mr. Terrific was once the third-smartest man on Earth. Now his amplified genius is about to span the cosmos as he prepares to ascend to godhood — and only the Justice League can hold him back!

Back in Justice League Unlimited #22, Mister Terrific absorbs the Justice League’s collective powers and arrives at the conclusion that he alone can fix a broken universe with his new combination of unmatched intellect and the Justice League's complete collection of superpowers, which he acquires when he gets his hands on the Power Bank holding them all within a single object. Feeling superior to the entire Justice League, Mister Terrific has started to understand Darkseid's ideology, and he now has everything he needs to prove himself the villain's equal and overpower all his former teammates.

Mister Terrific possesses one of the sharpest minds in the DC Universe, but once he absorbs the Justice League’s collective powers, pure logic convinces him that authoritarian control is the most efficient way to fix the universe. Without a selfless heart to temper his calculations, Michael Holt’s brilliance turns clinical and ruthless, echoing the exact same hubris that makes Darkseid impossible to bargain with. Batman, one of the only two DC humans brighter than Mister Terrific, tempers his obsessive strategic mind with compassion, which allows him to understand that efficiency without humanity inevitably becomes oppression.

Bruce Wayne isn’t the only Batman in the DC multiverse. Discover 45 versions of the Caped Crusader and which one is the most powerful of all.

Batman has proven this restraint virtually every time he has gained similar upgrades, and he has always used those temporary boosts strictly to save lives before he willingly gives them up. Bruce Wayne has sat upon the omniscient Mobius Chair, wielded a Yellow and Green Power Ring, and has temporarily acquired Kryptonian-like physiology, yet he has never let godhood seduce him into believing he should rule or reshape the world. The belief that "absolute power corrupts absolutely" is ultimately the difference between Batman's legendary heroism and Mister Terrific's tragic transformation into a Darkseid-like supervillain.

What do you think about Mister Terrific's heel turn?

Across decades of DC stories, the team's roster repeatedly changes as its members confront alien warlords, ancient demons, powerful sorcerers, and Darkseid.

#3475. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3474. These Early Black Friday Ring Camera Deals Start at $24.99

If you’re browsing home security options, Ring has one of the best early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar. Right now, you can add an indoor camera and another one at your front door for less than $65. The Ring Indoor Cam 2K is 58% off at $24.99 (originally $59.99), while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is 60% off at $39.99 (originally $99.99)—both at their lowest-ever price.

Both offer features like 2K video and two-way talk, but the indoor cam is the simpler purchase if you mainly want to check on a pet or kids and see what’s happening near an entrance. It plugs into an outlet, so there’s no battery to recharge, and its low-light color video helps preserve detail when lights are off or dimmed. However, since it’s a fixed-view camera, keep in mind that you’ll need to position it carefully.

The Battery Doorbell is the better pick if alerting you to visitors, deliveries, and potential intruders is your priority. It has a 140-degree horizontal and vertical field of view that provides head-to-toe framing, plus up to 6x zoom for better detail. You can install it without wiring, though you’ll need to recharge its built-in battery. It also requires a 2.4GHz wifi network.

The main catch with both devices is the ongoing subscription cost: Live viewing, two-way talk, and basic real-time notifications all work without a subscription, but reviewing saved footage requires a paid plan, starting at $4.99 per month or $49.99 annually for one device; coverage for multiple devices at one location starts at $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually.

At these prices, the Ring Indoor Cam 2K is perfect for occasional live check-ins, while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is better suited to monitoring your front entrance. Buying both makes sense if you already have a Ring plan that covers extra devices.

#3472. Apple TV's Best Sci-Fi Series Officially Confirms Major Season 2 Change

Lade Omotade is a News and Features Author at Collider, covering everything from casting announcements and streaming trends to behind-the-scenes stories and the cultural impact of today's biggest film and TV franchises. Since joining the team in 2024, she has written more than 1,000 news stories, with her work also cited by outlets like AOL and IMDb.

After a phenomenal first season that broke viewership records, Apple TV's best sci-fi series will return for another run, but sadly, not this year. The acclaimed drama premiered on November 7, 2025, with a perfect 100% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes, while setting a new Apple TV record for a drama series premiere. Before Season 1 ended, it had become the platform's most-watched series in history, surpassing both Severance and Ted Lasso. It also received 18 Emmy Award nominations and took home six, including Outstanding Lead Actress and Outstanding Writing for a Drama Series.

Now sitting at 99% on Rotten Tomatoes, Pluribus remains one of Apple TV's standout sci-fi achievements. Set in post-apocalyptic Albuquerque, New Mexico, the nine-episode first season follows the most miserable person on Earth, who must save the world from happiness. Vince Gilligan created the sci-fi masterpiece after finding success with Breaking Bad, its spin-off Better Call Saul, and The X-Files.

Rhea Seehorn leads Pluribus as Carol Sturka, a romantasy author and one of only 13 people in the world immune to the hive-mind virus that kills a large fraction of the human population and infects the rest with artificial happiness. Season 2 will continue the brilliant plot, now closer to our screens as filming is underway; however, no premiere date has been announced. In the meantime, the series has made a major change ahead of its return, promoting an important recurring character, as Deadline reports.

Samba Schutte has officially been promoted to series regular after masterfully portraying Koumba Diabaté in Pluribus Season 1. Mr Diabaté is one of the immune characters, a Mauritanian who chooses to see the bright side of the situation. Rather than go into panic mode and try to save the world like Carol, he embraces a hedonistic, luxurious lifestyle in the penthouse suite at The Westgate Las Vegas Resort & Casino. For his performance, Schutte received a Saturn Award nomination for Best Guest Star in a Television Series.

In addition to Seehorn and Schutte, Pluribus Season 2 will see Karolina Wydra and Carlos-Manuel Vesga reprise their roles as Zosia, Carol's artificially happy chaperone, and Manousos Oviedo, the extremely paranoid Colombian immune, respectively. Further casting details, including new and returning cast members, have not yet been revealed. Sony Pictures Television produces Pluribus for Apple TV, with executive producers Gilligan, Gordon Smith, Alison Tatlock, Diane Mercer, Jeff Frost, Jenn Carroll, and Trina Siopy.

#3471. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

#3470. 'Game Of Thrones Meets Outlander' Fantasy Series Reveals New Title & 2027 Release Date

Game of Thrones fans looking for a new fantasy series with the same political intrigue may have found the perfect replacement, with an exciting new update on the next entry in the saga.

It's been over 15 years since the most recent entry in the A Song of Ice and Fire series, with A Dance with Dragons arriving back in 2011. While George R.R. Martin continues working on the long-awaited The Winds of Winter, there's still no official release date in sight. HBO has kept Westeros alive through its expanding slate of television adaptations, but readers hoping for another sprawling fantasy epic that scratches the same itch have had to look elsewhere.

One such alternative has been a major hit among fantasy readers, and the New York Times #1 best-selling adventure features "the page-turning politics of Game of Thrones [and] the worlds-spanning romance of Outlander," according to the author's official website, with a brand-new release just announced for 2027.

Ilona Andrews' Maggie the Undying series is officially returning in 2027, with the bestselling author revealing some exciting new details about the next installment in the fantasy saga.

On November 10, 2026, Ilona Andrews officially announced that the second book will be titled This Crown Will Not Rule Me, with a confirmed release date of September 21, 2027. The announcement also included a first look at the novel's cover artwork by Helena Elias, alongside a new story synopsis, which you can check out below.

For those unfamiliar, Ilona Andrews is actually the pen name of husband-and-wife writing duo Ilona and Gordon Andrews, who are best known for their bestselling Kate Daniels, Hidden Legacy, and Innkeeper Chronicles fantasy series.

Their latest series, Maggie the Undying, is a planned trilogy that began with This Kingdom Will Not Kill Me in March 2026. It follows Maggie, a devoted fantasy reader who unexpectedly finds herself transported into the world of her favorite unfinished book series.

The newly revealed description for This Crown Will Not Rule Me teases a dangerous new adventure:

The kingdom of Rellas is safe—but for how long? Having averted a fateful attack on the capital, Maggie must now keep its people safe from an even deadlier struggle for the crown. Unfortunately, her allies keep getting in her way: Everard, who is ever the more insistent on making Maggie his duchess; the knight Arvel, who is determined to uncover her secrets; and a mysterious religious sect that continues to pester her for unknown reasons. If that’s not enough, the plot is no longer as Maggie remembers.

Beyond the political intrigue, the sequel introduces a dangerous "monster extermination" known as the Culling, which is arriving a year earlier than expected with "thrice as many nests." With Maggie's knowledge of the original story becoming increasingly unreliable, her apparent immortality may not be enough to save everyone she cares about.

The first book in the series has already proven enormously successful, becoming a New York Times and USA Today bestseller and earning a nomination for Readers' Favorite Fantasy in the 2026 Goodreads Choice Awards. With that kind of momentum behind it, Maggie the Undying is quickly establishing itself as an exciting alternative for fantasy readers looking for their next Game of Thrones fix.

#3468. Why Casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond Is a High-Risk, High-Reward Gamble for Denis Villeneuve

Throughout his 64 years in movies, James Bond, the hard-living superspy, has been the star of the 007 franchise. But by granting Robert Pattinson a license to kill, the producers of the next Bond film are making a bet that one of the most famous men on the planet can slide into a role shaped by the likes of Sean Connery, Daniel Craig, Roger Moore, and Pierce Brosnan without bringing any Edward Cullen-sized baggage.

It’s quite a gamble. After all, Connery, Craig, Timothy Dalton, and poor, delusional George Lazenby were relative unknowns when they were tapped to play the secret agent, and Brosnan and Moore were TV-famous but unproven as film stars. That’s not the case with Pattinson, who has been one of the most recognizable people on the planet for two decades, and who is currently anchoring another massive franchise in “Batman.” So why did director Denis Villeneuve, producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal, and Amazon MGM Studios decide to hand over the keys to the Aston Martin to such a prominent and expensive candidate? Related Stories ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

Well, some of it has to do with Villeneuve’s comfort level. He’s worked with Pattinson on “Dune: Part Three” and knows what the mercurial star can bring to a role. Clearly, he wants to build a darker, brooding Bond. Then, there’s also the need to have insurance. Amazon is launching a new iteration of 007 into a world that looks very different than it did in 2019 when the last chapter, “No Time to Die,” was conceived and shot (it wouldn’t be released until 2021 thanks to COVID). We’ve lived through #MeToo, a pandemic, wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the fraying of the Western World and, with it, the “special relationship” Bond has sworn to protect. From the start, Amazon was interested in picking a higher-profile actor to outfit in one of Bond’s signature tuxedos. Before the search began in earnest last May, executives were high on the idea of Jacob Elordi.

Plus, some of the other finalists, a group that included Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, and Nicholas Hoult, lacked the kind of sex appeal and danger that the part required. Hoult apparently impressed executives with his audition, but came up short, as he did when he was in contention for Batman (losing out to Pattinson) and Superman (getting Lex Luthor as a consolation prize). He remains very well liked in the industry. With a salary estimated at roughly $2.5 million, Hoult would have been a cheaper option than Pattinson, who one industry source speculated would cost north of $10 million to hire.

But the higher price tag may be worth it. This isn’t just the first Bond to be released under Amazon’s ownership — it’s the first to be produced without the Broccoli family at the helm. The keepers of the 007 flame sold their creative control to Amazon in 2025, leaving the series without a guiding force. Both Heyman and Pascal are old hands, having overseen the casting of the Harry Potter and Spider-Man franchises, respectively, but those are still big shoes to fill.

What’s in it for Pattinson? Well, a chance to put his stamp on an iconic role, as well as an opportunity to reunite with Villeneuve, one of the hottest directors in Hollywood. His commercial bona fides have also, arguably, never been higher. Not only has he shown he can anchor a superhero film with “The Batman” and its upcoming sequel, but he’s also opened more idiosyncratic fare, such as the recent A24 hits “The Drama” and “Primetime.” Clearly, he can bring in the younger audiences driving the box office turnaround while retaining a kind of indie cool that could take Bond in a new and exciting direction. Will he be our perviest 007?

Plus, the recent shake-up at DC Studios, with James Gunn and Peter Safran replaced by former Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham, may spell trouble for Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” series. Although it was conceived as a trilogy, the sequel was delayed multiple times as Reeves dealt with personal matters, forcing him to leave production last month, with Steven Soderbergh stepping in to finish shooting. DC may not want to wait as long to make another installment, and there’s a sense that Latcham may want something brighter and more mainstream than Reeves’ moody, hard PG-13 take on The Dark Knight.

But Pattinson better get ready for a lot more scrutiny than the questions that greeted his casting as Bruce Wayne. “With Batman, there’s a mask to hide behind,” said one industry source. “With Bond, your face is front and center.”

Even Craig, widely considered to be the best Bond since Connery, faced fierce blowback when his casting was announced. He was too blonde, too unconventionally handsome. A website, CraigNotBond, sprang up where fans vented their displeasure.

But when “Casino Royale” debuted in 2006, and Craig showed that he was perfectly capable of kicking ass and ordering his martini shaken, not stirred, the haters were quickly silenced. Will Pattinson be able to pull off the same stunt? It’s a high-risk, high-reward gamble. Just the kind of bet James Bond lives to make.

#3465. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers

#3464. The Stop-Motion Tool That’s a Constant in This Crazy, AI-Mixed-Up World

A lot is happening in front of the camera in “Wildwood” — the general Millennial chaos of Portland, Oregon, swarms of baby-napping crows, an army of wolves with cannons and trebuchets — and just as much behind the camera in Laika Studios’ latest stop-motion epic. But for all the innovation and blending of CG and stop-motion required to tell the story of Prue McKeel’s (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) impossible quest into the impassable woods, some key tools have stayed the same for Laika since “Coraline.”

One such tool is Dragonframe, the frame-grabbing software developed by Jamie and Dyami Caliri in 2008, and essential to helping Laika animators craft the naturalistic performances that “Wildwood” director Travis Knight wanted to create. Related Stories Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber Why Casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond Is a High-Risk, High-Reward Gamble for Denis Villeneuve

“Back in the old days, like the Ray Harryhausen days — it was still the same as how we do it: You have a puppet; you have an object; you move it a tiny bit; you take a picture; you move it a little more; you take another picture. But you had no way of knowing exactly what the frame that you just took looked like and how it related to the frame that you’re about to take,” Knight explained on an episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast. “You had these gauges where you could try to approximate the distance something moved, but it was this act of faith. You didn’t really know; you had to wait until you developed the film to see how it moved. And that’s why a lot of early animation has that kind of herky-jerky quality.”

Dragonframe and other frame-grabbing software systems take a lot of the guesswork, if not quite all of the faith, out of that process. Laika animators can check what they’ve just done on a computer, moving between the most recent frames taken and the one that an animator is currently on. This allows animators to ensure that whatever motion they’re puppeting, be it walking, running, flying, or the unfathomable wrath of nature flowing out through a giant tower of living vines exploding forth from the Earth, flows together.

“Whether it’s a 20-frame shot or a 1000-frame shot, you can look at all the frames that precede it to make sure that the object or the puppet is moving the way it should,” Knight told IndieWire.

Laika has used Dragonframe on every one of its films, but just because a tool is that useful and reliable doesn’t take the artistry and effort of animating out of the equation, or lower the particular stakes of stop-motion.

“2D animation, CG animation, they’re iterative. You can set key frames. You do your breakdowns. You do your in-betweens. You can go back and refine and keep going and reworking things until you get the perfect performance. With stop-motion, it’s progressive. You start on frame one, and the animator, coaxing life with their hands into this puppet, is working their way through a frame at a time. You don’t get to go back and change it.”

That lack of take-backs permanence, though, also helps stop-motion animators be intentional and certain in their choices. “You’re contorting your body into all these positions to get these puppets to move properly. It’s mentally very draining because you have to do all this three-dimensional chess as you’re trying to figure things out, because it is technical, but it always has to feel organic,” Knight said. “ It’s human ingenuity, it’s human creativity, it’s devotion, it’s care, it’s time.”

All that care and time goes into pulling off the magic trick of making steel, silicon, and fabric objects feel fully alive. That’s been the game for stop-motion since Ray Harryhausen. Whenever Laika develops new processes or sticks with tried-and-true tools, it’s to give animators the ability to do that. “[We don’t want] to get in the way of seeing this puppet as a person. The finest stop-motion animators can do all that with their hands. But we’ve developed different techniques and tools where some of the less experienced animators can actually get to that same level,” Knight said.

#3462. iOS 27’s Find My app adds convenient feature I’ve long wished for

iOS 27 is packed with new features, including several for the Find My app. One upgrade to Find My—custom sharing durations—grants a feature request I’ve had for years.

Apple’s Find My app is a great way to share your location with friends or family members on either permanent or a temporary basis.

But the “temporary” option just got a very welcome upgrade in iOS 27.

That’s because you can now set up location sharing in Find My for a custom duration. Per Apple:

users [now] have more control over how they share their location with friends and family using Find My, with new options to share for a custom duration — either for a number of minutes, hours, or days — or even set a date and time for when sharing will stop. This makes it easy for users to share their location while attending an event, or for a long weekend getaway with friends and family.

Until iOS 27, you could only choose from a very limited set of “temporary” options for sharing: for one hour, or until end of day. The only other option was “indefinitely.”

The main time I find myself adding new people to share my location with, I’m either traveling or they’re visiting me. On these occasions, the “one hour” and “until end of day” options never cut it.

So of course, I have to choose “indefinitely.” Then there’s the decision after the trip ends of either continuing to let location sharing happen, or ending sharing immediately (if I remember to). And the latter option has always felt a little awkward to me. I’d much rather schedule the sharing duration upfront.

And now with iOS 27 I can. When sharing location with someone, a new ‘Custom’ duration option allows choosing an end date and time, and/or manually setting a given number of days, hours, and minutes for sharing to continue.

It’s a great change, long overdue, and works perfectly for the scenarios Apple outlined.

Have you ever wished for custom sharing durations in Find My? Let us know in the comments.

#3461. 7 Most Hopeless War Books of All Time, Ranked

Whether they’re on a screen or on a page, great war stories play a key role in educating the wider public about the horrific realities of armed conflict. Particularly in the 20th and 21st centuries, the lived experiences of the World Wars, the Vietnam War, and more have inspired some brilliant and bleak novels, many of which rank among the greatest works of literature ever written.

These novels span many genres, from tragicomedy to drama to science fiction, but what they all share is a grounded emotional and psychological realism that makes for a truly devastating read. They’re not easy, but they are inventive, intelligent, visceral, and above all honest, which is the quality that you want most of all in a story about humanity’s darkest chapters. So, without further ado, here’s our ranked selection of some of the most hopeless war books of all time.

Joseph Heller’s debut novel, which has been adapted multiple times, Catch-22 is a satirical war story set during World War II. The book uses a non-linear third-person narrative, exploring events from 1942 to 1944 from the perspectives of multiple characters. Primarily, it’s the story of Captain John Yossarian, a U.S. Army Air Forces bombardier based on the Mediterranean island of Pianosa who desperately tries to cling to his sanity while dealing with the relentless absurdities of war and military life.

Primarily a satire of military bureaucracy, Catch-22 derives its title from a bureaucratic fallacy: an insane person should not fly missions, but anyone who asks not to fly on grounds of insanity must be sane enough to fly them. The book explores how this rule, and other equally counterintuitive military reasoning, slowly grind away at a soldier’s sanity. It’s easily one of the most important war novels of all time and a decidedly bleak narrative; the only reason it doesn’t rank higher on this list is that the hopelessness is balanced by Heller’s wit and dark sense of humor.

Written by novelist Tim O'Brien and based on his experiences as a soldier in the Vietnam War, The Things They Carried is a collection of linked short stories revolving around a fictional platoon of American soldiers fighting in the war. A semi-autobiographical work of metafiction, the book explores personal stories of love, loss, and trauma as well as the importance of storytelling, especially when it’s the stories of the people you love. Though fictionalized, the story is inspired by real people and events that O’Brien encountered during the war.

The Things They Carried is a powerful book that blurs the lines of fiction and non-fiction but ultimately delivers a deep truth about life and war. Since the time it was first published in 1990, the collection has received near-universal critical acclaim and become an international bestseller. The book has won several accolades as well and was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Critics Circle Award.

Kurt Vonnegut’s Slaughterhouse-Five, or, The Children's Crusade: A Duty-Dance with Death is a genre-blending anti-war novel partially inspired by Vonnegut’s own experiences and those of other people he knew who served in World War II. The narrative follows Billy Pilgrim, an American soldier who becomes unstuck in time and experiences his own life in a non-linear fashion after an encounter with fourth-dimensional aliens. Over the course of his life, Billy’s experiences, particularly the trauma of surviving the bombing of Dresden, drive him to adopt a fatalistic worldview as death loses all meaning for him.

One of the most acclaimed war novels and sci-fi books of all time, Slaughterhouse-Five is a highly original book that uses its metafictional narrative to process the author’s personal experiences. Like Billy Pilgrim, Vonnegut also survived the Dresden bombing, and the book is largely his attempt to finally put what he experienced into words. The novel was Vonnegut’s first bestseller when it came out in 1969 and has been highly acclaimed ever since. It’s also been banned in multiple places in the United States as recently as 2024.

Ernest Hemingway’s A Farewell to Arms is a novel set during World War I that follows the story of an American medic, Frederic Henry, who serves in the Italian Army. The book primarily explores Frederic’s romance with English nurse Catherine Barkley, which provides the sole light in his life as the war turns bloodier and more brutal than ever. Eventually, he leaves the army and seeks out Catherine, hoping to start a new life in Switzerland.

A Farewell to Arms is a truly tragic war romance, mainly because, unlike in many war novels, there is some hope to be found in the book: the hope of love and family that Frederic feels thanks to Catherine. However, by the end of the novel, that hope is cruelly taken away, not in a high-stakes battle but in a painfully normal, everyday manner that is all the more heartbreaking for its simplicity. A Farewell to Arms has been widely hailed as one of Hemingway’s greatest novels, and it has been adapted as films, a play, and a TV miniseries. In 2025, the novel entered the public domain and is now freely available online.

Written by Joe Haldeman, The Forever War isn’t a war book in the traditional sense: it’s a military science fiction novel that explores an interstellar war between humans and an alien civilization known as the Taurans. The book follows William Mandella, a physics student drafted into an elite task force to fight in the war using advanced weapons and near-lightspeed technology. Due to the relativistic nature of time, every time William returns to Earth, he finds a world that’s drastically different in its culture, language, and even biology, leading to an ever-increasing sense of alienation.

Published in 1974, The Forever War was highly acclaimed by critics and won multiple accolades, including the Nebula, Hugo, and Locus Awards. Despite its science fiction narrative, the book is inspired by Haldeman’s real experiences serving in the Vietnam War and is arguably more realistic than most historical books. It’s also unique in the sense that, while the story has what you could call a happy ending, it also delivers a bleak message about the inherent meaninglessness and alienation of war. The book was followed by three sequels: 1997’s Forever Peace, 1999’s Forever Free, and the 1999 novella, A Separate War.

A German semi-autobiographical novel by Erich Maria Remarque, All Quiet on the Western Front is one of the most famous war books ever written. The novel follows Paul Bäumer, a young man who, along with his classmates, enthusiastically signs up to fight in World War I. Over the course of the war, Bäumer learns firsthand about the horrors of war, the pain of loss, the alienation from civilian life, and the utter meaninglessness of the patriotic fervor that led him to join military service.

Since its publication in the late 1920s, All Quiet on the Western Front has been widely hailed as the greatest war novel of all time. The book is a bleak, painful, and necessary narrative that exposes the true cost of warfare on the individual psyche and soul — a message that got it banned and burned in Nazi Germany. Today, the novel is universally acknowledged as one of the greatest literary treasures of human civilization, and it has received multiple film adaptations, most recently Edward Berger's 2022 German adaptation, which won four Academy Awards.

Written by Dalton Trumbo, Johnny Got His Gun is a highly influential war novel that isn’t nearly as talked about as it ought to be. Set during World War I, the book is centered on Joe Bonham, a young American soldier who wakes up in a hospital bed and slowly realizes that he has lost all his limbs, eyes, ears, mouth, and nose. Trapped in his own body, his only hope is death, but even that is rendered impossible by military “regulations." All he can do is reminisce about his old life and hard-learned lessons about war.

Despite being an anti-war novel published during wartime, Johnny Got His Gun was quite acclaimed in 1939 and became a popular text among the American left of the time. The book has had a significant influence on American literature, shaping political discourse and literary craft with its stream-of-consciousness critique of war. Trumbo wrote and directed a film adaptation, released in 1971, which became a cult film, and the book has also inspired several other works of cinema and theatre, not to mention the Metallica song “One."

#3460. Why Clemenza Didn't Return For The Godfather Part II

The Godfather Part II continued the story of Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) after becoming the new Don of the Corleone family, and while most of the cast from the first movie returned, the character Peter Clemenza was notably absent. Played by Richard S. Castellano, Clemenza was one of Vito’s caporegimes and oldest and most trusted friends, who was instrumental in Michael cementing his power, and his absence was conspicuous.

In 1972, Francis Ford Coppola brought what’s now considered one of the greatest movies of all time and the best in the gangster genre: The Godfather. Based on Mario Puzo’s 1969 novel of the same name, and with a screenplay co-written by Puzo and Coppola, The Godfather was a massive critical and commercial success and made way for one of the greatest movie trilogies of all time.

The Godfather introduced viewers to the Corleone family in New York City, led by Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando). When Vito decided to hand over his empire to his youngest son, Michael, conflict with the rest of the city’s crime families was triggered, putting the lives of Vito’s loved ones in great danger, while Michael was pushed to take the lead despite staying out of the family business his whole life. The Godfather was followed by two sequels, and though most of the cast returned in The Godfather Part II, Castellano’s Clemenza didn’t come back.

Throughout The Godfather, Clemenza was tasked with getting rid of some of the Corleone family’s enemies, most notably Don Victor Stracci during the infamous “baptism killings” and he planted the gun for Michael to use to kill Sollozzo and McCluskey.

The Godfather Part II arrived just two years after The Godfather, and is obviously both a sequel and a prequel, picking up the story of Michael now as the new Don of the family while also going back in time to explore the origin story of Vito. The “present” timeline notably didn’t include Clemenza, which was strange given his strong connection to the Corleone family and his place as one of their most trusted capos.

Coppola said in a DVD documentary (via Mental Floss) that Castellano had declined to return as he wanted more money and dialogue approval. The latter demand came after he ad-libbed the now-famous “take the cannoli” line in the first movie at the urging of his wife, Ardell Sheridan. However, Castellano denied this in an interview in 1981 (via New York Post) and explained he didn’t return in The Godfather Part II as he disagreed with how Clemenza had been written.

According to Castellano, the original script had Clemenza testifying against the Corleone family, which he - quite rightly - claimed was completely off-character. Castellano added that the demands on him were “impossible” as he had settled on a price, and he was required to gain weight after losing 194 pounds to play young Clemenza. He also claimed Coppola promised to tell the press he had turned down the role for artistic reasons, but Coppola ended up saying something entirely different.

Despite Castellano not returning to play Clemenza in the present timeline in The Godfather Part II, Coppola found a way to give him closure and fill in that space. Bruno Kirby was cast as young Clemenza for the flashback scenes to Vito’s backstory, and in the present timeline, Clemenza was killed off-screen, with the betrayal of the Corleone family given to someone else. Fredo mentioned that Clemenza died of a heart attack, but Cicci implied he might have been murdered.

Ultimately, Clemenza was replaced by Frank Pentangeli (Michael V. Gazzo), who was given the storyline of testifying against the Corleone family. It was a smart move: seeing Clemenza betray the Corleone family would have felt like too much of a swerve, even if it also felt strange not seeing him in The Godfather Part II. Pentangeli was, instead, retroactively established as another long-term Corleone capo who had worked with Vito in his early career in the olive oil business.

Having been a key figure under Clemenza's leadership running the Corleone's family operations in New York, Pentangeli inherits the operation, kicking off an almost-immediate set of conflicts as he seeks to consolidate his position, but Michael refuses to allow him to take out his rivals, the Rosato brothers. Because of Michael's keenness to establish strong relations with Hyman Roth (Lee Strasberg), who is aligned with the Rosatos, he refuses, and Pentangeli is incensed by the insult.

Pentangeli quickly becomes the heart of the story as the walls close in on Michael and the Senate hearing investigating organized crime and allegations of his crimes threaten to crumble his empire. Gazzo's performance is great, and earned him a Best Supporting Actor nomination at the Oscars - which he ultimately lost to Robert De Niro for the same movie, understandably. Any other year, he would have had a strong chance of winning.

Even with the Rosato brothers and Roth pulling the strings, it would never have worked for Clemenza to be the one to betray the Corleones: it had to be someone like Pentangeli, who inherited his power, and like Michael, immediately faced a challenge. Those underworld politics were a great foundation for the entire subplot, which ultimately saw Michael using Frank's brother Vincenzo to intimidate him into recanting his Senate statement in fear. It's at this point that Gazzo really earns his plaudits, and his arc subtly reflecting Michael's own precarious position in the first movie only works because of how well he sells it all.

Ultimately, Robert Duvall's Tom Hagen using Frank's knowledge of Roman history and how traitors' families would be spared if they killed themselves is a brilliant, chilling end to his story, and shows both the dark morality of this world and the complex parallel with Ancient Rome. There's also an incredibly compelling mystery left unanswered, which was only explained in the original script: Frank's children were under Vincenzo's protection in Sicily, and his brother turning up was supposed to be a reminder not to betray his blood oath and the Mafia's code of silence, or retribution would be taken on his kids.

It's an unfortunate cut, but the fact that Gazzo's performance so thoroughly convinces of the threat without it ever having to be spelled out is the final testimony to how great he was as Clemenza's replacement. Ultimately, Castellano's unwillingness to sign on for the sequel may have led to the loss of a great character, but it worked out better for The Godfather Part II.

The Godfather Part II is a continuation of the Corleone crime family saga. The film explores Vito Corleone's early life in Sicily and 1910s New York, while Michael Corleone navigates the 1950s, seeking to expand the family's influence into Las Vegas, Hollywood, and Cuba.

#3459. Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber

This year’s TIFF and Venice were quieter in terms of breakout sales, especially when compared to last year’s splash for “Obsession,” and several awards contenders were scooped up before they even premiered at the festival. But other smaller buyers have emerged in recent weeks to release some of the more critically acclaimed titles that didn’t land major sales ahead of time.

The festivals are long done, but we’re still tracking every sale that happens, so check back frequently.

Distributor: Kino LorberDirector: Maiken BairdFestival: TIFF DocsBuzz: This documentary about Palestinian-American author and intellectual Edward Said earned strong reaction in its premiere at TIFF and festivals like NYFF and IDFA, in part because though he’s been dead for over 20 years, his writing and his views have been far more relevant in a post-October 7 landscape. IndieWire’s review out of TIFF praised the construction of the documentary and how it manages to be decades-spanning and comprehensive in a manageable running time. And Anne Thompson spoke with the filmmakers about the challenges of making the documentary and the fear that it being about Palestine would pose barriers to a distributor stepping up to buy it. Thankfully, Kino Lorber did just that, and it will be planning a theatrical release for 2027. Related Stories ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They? ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie

Distributor: Cohen Media GroupDirector: May el-ToukhyFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: Venice’s top prize winner of the Golden Lion has found a U.S. deal, this one made out of AFM with Cohen Media Group. Not only did el-Toukhy (“Queen of Hearts,” “The Crown”) movie win the Golden Lion this year, star Mathilde Arcel also won the Volpi Cup for Best Actress. The Danish film, also Denmark’s official Oscar selection, is a period drama set after World War II about a former housekeeper now set to be married to the household’s wealthy patriarch. But as she plans an extravagant dinner party to celebrate the occasion, hidden aspects of her past begin to resurface. Namely, it has to do with Danish witch hunts of those associated with Nazis after the war, and our positive review called it an “angry, despairing film” with a “Haneke-level bleakness in its assessment of human nature.” Cohen Media Group also recently bought an Isabelle Huppert comedy called “All About Corinne” that played at TIFF and premiered at Locarno.

Distributor: Sony Pictures ClassicsDirector: Niki ByrneFestival: TIFF Special PresentationsBuzz: Sony Pictures Classics have acquired all rights in the United States, Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, United Kingdom, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore) to “The Julia Set,” written and directed by Niki Byrne. The film had its world premiere at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival and follows a gifted young math prodigy (“One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti) who is “recruited into an elite prep course culminating in the most punishing exam in mathematics, while at the same time falling into a romantic relationship with her charismatic teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney).”

Distributor: Strand ReleasingDirector: Hanaël El YousfiFestival: TIFF DiscoveryBuzz: This directorial debut follows two friends, one Muslim and one Jewish, spending a carefree summer in Marseille, only to see the expectations and tensions between their traditional families start to get in the way of their friendship and leads them to take hold of their own destinies. El Yousfi both wrote and directed the feature, co-writing it with Raphaël Chevènement and Mia Grace Brown. It had its international premiere at TIFF, but it actually had a small bow at a French festival called the Angoulême Francophone Film Festival, where it won an Audience Award and a Special Prize for its cast. “The Daughters of Abraham” first opens in France on December 30. But Strand, a Culver City-based distributor behind recent releases like Mexico’s Oscar submission “On the Road,” “In a Whisper,” and the 4K restoration of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin,” will release it in North America in 2027.

Distributor: Black BearDirector: Nahnatchka KhanFestival: TIFF MarketBuzz: This market title is a rom-com starring an indelible trio of Greta Lee, Rebecca Ferguson, and Carrie Coon, and it wrapped production in September. Read more about the film here.

Distributor: 1-2 SpecialDirector: Jacqueline LentzouFestival: Venice OrizzontiBuzz: This Greek coming-of-age story won filmmaker Jacqueline Lentzou the Best Director prize in the Horizons section of the Venice Film Festival, but 1-2 Special picked it up after its North American premiere at NYFF and head of additional screenings at BFI London Film Festival, the Chicago International Film Festival, and the Busan International Film Festival. Blending what the release describes as both the “cosmic and the mundane,” the film follows a 15-year-old girl who meets a new classmate named Phaedra but also begins to notice signs and symbols from a dream world surfacing around her, ultimately leading her to an ethereal transformation. This is Lentzou’s second feature after 2021’s “Moon, 66 Questions.” 1-2 Special is planning a theatrical release for 2027.

Distributor: Sony PicturesDirector: Roshan SethiFestival: TIFF CentrepieceBuzz: This action-thriller starring Michelle Yeoh as a surgeon who is abducted and forced to operate on a mysterious patient is a bit of a departure for Sethi. Sethi’s previous film was the charming rom-com “A Nice Indian Boy,” and he’s also the co-creator of the medical drama “The Resident.” But reviews for the film were solid, and it’s not typical for the majors to buy festival titles, but Sony is already dating it for release on April 2, 2027.

Distributor: Universal Pictures and Blumhouse Atomic MonsterDirector: Joshua GiulianoFestival: TIFF Midnight MadnessBuzz: IndieWire first broke the news about the film originally set up at the Independent Film Company and Shudder being picked up by Universal and Blumhouse Atomic Monster for a deal that could surpass $10 million as the companies hope to find the next “Obsession,” just as they did last year. Read more here.

Distributor: HBO Documentary FilmsDirector: Rebecca HunttFestival: TIFF DocsBuzz: “Rapinoe” about US Women’s National Soccer star Megan Rapinoe was the opening night documentary at TIFF. Rapinoe was in attendance at the premiere screening of director Rebecca Huntt’s (“Beba”) film, which grapples more with Rapinoe’s progressive politics, such as her kneeling in solidarity with Colin Kaepernick, and her coming out story, than it does on the stories from her soccer career about how she led the US Women’s team to two World Cup titles, an Olympics Gold, and the Ballon d’Or. HBO Documentary Films has North American TV and streaming rights to the film. THR first reported the news.

Distributor: Roadside Attractions and VerticalDirector: Lauren Miller RogenFestival: TIFF Gala PresentationBuzz: Lauren Miller Rogen directs her husband Seth Rogen alongside Anna Kendrick and Kate Berlant in this comedy about parenthood and prospective parenthood. It follows a childless couple who begin debating the merits of having kids when their divorced friend and her child move in with them. The cast is stacked, including Issa Rae, Dan Stevens, Zach Cherry, Ed Helms, Ashley Park, Sharon Stone, and David Strathairn in supporting parts.

“Babies” is described as heartfelt and poignant in what is shaping up to be a strong year for Seth Rogen. The movie launched sales at TIFF nearly a year to the date prior to its Roy Thomson Hall premiere. The distributors are planning for a release in early 2027.

Distributor: Focus FeaturesDirector: Simon StoneFestival: Telluride and TIFFBuzz: Andrew Scott is said to be fantastic in this performance based on the true story of “Chariots of Fire” and “Gandhi” star and thespian Ian Charleson, who died of AIDS at the age of 40 but managed to raise awareness for the epidemic after his death. Focus has already dated the film for late November, the same time slot it gave “Hamnet” last year.

Distributor: NetflixDirector: Danny BoyleFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: The opening night film for this year’s Biennale, “Ink” is the story of the birth of The Sun tabloid in the ’60s and the collaboration between editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) and Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) that made it the notorious publication it is today. Netflix didn’t acquire worldwide rights to the film, so it could easily be something it sees as both commercial and an awards play.

#3458. Samsung’s Newest Flagship Soundbar System Is $500 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Samsung’s flagship soundbars have reached the point where the yearly upgrades are more about refinement than reinvention, and that is pretty much the story with the Samsung HW-Q990H—and with Black Friday approaching, this 2026 model is already seeing a $500 discount, bringing its price down to $1,497.99 from $1,997.99. That's its lowest price to date.

Samsung kept the same 11.1.4-channel setup from the older HW-Q990F, including the soundbar, wireless subwoofer, and two rear speakers, but leaned harder into software this time around—features like the SpaceFit Sound Pro automatically adjust the sound depending on your room layout, and unlike some auto-calibration features that barely change anything, this one reportedly shifts the audio balance in noticeable ways. Sometimes it improves dialogue clarity and bass response. Other times, you may prefer tweaking things yourself with the built-in seven-band EQ.

The system also handles basically every major audio format, supports wireless Dolby Atmos with compatible Samsung TVs, and includes 4K 120Hz HDMI passthrough for people gaming on a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X. That said, while the bass is strong for a compact subwoofer, it compresses when you push the volume near maximum, so it's not perfect for huge spaces or people who want nightclub-level output. More importantly, if you already own the HW-Q990F or even the older HW-Q990D, upgrading probably will not feel dramatic enough to justify the cost. But for someone starting from TV speakers or an entry-level soundbar, this system can completely change how movies, games, and even sports feel at home.

But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.
