#3456. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

#3455. It's Your Last Chance to Get This Early Black Friday Deal on a 65-inch Samsung OLED TV

This is one of those rare opportunities that don't come very often in the consumer tech space: Right now, you can get a 65-inch OLED TV from Samsung for $899.99 (originally $2,099.99) from Best Buy during its early Black Friday sale. This 2026 TV is considered an "entry-level" OLED, but it's still an incredible value for the money and the lowest price it has ever reached. #3454. Robert Pattinson as James Bond Proves That IP Is No Longer the New Movie Stars

Every James Bond casting announcement marks the start of a new era. The fictional MI6 agent has been one of pop culture’s few constants over the past seven decades; and each time a new actor steps into the role, it tells us something about the entertainment landscape we currently inhabit. Bonds can be intensely serious or silly and self-deprecating, and actors have entered the franchise at ages ranging from their late twenties to mid-forties. The role always goes to a member of the Commonwealth, but the variation that’s possible within those parameters has turned the franchise into a vertical wine tasting that illustrates what male movie stardom looks like in each decade. Related Stories Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber The Stop-Motion Tool That’s a Constant in This Crazy, AI-Mixed-Up World

The first Bond of the Amazon MGM era was destined to be even more of a turning point than usual, no matter who landed the role. The next film in the franchise will be the first one ever produced without the involvement of the Broccoli family, who have carefully guarded each iteration of the character since “Dr. No” came out in 1962. It marks the biggest movie investment that Amazon has ever made, as the tech giant spent nearly $10 billion to acquire MGM (of which Bond was the clear crown jewel) and then wrestle full control away from the Broccolis.

With Denis Villeneuve at the helm, it arguably marks the first time that Bond has been rebooted by a true auteur director with a distinct preexisting style and fan base. And it follows a Daniel Craig era that many feel took the idea of a dark, realistic James Bond to its logical endpoint with no obvious direction to go next.

When Robert Pattinson was officially announced as the seventh actor to play 007 on Monday morning, the latest era of the Bond franchise officially took shape. But it also marked the end of a larger Hollywood era in which blue chip legacy characters were seen as infinitely more important than the people playing them. We spent much of the past decade declaring that intellectual property is the new movie star(s). But casting the current Batman actor as James Bond proves that is no longer the case.

That line of thinking began to take shape in the 2010s, an era of Hollywood that will forever be defined by the phrase “cinematic universe.” As moviegoing became less of a consistent consumer habit and more of an event-driven hobby, the industry found that putting an A-list movie star or two in a new film was no longer enough to guarantee a big opening weekend. What did work, though, was slapping a Marvel logo in front of something and watching the box office dollars flow in.

Top-tier franchises were places where you went to build your star power, not cash it in. A new Bond or Spider-Man announcement was often the mainstream world’s introduction to a rising star that would be a household name within a few years. The approach was certainly better for the producers who steward these franchises: it ensured that the real value was contained in the stories and iconography that they controlled, making it relatively easy to bring in massive box office hauls with interchangeable actors who often moved onto bigger things before they became too expensive or demanding.

As that formula becomes less workable, it’s fair to wonder where we’ll start going to find our new stars. If you were casting a new Spider-Man in this environment, you probably wouldn’t pick an obscure theater actor like Tom Holland. We’re already seeing more stars come out of independent genre films, one of the few niches that can still be profitable without star power. “Obsession” gave the world its biggest breakout star of 2026 in Inde Navarette, and now she’s heading to the Marvel Cinematic Universe to help lead the “X-Men” franchise. But legacy franchises were once Hollywood’s most reliable path to minting new stars, and the industry will have to get creative if it doesn’t want the pipeline of bankable stars to fizzle out.

From an artistic standpoint, there’s every reason to believe Pattinson will make an excellent Bond. He has already worked with Villeneuve on the upcoming “Dune: Part Three” and has proven himself to be one of his generation’s most versatile leading men. He’s equally capable of playing brooding heroes and sniveling villains; a 2026 slate that includes “The Drama,” “The Odyssey,” and “Primetime” is evidence of both his range and consistent box office appeal. But from a business standpoint, it’s a decision that you wouldn’t make if you didn’t have to.

His deal reportedly costs more money for less commitment than any of the other finalists who screen tested. You’ll be juggling a production and promotion schedule that also includes “The Batman” franchise and other major films. In the run-up to the movie, more eyes will be on the man himself than the timelessness of the brand. And when the time eventually comes to replace him, expectations for the level of actor you need to land will be higher than ever before. It’s the kind of move you make when you simply cannot afford to fail. Nobody would deny that that’s the exact situation Amazon MGM finds itself in, but the mere fact that something as reliable as a new James Bond movie could place a studio in such a position is notable in and of itself.

It would be reductive to say that the pendulum has entirely swung back towards favoring movie stars. The old model where you could regularly deliver hits by putting George Clooney and Julia Roberts on a poster is certainly nowhere to be found. It might be more accurate to say that we’re in a “more is more” era of Hollywood, where no film is ever guaranteed to become the kind of cultural event that’s required to turn a profit on these massive tentpole budgets. With more competition for audience attention spans than ever before, you need to pair the power of Bond and the power of Pattinson and Villeneuve to feel truly comfortable with your investment.

#3451. BritBox’s Masterpiece Detective Thriller Gets Major Season 3 Update From EP

Greer Riddell is a London-based film and television journalist writing about comedy, streaming and the evolving media industry in the UK and USA. She works at Collider, covering the latest in film, television and entertainment through interviews, features, reviews and industry coverage.

Her recent brand collaborations include HBO, Warner Bros., Netflix, Hulu, Sky, Disney+ and DC Studios. She has covered titles including Saturday Night Live UK, Rivals, Scrubs, Stuart Fails to Save the Universe, Ludwig, Supergirl and Stranger Things.

Her recent interviews include Florence Pugh, Mike Faist and Christopher Abbott for Netflix's East of Eden, Taika Waititi and Jenna Ortega for Klara and the Sun.

Editor's note: The below interview contains minor spoilers for Ludwig Season 2.

David Mitchell's breakout role as Mark Corrigan in Peep Show saw him play a neurotic overthinker who could turn even the most mundane interaction into an existential crisis. Now, in Ludwig, he takes on another socially awkward, semi-reclusive character, but John Taylor has a much more productive way of putting his obsession to use. Under the pseudonym Ludwig, John is an acclaimed puzzle setter whose methodical mind and extraordinary ability to recognize patterns also happen to make him excellent at solving murders.

That talent might have remained undiscovered if it weren't for his sister-in-law Lucy (Anna Maxwell Martin), who forces the reluctant John into impersonating his twin brother, a DCI in the local police force, after he mysteriously disappears. The mystery surrounding James' whereabouts continues into Season 2, but John no longer has to hide behind his brother's identity in this “soft murder” take on The Parent Trap. Instead, the Cambridge Police Authority has brought him in as a "Crime Consultant".

With the second season having just finished its run on BritBox, Ludwig executive producer Kenton Allen joins Collider to discuss the series' success, the challenges of continuing the same story with a new dynamic, and why comedy actors seem so well suited to murder mysteries. He also discusses whether Ludwig could become a long-running detective franchise, teases the series' Christmas special featuring Poirot himself, David Suchet, and shares what audiences can expect from Rabbit, the U.S. adaptation currently being developed by Humphrey Ker (Welcome to Wrexham) and Megan Ganz (It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia).

COLLIDER: When I was doing my research for Season 2, I watched a couple of podcast appearances by you, and something that I thought was really interesting is that David Mitchell actually said he'd be interested in playing a detective, and he fits so well with that! Now, when I watch Ludwig, it's like, well, why was he doing anything else? What do you think it is about David and his performance that makes him such a good Ludwig?

ALLEN: I think it's a number of things, really. I think that you are correct when you say he fits it really well because it was written for him. I don't know whether you know the story, but a few years ago we were shooting another show. Do you know the story?

ALLEN: So he rang me and said, "I've got a secret I need to tell you." I'm slightly worrying what that secret might be. And his secret was he wanted to play a TV detective. And then I spoke to Mark Brotherhood, and that began Ludwig ultimately. So it was written for David, and Mark Brotherhood is sort of a bit like David but from the North of England.

I suppose that David, I sort of have this firm belief that the really great actors, particularly in this sort of genre, have come through half-hour comedy. And so if you look at British TV and you think of things like Cracker — Robbie Coltrane, I know Cracker wasn't a detective, but he sort of was — and you think of Alan Davies and Jonathan Creek, and Alan Davies came through 30-minute TV, and you think of David Jason and A Touch of Frost, and there's a great lineage of comedy half-hour sitcom actors stepping up into one hour. Some people call them “cozy crime,” a phrase I don't like. We prefer “soft murder.”

ALLEN: Yeah. Well, you need an actor that can play that, you know, that can do the serious business of investigating murders, but can also bring the charm and the wit and the irreverence to it. And I think that David brings that to Ludwig, and he has a light element to David in his real life, which I tease him about regularly.

I think he sort of embodies who Ludwig is, which is an outsider, a loner, somebody who prefers his own company to the company of other people, somebody who's very clever but is also quite shy, et cetera, et cetera.

I was intrigued by that connection between comedy and drama. So you mentioned the example of Alan Davies, David Jason, and there's also been a lot of talk around, perhaps this year especially — I went to the Edinburgh TV Festival, and they were all talking about how comedy, British comedy, has this huge resurgence. Is that comedy side of things one of the reasons why Ludwig has done so well, that tone, and what do you think comedy brings as an advantage to the mystery genre?

ALLEN: I don't think it's comedy, really, that brings something to the genre, but I think that in these sort of shows, these sort of murder-of-the-week shows, I think that in a world which is increasingly confusing and upsetting and there doesn't seem to be any answers to anything, I think spending an hour with somebody who is clever and entertaining and fallible and has all sorts of issues, but is capable of sorting out a whodunnit in 60 minutes, is rather reassuring.

There is some order in the world. Puzzles do get solved. Bad people do get caught. I think it's to do with that. I think the comedy, I think people, I think there's a bit of weariness about very hard murder shows. Some American television executive once described to me, "dead women in the trunk of a car" show, which is not a genre of television.

ALLEN: Isn't it? What a charming phrase. But I think there is a weariness of that very graphic, very violent, often women or children being kidnapped or murdered. I think people have had their fill of that. Particularly in a world which is, the news headlines are particularly unpleasant and disturbing and upsetting. I think escaping into a world where problems get solved, but we don't focus too much on the grisliness of the murder and focus more on the how was it done and who did it, I think there's some comfort in that. So, I think there is some comfort viewing in it.

The same there is in Traitors, when you're watching them get murdered, but they're not actually getting murdered. It's just reassuring, I think, to know that despite the chaos outside your living room or wherever you happen to be watching, that there is some north star, which is problems can still be fixed.

That first season, we had that added tension of John impersonating James and when was everybody going to find out, and then everybody found that out at the end of the first season.

So, you've got to come back to Ludwig in a sort of new dynamic in a different way. How can he still be involved with the police investigations in this new season? How did you ensure that this second series maintained that same level of suspense, and how did it keep audiences just as gripped?

ALLEN: Yeah. Well, I think the plan was always, from day one of developing the show, that Ludwig could only pretend to be his brother for one season because I think it stretches credibility to think that he could get away with that for more than a couple of weeks. So we always imagined that he would become, he'd be so good at solving murders and his clear-up rate would be so good and make Cambridge's CID look so good that they want to keep him on as a consultant.

So he becomes a consultant in the second season. But we still don't know where his brother is, why his brother's disappeared, and the evolving mystery about what is going on with Joanne Kempner (Sian Clifford). What is this greater conspiracy? Is his brother involved in it? Is the Kempner family really a decade-long, multiple-decade murdering dynasty? What is that all about?

I think that's the thing that keeps pulling you through the show. As much as John, Ludwig being a really good detective, he's still got an ulterior motive, which is what the hell is going on with his missing brother?

And also, he's got this developing relationship with Lucy and this sort of surrogate family with Lucy and Henry, which is evolving as well. The more time they spend together, the more time they realize that they're sort of codependent.

I really liked Anna Maxwell-Martin's character being perhaps a bit more involved in this season. She's doing her own detective work now at the newspaper. What has having Lucy more involved allowed you to explore that was not possible in Season 1?

ALLEN: Well, it's allowed us to explore what a brilliant actress Anna Maxwell Martin is more. If you've got Anna Maxwell Martin, give her something to do. That's from a producing point of view, but from a story point of view, it enables them to become a kind of investigating duo, Ludwig and Lucy, I guess, and it enables her to follow up leads on the bigger, the wider conspiracy and the mystery of her husband's disappearance, while Ludwig is pulled into various murders.

And I think it just gives a bit more urgency to the show, and I think it raises the stakes that Lucy is no longer the passive — we never wanted her to be a kind of passive wife who'd been abandoned by her husband, was just sort of slightly sad and... Just sort of a typical abandoned wife. The character was not that, and Anna Maxwell Martin certainly didn't play her like that. So she's obviously going to want to get involved. Her husband's missing. That is true. She's not going to sit around and ask Ludwig every week, every day, "Anything else happened in the investigation of my missing husband?" You know, she's going to get amongst it.

ALLEN: Yeah, and her photojournalism comes out of her day job, which is a photographer. So she goes for it, like any modern woman would, don't they? They wouldn't — you wouldn't sit around and go, "Oh, I don't know. I'm just going to sit here and make tea and wait for somebody to tell me where my husband is." She's not going to wait for permission to get involved, I think.

With Lucy, as you said, there's a bit of surrogate family there, but John and Lucy almost act a bit like an old married couple, and there seems to be a bit of history between them. Do you think it's fair to say that John sees Lucy as the one that got away and then perhaps married the wrong brother?

ALLEN: Yeah. I think so. I don't think Lucy thinks that. I think Lucy picked James and obviously married him and has a family with him. I think that Ludwig, though he probably never says it out loud to her in this season, feels that there was something else there, and if only he'd been less on the back foot, maybe he and Lucy could have been together.

But it's obviously the thing that dare not speak its name because she's married to his brother! I think that's in the Bible. You don't go out with your brother's wife. So it's completely forbidden fruit, and obviously neither of them can go there, whatever they're feeling. There's a son, Henry, in the mix, and there's a marriage, and there's all sorts of other things that are in the way of them ever truly saying how they may or may not feel about each other.

Well, it's interesting to watch any way, that sort of there's a devotion there, but perhaps in the past.

ALLEN: It's interesting growing up with identical twins and falling in love with one or both of them, and then we know they're not Mormons. No, she had to pick a brother, and she picked James.

What I really like about Ludwig is that there is obviously the overarching mystery, but then we also have the murder-of-the-week. How do you actually balance keeping those murder-of-the-week stories self-contained and interesting throughout, but also work out how much to feed into each episode of that central mystery that keeps us watching every episode week by week?

ALLEN: You work with a brilliant writer called Mark Brotherhood! And then, one of the answers to that question is a bit technical, but it's sort of true, which is our show is made principally for the BBC, and a BBC show is 59 minutes long, and typically a network show that has commercials in it, they're typically about 44 minutes long. So just in the maths of it, we have 15 more minutes of airtime to play with than you would on a normal commercial procedural. And often when you look at a sort of non-commercial procedural television, you'll see that they have to have more story in them because you've got this other screen time to fill, and you can't have eight more suspects. That doesn't work and is a bit boring. So, I think the nature of making it for the BBC originally means that there's naturally some time there to devote to the bigger conspiracy.

You could make the show at 45 minutes, but I think you'd find that the — and in fact, we're making, we're going to make a pilot for ABC, which we announced a couple of weeks ago. So that'll be very interesting about compressing both the story of the week and the conspiracy into a shorter running time. And the fact that a murder mystery, a story of the week, can sustain so much entertaining screen time. You can see shows where that aren't very entertaining, where it's all they've got, and that can become a little one-note. So I think it's just balancing what we're interested in, and you're led by Ludwig as well, and what is going on in his sort of quasi-professional life and his domestic life and how those two things are balanced out.

Britain has a history of such long-running murder mystery series and detective series. Do you see Ludwig becoming a long-running series, or is that overarching mystery with James' disappearance sort of giving it a natural limit to the story?

ALLEN: We've just wrapped the first three episodes of Season 3. We start shooting the second three episodes on Monday. We shall see.

Okay, I will come back to that at some point then, when I've watched the third season.

ALLEN: Yeah, I mean, you would need to ask that question at the end of the third season. I would say that people don't stop getting murdered.

Yes, there's not going to be many people left in Cambridge. I do keep thinking that.

ALLEN: Well, there's lots of people moving around all the time, but I don't think we'll have found all the murderers in Cambridge by the end of Season 3.

You brought up the fact that there's going to be a pilot made for ABC based on Ludwig, called Rabbit. It has a good audience. People are enjoying it. What was it about the American adaptation that you wanted to explore a bit differently from the original series?

ALLEN: I can't really talk too much about it. For obvious reasons, but I would say that if we get it right, Rabbit will be a brilliant cousin to Ludwig. Just in terms of where it's set and what the attitude is towards crime and crime prevention in North America as opposed to Cambridge, there's some big differences. Our police don't carry guns.

ALLEN: American police do carry guns. There's lots of cultural differences that I think will make it an interesting companion piece to Ludwig. I don't think it will be — it's a bit like the American Office, I guess, in that, you know, the American Office started off relatively like the British Office, but it took on a life of its own quite quickly. And I think that's what we're hoping to do with Rabbit, which is why it's called Rabbit and not American Ludwig.

So, watch this space, but I think there's plenty of cultural differences just between the two settings that give the show its own distinctiveness. And then I think there is a writer, obviously Megan Ganz, working with Humphrey Ker and Jon Steinberg and Dan Shotz myself. So it's seeing the fundamental setup through a different lens.

I'm looking forward to seeing what that becomes.

ALLEN: Yeah. Particularly the creators, Mark Brotherhood, myself, David Mitchell, nobody wants to make a facsimile of a show that we're making and is on air. So it has to have some reason to exist. And I think that Megan Ganz and us have found a very cute, smart way of making a cousin rather than a copy.

So fans of Ludwig will start watching Rabbit as well, and then they've got both shows to enjoy. You brought up the "cozy crime," or what we're going to call "soft murder."

ALLEN: Cozy crime is dead. Soft murder lives!

So it's become quite a significant British export to North America through BritBox.

Well, there's a whole page on BritBox as a category. Detective stories have become a thing. From your experience, why do you think international audiences respond so strongly to these sort of British murder mysteries?

ALLEN: I think that I don't think it's exclusively British because I think there are some examples in the States now of this, and our inspiration for Ludwig, a lot of it came from shows like Columbo and Monk, which were sort of murder-of-the-week shows. I think that international audiences enjoy seeing less grisly forms of ways to kill people, as we've discussed.

We very deliberately set the show in Cambridge, England, because it gives you a great mix of ancient and modern and hasn't been photographed very much in contemporary television. And I think that feels fresh, like Inspector Morse and Oxford felt fresh 30 years ago. Hopefully audiences are enjoying seeing a different slice of British life.

And obviously we're brilliant. We have brilliant actors, brilliant writers. Our on-camera and off-camera talent is world-class. So I think we're, you know, we've always been brilliant storytellers, and we have brilliant actors and brilliant directors and brilliant designers and brilliant everything. I just think hopefully it's an elevated form of a very familiar genre.

The world is not short of shows where people get murdered, but I think there's a lot of shows where people get murdered in a very unpleasant way. And we don't really feature the unpleasantness. We don't really, we don't ever revel in it, really, and we don't deal with it — we rarely deal with the impact on relatives and all of that. I mean, it is a slight fantasy career. Murder is very serious and devastating, obviously, but we use it for entertainment.

David Mitchell's 6-part crime series returns.

I was very happy to see that Ludwig is coming for a Christmas special because, obviously, we get to see more Ludwig, but I really do love Christmas specials and I think more shows should do them. I also saw that David Suchet is going to be a part of that, which is very exciting. People who love murder mysteries will absolutely love that. Is there anything you can tease?

ALLEN: Well, it's, it's rather wonderful, really, because we all, David in particular, are huge fans of Poirot, who is probably the greatest detective of all time. A fantastic Agatha Christie creation, and David Suchet's interpretation of that character is, we think, probably the best detective on screen there has ever been. So obviously David Suchet does not play Poirot in Ludwig, but we have got Poirot meets Ludwig in the show.

ALLEN: It's Christmassy. It is a special to me. It's the highest accolade any television show can ever have, which is to have a Christmas special. It'll be scheduled around Christmas in the UK, and I think on BritBox. We're still working that out. There's snow, there's mince pies, there's Christmas crackers, there's murder!

Ludwig Season 1 and Season 2 are both streaming now on BritBox.

#3450. Macaulay Culkin Officially Revives Home Alone With New Sequel

Macaulay Culkin officially revives Home Alone.

Culkin stars in a new sequel to the classic film that comes from one of the most unlikely of places. Culkin's best roles involve a number of TV shows and movies across the board, especially as his career has seen a resurgence in recent years. But his role as Kevin McCallister in the first two Home Alone movies will forever remain a classic part of both his career and cinema history. He's even reprised his role across various ad campaigns, lending his talent to nostalgic approaches to the movie and its cinematic importance.

Now, Collider has confirmed Culkin is back as Kevin McCallister for a McDonald's holiday campaign, advertising a limited-time Home Alone meal. The meal, which arrives in the US on December 1, 2026, consists of either a Sausage, Egg & Cheese McGriddles for breakfast, or a Big Mac for the rest of the day. It comes with movie-inspired Little Nero's Pizza McShaker Fries and a Lovely Cheese Pizza Dipping Sauce, useable for both fries and a customer choice of McNuggets or McCrispy Strips.

In addition to the food, each meal also comes with a collectible sock featuring McDonald's characters pulling inspiration from the Home Alone movies. There's also the Everything Sundae McFlurry, a separate dessert item that comes equipped with Oreos, M&M's, and hot fudge.

As for Culkin's role, he stars as Kevin in an ad wherein he's a McDonald's employee manning an empty restaurant during a snowstorm. The advertisement shows off the food, which he makes for himself in a comedic montage. Check out the full advertisement featuring his return as Kevin below:

In addition to the Home Alone-inspired food and collectible socks, customers in Los Angeles can sign up to participate in the Home Alone challenge pop-up on December 4 and 5, happening from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. PT. The free, first-come, first-serve event requires online registration, with reservations limited to groups of eight people or less. It's an additional element to the food-centered campaign, and one that puts the movie first with plenty of promising surprises.

The Home Alone meal is the second time Culkin has returned as McCallister for an advertisement role. His latest rendition was in a 2018 Google Assistant commercial, where he utilized the technology for a more modern take on the movie. According to the report, Culkin was drawn by the idea of associating McDonald's "comfort food" with the movie, having "no notes" about the meal when it was presented to him.

With the meal only two weeks away, it won't be long until the taste of Little Nero's in fry form, coupled with a cheese pizza sauce, all arrive at McDonald's. The breakfast option coupled with the regular lunch and dinner menu means there will be plenty for customer to enjoy, while the socks add a fun collectible item to the mix. The commercial makes for a fun reprisal of Culkin's Home Alone role, while adding the comfortable mix of McDonald's food to a nostalgic blast from the past.

#3449. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3448. Cary Grant, Clint Eastwood, and Christian Bale: The Stars Who Almost Played James Bond

When director Denis Villeneuve selected Robert Pattinson to play secret agent 007 in the next James Bond movie, he broke with tradition by casting an undeniable movie star in the role. Earlier Bonds were either relatively unknown (Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Daniel Craig, Timothy Dalton) or big names in television who hadn’t yet proven themselves on the big screen (Roger Moore, Pierce Brosnan). Yet Villeneuve and producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal’s choice of Pattinson isn’t completely at odds with the franchise’s history. At several points in the last 64 years, some of the box office’s biggest draws have flirted with the role and either turned it down or been rejected by the filmmakers. Related Stories Robert Pattinson as James Bond Proves That IP Is No Longer the New Movie Stars Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber

Right from the beginning, Bond producers were torn between going after a bankable name and letting the character be the star. Cary Grant was one of the world’s most famous actors when producers Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and Harry Saltzman began pre-production on “Dr. No,” the first feature film to showcase James Bond. (The character had previously been played by “The Shining” hotel manager Barry Nelson in a 1954 TV adaptation of “Casino Royale.”) He was also a close friend of Broccoli’s — so close, in fact, that he was best man at the Broccoli’s wedding.

Alas, that personal relationship wasn’t enough to get Grant to play Bond as Broccoli wanted. Grant was already starting to wind down his career and wanted to leave the public with their impression of him as a dashing young man. By 1966, he was done, so signing a multi-picture contract to star as Bond in 1962 didn’t appeal to the soon-to-be retired actor. Broccoli and Saltzman’s requirement that their Bond sign a long-term contract was also an obstacle for two other famous actors they approached. Both James Mason and Peter Lawford bristled at the idea of being committed to Bond for three or more films.

Rex Harrison and David Niven both wanted the part but were turned down in favor of Sean Connery, whose most prominent role to date was in the Disney movie “Darby O’Gill and the Little People.” “Dr. No” and its sequels made Connery a star, and for many viewers he remains the definitive Bond. By the time the sixth 007 movie, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” rolled around in 1969, however, Connery was tired of the role and stepped away — launching the first major search for a new James Bond.

Given that Connery wasn’t a household name when he made Bond an international icon in “Dr. No,” Broccoli and Saltzman were less inclined to go after a major movie star than they had been during the James Mason and Cary Grant discussions; most of the people seriously considered for “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” weren’t particularly popular at the time, and are even less well known now. (Few modern movie buffs would be able to pick John Richardson or Anthony Rogers out of a lineup, though the more famous Terence Stamp did meet with Broccoli about the role.)

The most popular actor Broccoli and Saltzman pursued was “Batman” star Adam West, who turned the part down because he felt 007 should be British — a response that would be repeated by other actors the next time a new Bond was needed, which turned out to be a lot sooner than Broccoli or Saltzman would have liked. Male model George Lazenby had almost zero acting experience when he secured the coveted role, but he took his good fortune for granted. In one of the great cinematic miscalculations in history, he assumed James Bond’s days were numbered in the age of “Easy Rider,” and declined to return for more 007 adventures.

Back at square one, Broccoli and Saltman decided to reverse course and once again go after big movie stars, including American ones. They offered “Diamonds Are Forever” to Clint Eastwood, who, like West, turned down the role because he felt Bond should be British. He would, however, direct and star in his own Bond-esque spy adventure, “The Eiger Sanction,” a few years later. Burt Reynolds, as famous for the hits he turned down (“Die Hard,” “Pretty Woman”) as for the ones he made, turned down Bond for the same reason.

John Gavin, best known today for his roles in Alfred Hitchcock’s “Psycho” and Douglas Sirk’s “Imitation of Life,” had no such reservations about playing Bond, and was the first American cast in the role. Unfortunately for him, Connery had second thoughts and decided to come back one last time, so Gavin was out, and Connery was in for “Diamonds Are Forever.” Gavin was briefly considered again for the eighth Bond picture, “Live and Let Die,” but by then the producers decided 007 should, in fact, be British and went with television star Roger Moore.

Moore had actually been offered “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” but had to turn it down due to an episodic series commitment. He became one of the longest-running Bonds, starring in seven 007 movies between 1973 and 1985. However, he began grumbling about leaving the series as early as 1979, leading the filmmakers to open discussions with Timothy Dalton (who turned down the role in “For Your Eyes Only” before committing to the series with 1987’s “The Living Daylights”) and James Brolin, whose bags were packed to play what would have been (again) the first American Bond in “Octopussy” when Moore had a change of heart.

The tradition of actors who either turned down or missed out on Bond in earlier films coming back to play the character was a sturdy one: just as Moore and Dalton would play the character in multiple films after initial false starts, Pierce Brosnan lost out on “The Living Daylights” due to a scheduling conflict (with his series “Remington Steele”) before replacing Dalton in 1995’s “GoldenEye.” Before the producers committed to Dalton in “Living Daylights,” a wide range of actors were considered and approached. Brosnan was the frontrunner, but Sam Neill came close, and the studio wanted Mel Gibson, but Broccoli overruled it, once again wanting a Brit (never mind the near-casting of James Brolin).

Although Brosnan was perhaps inevitable as Dalton’s replacement given the producers’ thwarted desire to have him in the 1980s, Hugh Grant, Sean Bean, and Liam Neeson were all considered for “GoldenEye.” Neeson turned the part down, later admitting that his girlfriend (and eventual wife) Natasha Richardson didn’t want him to play it. The producers wanted Bean but were overruled by MGM. Luckily for the actor, he made a strong enough impression to score a role as the picture’s villain.

Brosnan would play Bond four times, from “GoldenEye” through 2002’s “Die Another Day.” After that, the producers decided to make a change (reportedly because Brosnan’s salary demands were getting too high) and reboot the franchise with “Casino Royale.” Several now noteworthy actors were considered before Daniel Craig snared the part and became (after a brief initial flurry of internet outrage) the franchise’s most beloved Bond since Connery; Clive Owen, Sam Worthington, and Matthew Rhys were all in the running, and Henry Cavill was high on director Martin Campbell’s list.

Most intriguingly, Christian Bale turned down the part, which producer Barbara Broccoli said was his for the asking after she saw his stunning turn in Mary Harron’s “American Psycho.” Bale, amusingly, said he didn’t want to play Bond since he had already just played “a serial killer.” He also, according to the book “Christian Bale: The Inside Story of the Darkest Batman,” felt the role played into “despicable” stereotypes. Bale’s loss was Craig’s gain, as he led the Bond franchise into one of its most artistically and commercially successful periods — leaving Robert Pattinson with sizable shoes to fill.

#3446. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3445. Opera One for iOS adds Data Saver feature, cutting browsing data usage by up to 80%

Opera today announced that its Data Saver feature is now available on iOS, in a press release that also revealed a 20% year-over-year increase in the browser’s monthly active users. Here are the details.

In a press release published today, Opera celebrated a 20% year-over-year increase in monthly active users on iOS last month, “building on its established presence in Asia and Africa while expanding its reach in the US and Europe.”

In the US alone, growth was even stronger, with monthly active users increasing 46% year over year.

In both cases, that outpaced the 16% year-over-year growth Opera reported on PC just a few days ago, when the company also announced it had surpassed 100 million monthly active users for the first time.

Behind this growth across both desktop and mobile is a broader shift in consumer expectations – users are increasingly reconsidering the default as their understanding of what a browser can do evolves.

In today’s announcement, Opera also touted the arrival of Data Saver on Opera One for iOS, which the company says can reduce browsing data usage by up to 80% by compressing images and text on its servers before they reach the user’s device.

For users, this can make a difference when travelling abroad on expensive roaming data, topping up a prepaid plan or running low on a monthly data bundle. Data Saver can also help when browsing on a weak connection.

#3443. ‘Minotaur’ Review: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Riveting Comeback Remakes Claude Chabrol and ‘Unfaithful’ for a Hopeless Wartime Russia

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 19, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release the film in theaters Friday, November 20.]

Andrey Zvyagintsev nearly died and then came back to life in 2021 amid COVID complications, but unlike another Cannes filmmaker who resurrected from near-death only to make bad art, the Russian auteur’s riveting comeback “Minotaur” is not only a return to form — it’s also exactly the kind of hopeless, coldly gazing, and politically indicting film only the director of “Leviathan” and “Loveless” could ever make.

Based on Claude Chabrol’s 1969 erotic thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” which itself inspired Adrian Lyne’s deliciously lurid adaptation “Unfaithful” with Diane Lane in 2022, “Minotaur” follows a feckless, selfish man down a dark rabbit hole of his own digging amid the news that his wife is having an affair. We’ve seen this story before, and we know where it’s going. But Zvyagintsev, with a camera as still and gimlet-eyed as the Sphinx except when it’s gliding through the saddest rooms in the world like a seeking serpent, delivers an outcome and a movie more hopeless and on-brand than you could’ve dreamed of. His screenplay, co-written by Simon Lyashenko, is as tight as a drum, or as a rug you wrap up a dead body inside. Related Stories Cary Grant, Clint Eastwood, and Christian Bale: The Stars Who Almost Played James Bond Robert Pattinson as James Bond Proves That IP Is No Longer the New Movie Stars

Even without knowing the plot of Chabrol’s or Lyne’s film, you know everybody is doomed to their own resigned lot in life when you’re in a Zvyagintsev picture, the same director who tore an already estranged couple apart with the disappearance of their son in “Loveless,” only for the boy never to be found because, well, that’s life under Mother Russia.

But in the Russia of “Minotaur,” which was actually shot in Latvia because the days of shooting politically trenchant material in Russia are done, Gleb Morozov (Dmitriy Mazurov) is the CEO of a shipping company. He lives in a Russian suburb, ensconced from life’s daily horrors, in a modernist home made of glass, steel, fine wood, and concrete. It’s autumn 2022, and Russia is mobilizing into Ukraine, with the town’s mayor mandating that Gleb assemble a list of his employees to be drafted into service. Videos of bombings, meanwhile, are entering people’s social media feeds.

Life at home for his wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) is an empty chain of days; she’s an unemployed housewife whose existence revolves around getting their son Seriosha (Boris Kudrin) to school on time. A woman for whom getting the right presents and ordering the right food for his birthday party is a full-time job to fill the vacant space of a day. But as “Minotaur” quite quickly reveals, she’s having an affair with a 33-year-old photographer, Anton (Yuriy Zavalnyouk), whom she visits almost daily under the guise of yet another appointment. It’s something to live for, a thrilling escape from a miserable life of staring into the void, waiting for her husband and son to come home.

Lebedeva, who is astonishing here, feels less like a doomed Chabrol heroine than someone cut out of Antonioni. A forcefield of ennui with an elegant trenchcoat around her, and with the furtive glee that comes with having a secret, she makes her way a few times a week down the road to her assignations with a younger, virile artist in the sort of apartment where a woman as beautiful and rich as this would ordinarily never deign to be.

It’s no secret to the audience that Gleb, who has a history of infidelity and jealousy, is going to find out what she’s up to, nor is it a shock how he reacts. It’s mildly frustrating that Zvyagintsev, for his first film in nine years and after a brush with death, chose material that is very much familiar to his already savvy cinephile audience.

But the thrill of “Minotaur” is in how the filmmaker repositions the inevitable violence wrought from being cuckolded, the stuff we recognize from classic noir movies, into the political context of life in Russia amid its invasion into Ukraine. Imagine a Hitchcock thriller situated in the saddest, crummiest, most totalitarian corners of our times — and with an unfliching camera that offers no reassurance — and you’ll have some idea of just how bleak this unfeeling movie can get.

Mikhail Krichman, cinematographer on all Zvyagintsev’s films, returns on “Minotaur” with a glacial, widescreen gaze that encourages the viewer to examine everything around them. There’s a hypnotizing 360-shot that starts with Galina and Anton day-drinking and then getting into bed, with composers Evgueni and Sacha Galperine’s worrying score pressing upon them, only to come back to the pair in an unchanged, postcoital position. But they can’t stop what’s coming to them, which is nothing good.

Zvyagintsev loves a red herring almost as much as a cosmically depressing visual joke, like the tiny picture of Putin hanging over a boardroom. Or the detectives who eventually show up at Gleb and Galina’s house, only to later look at some serious hard evidence that could solve their wild goose case and instead think, eh, let’s just go to lunch. Or this film’s last shot, which does not leave the viewer in an easy state of mind despite the comforting falsities that its characters embrace as they float above it all.

Zvyagintsev’s latest film, like all of his others from the fraught father-son journey of “The Return” to the slinking, snaky noir of “Elena,” is devoid of easy resolution, least of all hope. It may feel too familiar to those who have followed this filmmaker’s work closely, but “Minotaur” is capable of crushing you with its final suite of images that refuse to let you forget that the world we are living in is hell.

The actors are exquisite, transcending whatever allegorical mouthpieces you might read into them as, like when Lebedeva’s Galina, absolutely wasted after not hearing back from Anton for at least 24 hours and then drinking an entire bottle of wine at a bar, berates her son and husband for ordering the same old shit for dinner every night when she’s not cooking. Margherita pizza, margherita pizza. “Where is me?” she yells at the husband she feels nothing for. The husband who has been instructing their son how to bash in the faces of bullies who come at him at school.

“Minotaur” isn’t the best movie of Zvyagintsev’s career, but the icily exacting power of his filmmaking is undeniable — and it sucks you in like a vortex. Rarely are you so glued to a tale you’ve heard so many times before. Andrey Zvyagintsev, welcome back. We missed, and we need you.

“Minotaur” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release the film later this year.

#3441. ABC Officially Confirms Devastating Grey's Anatomy News After Spinoff's Major Delay

An upsetting revelation about Grey’s Anatomy season 23 follows its spinoff’s already discouraging delay. Returning for a record 23rd season as part of ABC’s Fall 2026 lineup, Grey’s Anatomy was supposed to be replaced by its Texas-based spinoff during midseason, as the TV series would have had to take over Grey’s Anatomy’s Thursday night timeslot. However, massive delays made such a plan unfeasible, pushing back the Grey’s Anatomy spinoff from a 2026-2027 premiere to a 2027-2028 one. ABC nevertheless revealed even more dismal news regarding the long-running medical drama.

Grey’s Anatomy’s third spinoff is set to be based in rural West Texas and follow doctors at a medical center in the last town for miles. Such a setting pushes the Grey’s Anatomy spinoff to be completely different from the parent series, not only for the setting, but also for the type of storylines and traumas that reach the medical center in question.

Every Grey’s Anatomy spinoff that ever existed had been filmed in Los Angeles, which prompted Shonda Rhimes and Meg Marinis’s new brainchild to attempt to secure a tax credit so that it could do the same. However, California refused to award Grey’s Anatomy’s spinoff a tax credit twice, resulting in the production having to be moved to Albuquerque, New Mexico.

This inevitably delayed production enough that the Grey’s Anatomy spinoff couldn’t debut during the 2026-2027 midseason. However, another update regarding the popular medical drama is also upsetting, as Grey’s Anatomy season 23 will air its winter finale this week.

Grey’s Anatomy season 23 already having a winter finale date set up makes the current time particularly difficult for the medical drama, especially given that its Texas-based spinoff will be delayed for at least half a year if not more. Grey’s Anatomy season 23, episode 6’s trailer nevertheless promises an action-packed episode of medical chaos, hierarchical issues, and personal ones too, as Richard Webber’s wish to move the patient overflow to the VIP floor seemingly puts him at odds with both Grey Sloan Memorial’s new chief, Seth Norton, and his own wife, Catherine Fox.

While the news of Grey’s Anatomy season 23 already having a midseason finale is undoubtedly disappointing, its return has also been set up, and it’s the best possible outcome for the ABC medical drama. Unlike Grey’s Anatomy season 21, which had its midseason finale during the third week of November only to return in early March, season 23 will come back sooner.

Grey’s Anatomy season 23’s winter premiere is set for Thursday, January 7, 2027. This means the hiatus is only seven weeks long, which isn’t short per se, but it cannot be considered a long one either. Such a schedule mirrors Grey’s Anatomy season 22’s one from last year, when the ABC medical drama aired its midseason finale in mid-November only to return in January 2026.

Grey's Anatomy has made way for three spin-off series, though not all of them have been set in a hospital. Here's what they're about.

Grey’s Anatomy season 23’s return schedule would have inevitably looked differently had its Texas-based spinoff begun production earlier. However, the disappointment of a longer break for the record-breaking show would have been offset by another medical drama coming from the same minds that made Grey’s Anatomy the compelling drama that it is.

With the Texas-based Grey’s Anatomy spinoff’s debut delayed, having Grey’s Anatomy return in early 2027 is the best possible news for fans of the medical drama, particularly considering how Grey’s Anatomy alternated its return date between January and March consistently in the past ten years.

#3440. Apple HomeView launches tomorrow, but its first security update is already here

While the first HomeView units won’t reach customers until tomorrow, Apple today released a software update addressing nine security vulnerabilities. Here are the details.

Apple today released HomeView Software Version 27.2 (build 24V526), which contains some of the security fixes the company included in recent updates to its other operating systems, including iOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, and iPadOS 27.2.

These include a vulnerability that could allow a remote attacker to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages, as well as another that could allow a malicious Bluetooth device to pair without user interaction.

In practice, this means that users who get the device starting tomorrow are advised to update it as soon as possible, since the vulnerabilities have been publicly disclosed.

Here’s the full security content of HomeView Software Version 27.2

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data

Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory

Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management.

Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption

Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation.

Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction

Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks.

Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages

Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation.

Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined

Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code.

Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts

Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management.

Earlier today, Apple also confirmed that a software update coming next month will add support for security accessories to HomeView’s Siri AI, which currently refuses to unlock doors or open garage doors via voice commands.

Usually this is the time of year when early-year and summer awards contenders come back to theaters (see: “The Odyssey”). But even though it only left theaters not long ago, Sony is re-releasing “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” which is now the biggest domestic release of all time.

The studio is bringing the film back to theaters on December 4, with tickets going on sale November 19. #3436. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-new versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $152.99 for the Paperwhite and savings of $27 to $75 across five models that include the color-screen Colorsoft and the pen-equipped Kindle Scribe. As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. Its seven-inch, 300ppi glare-free display is larger than the previous generation’s 6.8-inch screen, with faster page turns, an adjustable warm light, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.
