#3434. ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

A very successful “values-based entertainment” company that was begat — in the parlance of its biblical heritage — from a film-filtering service that illegally edited “objectionable content” out of major Hollywood movies, Angel Studios has since become the world’s foremost purveyor of megachurch-approved multiplex content. The bigger they got (on the strength of projects like “The Chosen” and the QAnon cause célèbre “Sound of Freedom,” the latter of which pioneered a questionable ticketing model that continues today), the more that Angel removed from the films they released. Not just sex and swear words, but also anything that even vaguely resembled a soul. Related Stories ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Returning to Theaters with a New Rosario Dawson Cameo — and Box Office Records and Oscar Noms in Mind ‘Minotaur’ Review: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Riveting Comeback Remakes Claude Chabrol and ‘Unfaithful’ for a Hopeless Wartime Russia

With “Hershey,” a decidedly vanilla biopic about the most famous chocolatier who’s ever lived, the studio has taken its socio-religious project to its logical conclusion: They’ve made a movie that’s been stripped of any flavor whatsoever. It’s the cinematic equivalent of carob powder. It’s what Ned Flanders will force his kids to watch next Halloween.

Somehow unimaginatively bland and Splenda-sweet all at once, this godforsaken affront to good storytelling may not have benefited from any of the material that its distributor has deemed amoral, but “Hershey” is so mind-numbingly absent the most basic friction of the human experience that I wanted to fall to my knees and thank the lord that a few errant Kisses made it past The Angel Promise on a technicality. It’s too bad Milton S. Hershey never used his platform to baselessly sow doubt in a foreign election, because at least one of Angel Studios’ co-founders would clearly have been cool with including that (ecocidal fascism is fine, just don’t say “fuck” while you’re razing the Amazon, as that would offend Jesus).

As you may have gathered by now, I am probably not the target audience for this unrepentant godslop.

Not because I’m agnostic (“Hershey” is as secular as Angel Studios’ output gets, its overt religiosity limited to a brief scene in which the movie’s namesake pleads for help from an unspecified higher power), but rather because I stubbornly, blasphemously insist that a womb-to-tomb biopic should bear at least some faint resemblance to the stuff of real life. I couldn’t possibly care less about the facts (though I struggle to believe that Hershey and his wife literally danced with joy after learning that a twist of fate had spared them from being aboard the Titanic), but there isn’t a single moment in this film that feels like it was written by a real person, let alone lived by one.

Let’s back up a beat. To be clear, Angel Studios didn’t technically make this movie — that distinction belongs to the spiritually aligned production company Dandelion Media, who partnered with Hershey Entities for a fully authorized feature-length commercial meant to “bring [the chocolate brand’s] story into culture in a more immersive way.” The success of that marketing spend remains to be seen, but it can’t hurt to highlight Mr. Hershey’s ostensible purity at a time when the company that bears his name has been under fire for diluting its products with compound coatings in order to save money. And so we have a punishingly straightforward film that paints the Pennsylvania icon as a square-jawed, sweet-toothed wife guy who loved candy, orphans, and sitting way too close to the edge of the massive water tower that overlooks the town he remade in his own image.

Directed by Mark Waters, but absent any trace of the poppy confidence he once brought to the likes of “Mean Girls” and “Freaky Friday,” “Hershey” opens with its first and only stylistic flourish as a match cut transforms an immaculate chocolate Kiss into a small lump of coal — Milton Hershey’s life would turn out to be sweet, but it sure didn’t start that way. The film that follows sadly feels less like “Lawrence of Arabia” than it does an AI-generated adaptation of Hershey’s Wikipedia page, its algorithmic sense of human interaction rendered all the more uncanny by its ecclesiastical approach to conflict (and also by its blown out cinematography, which suggests a very literal interpretation of Angel Studios’ promise to produce “movies and shows that amplify light.”)

Adhering to the prosaic structure and candied morality that the Erwin brothers have made endemic to the world of faith-based biopics and their immediate kin, the film sees Hershey’s life as a blessed march towards his eternal reward — one that’s only slowed down by the litany of speed bumps that pop up along his path to heaven.

Young Milton’s very serious Mennonite mom is a major bummer, but she lets him out of the house to work for a local printer. The JRPG-like town where he grows up in the 1860s seems inhospitable to dreams, but its muddy roads make it appear as though the streets are paved with chocolate. His dad (Alan Ruck, a long way from “Succession”) abandons him pretty fast, but not before bending down to the kid like Zooey Deschanel in “Almost Famous” and telling him: “You’re a Hershey, and that means when you follow your dream, you don’t let anyone get in your way.” Apparently his dad’s dream was to not live with his family anymore, but so be it. A good example is a good example.

Every stumbling block is immediately followed by a burst of divine providence, as Sharon Paul and Timothy Michael Hayes’ script adheres to the grindset mindset of the prosperity gospel while Rolfe Kent’s saccharine score blends everything together into a tasteless slurry of unrefined sugar. The film insists that a little sweetness goes a long way, as an orgasmic taste of rock candy is all that Milton needs to make it through the day, but it doesn’t heed its own advice. Milton’s passion leads him to a job working for a saintly confectioner named Joseph Royer (a beneficent Richard Kind, as close to a live-action Bing Bong as he’s ever been), who just smiles it off when the kid forgets to turn off the peanut roaster and nearly burns down the whole shop.

Later, after sprouting into Finn Wittrock and starting his own caramel company, Milton is miraculously spared from ruin several times over by virtue of his non-denominational faith in himself and the universe. One low moment is redeemed by a massive order from overseas. Another resolves with a traveling salesman busting into the Lancaster Caramel Company with an offer to invest in chocolate — the future of snacking! “This chocolate,” Milton sniffs, “it could be good if it wasn’t so bad.” I know the feeling. The next time disaster strikes, he inadvertently stumbles upon the Hershey Kiss in the very next scene. The plotting is schematic enough to make “Bohemian Rhapsody” seem like “Last Days” by comparison.

Somewhere in there Milton enjoys a meet-cute with a woman named Kitty Sweeney (Alexandria Daddario), a grinning beauty who credits caramels with curing her shyness. Her job as Milton’s wife is to be his biggest cheerleader, and then — as the years melt away — to collapse in undiagnosed pain whenever he leaves the room. At one point it is implied that she and Milton have sexual intercourse, but only so the movie can leverage the couple’s inability to conceive a child into a robust philanthropic regime that allowed them to house and educate any number of white male orphans.

Of course, expecting this movie to acknowledge the Milton Hershey School’s history of racial and social discrimination would be as delusional as thinking its third act might address the labor disputes that unsettled Hershey’s chocolate factory in the late 1930s. Such things are simply not sweet enough to befit a story about how some vague belief and a little stick-it-to-em are all a man needs to prosper in this great land — even if a warts-and-all version of that same story would still be a model of American success.

Considerably less textured than the chocolate bars that have become synonymous with its title character, Waters’ film is so determined to launder one man’s dreams into reality that it comes to assume its own kind of dream logic in return — one divorced from the basic relationship between cause-and-effect or an event and its meaning.

In what might be the single most deranged movie scene of the year, Milton and his ailing wife Kitty literally dance for joy on the bow of a ship after learning that a twist of fate has spared them from being aboard the Titanic, even though upwards of 1,400 other people went to a watery grave that night. I’m not sure that qualifies as bringing the brand’s “story into the culture in a more immersive way,” but it’s definitely what I’m going to be thinking about the next time I bite into a milky and delicious Hershey Bar. After watching this perversely chalky film about the company’s founder, it’s a wonder that I can still remember what their signature product even tastes like.

Angel Studios will release “Hershey” in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.

#3433. Apple TV just debuted three new originals, including a heist thriller series

Each episode of “12 12 12” unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist and the 12 days following it. #3432. 10 Best Boxing Movies To Watch If You Love The Greatest, Ranked

Muhammad Ali could win a fight before throwing a punch. Opponents had to contend with his footwork, his mouth, and the unnerving confidence of a man who seemed to know the outcome. Often, he did. Yet the self-proclaimed greatest became a polarizing public figure, risking his career rather than compromise his convictions.

Prime Video's The Greatest, starring Jaalen Best, brings that complicated life to television. The authorized series explores the relationships and personal consequences behind Ali's victories. For viewers who finish the show wanting more, boxing cinema offers rich stories about people who discover that the toughest fight is often waiting outside the ring.

Some follow real champions. Others invent fighters whose struggles feel familiar, even when their records do not. Rocky and Creed offer underdogs worth cheering for, while Raging Bull makes rooting for its protagonist considerably harder. Even Million Dollar Baby, one of Clint Eastwood's best films of the last 30 years, has more on its mind than the final score.

These 10 films are ranked by their filmmaking, performances, lasting influence, and relevance to the themes of The Greatest. A great sports movie needs more than a convincing final bout. The best ones understand the person who has to climb into the ring, and what remains of that person when the crowd goes home.

There is an irresistible novelty to watching Muhammad Ali play Muhammad Ali. Released in 1977 and based on his autobiography, The Greatest follows the champion from his early career as Cassius Clay through his conversion to Islam, opposition to the Vietnam War, and historic return to heavyweight glory. Nobody could accuse the casting department of getting the leading man wrong.

Ali's charisma survives the awkward dramatic beats, although a great boxer playing himself does not automatically make a great actor. Director Tom Gries delivers a conventional biography of a thoroughly unconventional man. That limitation puts it last, yet it remains fascinating alongside the new series: here is Ali trying to tell his own story while he is still living it.

Denzel Washington received an Academy Award nomination for his portrayal of Rubin "Hurricane" Carter, the middleweight boxer whose career was derailed by a murder conviction. Norman Jewison's The Hurricane spends more time on Carter's imprisonment and struggle for freedom than on his actual fights, making it an unconventional addition to a boxing list. Its punches, however, still land hard.

The connection to Ali is compelling. Both were prominent Black athletes shaped by racial tensions, although their circumstances differed. Washington brings anger and dignity to a screenplay that simplifies disputed aspects of Carter's case. For fans of The Greatest, it broadens the conversation beyond athletic achievement to the consequences of becoming a public figure in a divided country.

James J. Braddock was hardly anyone's idea of a future heavyweight champion during the Great Depression. Injuries and poverty had pushed him toward the docks when an unlikely comeback turned him into a national sensation. Ron Howard tells the story with an old-fashioned Hollywood conviction that makes audiences forget they already know the outcome.

Russell Crowe gives Braddock bruised decency, while Paul Giamatti brings grit as manager Joe Gould. Cinderella Man is more traditional than the films ranked above it, and its inspirational machinery is occasionally visible. Nevertheless, the boxing is forceful. Its portrait of a fighter providing for his family contrasts with Ali, whose public battles were fought on a different stage.

Some boxing movies feature an opponent easier to handle than the fighter's family. David O. Russell's The Fighter follows Micky Ward (Mark Wahlberg), a Massachusetts boxer building a career while his half brother and trainer, Dicky Eklund (Christian Bale), struggles with addiction. Their family is loving, suffocating, and occasionally impossible to watch without wanting to intervene.

Bale and Melissa Leo won Oscars, but the film's real achievement is making Micky's independence feel as thrilling as any title bout. Its humor gives the material breathing room. Ali also had advisers convinced they knew what was best for him. The Fighter understands how hard it is to own a career when your family believes it owns a piece.

Choose the movie with the higher Rotten Tomatoes score.

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Ryan Coogler faced an unenviable assignment: bring Rocky into a new era without making the original hero look like a museum exhibit. He gave the spotlight to Adonis Johnson (Michael B. Jordan), Apollo Creed's son, who wants a boxing identity independent of his father's reputation. Sylvester Stallone's aging Rocky becomes the trainer rather than the attraction.

The fight choreography feels immediate, and Stallone delivers one of his most affecting performances. There's a direct link to the Prime Video series: Jordan's production company, Outlier Society, helped bring The Greatest to television. Creed ranks below the more accomplished films here, but its understanding of how athletes inherit and resist expectations makes it rewarding after spending time with Ali.

Clint Eastwood's Million Dollar Baby begins with familiar sporting ingredients: a stubborn trainer and a determined outsider everyone underestimates. Hilary Swank plays Maggie Fitzgerald, a waitress desperate to box professionally, while Eastwood is Frankie Dunn, the reluctant coach who eventually agrees to teach her. Their prickly relationship gradually becomes the film's emotional center.

What follows is darker than the usual underdog story. That turn earned debate, along with Best Picture and acting Oscars for Swank and Morgan Freeman. Among Clint Eastwood's greatest movies outside the Western genre, it's one of the most affecting. It ranks fifth because Ali's story takes a different emotional path, although few boxing dramas are better acted.

Will Smith had a difficult assignment in Michael Mann's Ali: persuade audiences to accept another actor inhabiting one of the 20th century's most recognizable personalities. He commits completely, reproducing Ali's physical swagger while finding the uncertainty beneath it. Smith received his first Best Actor Oscar nomination, and the performance remains one of the strongest arguments for his dramatic range.

Mann concentrates on the decade between Ali's first heavyweight title and his 1974 victory over George Foreman, covering events dramatized in The Greatest. The film shows how sporting achievement and political conviction became inseparable. The series has more room for relationships; Mann's film has a muscular visual style and Smith's transformation. They offer different routes into the same complicated life.

Some people admire Jake LaMotta as a boxer; others would cross the street to avoid him. Martin Scorsese's Raging Bull has little interest in reconciling those opinions. Robert De Niro plays LaMotta as a man whose aggression brings success in the ring and ruins nearly everything outside it. The performance won De Niro his second Oscar, deservedly so.

Scorsese's black-and-white photography makes the fights brutal, almost dreamlike spectacles. Yet the scenes that linger are confrontations in cramped apartments. LaMotta's story is the inverse of Ali's: a boxer unable to communicate what is happening inside him, however loudly he shouts. On filmmaking alone, Raging Bull could take first place. The two films ahead connect more directly to The Greatest.

50 years after its release, Rocky remains astonishingly good at making a small victory feel enormous. Sylvester Stallone wrote and starred in the story of Rocky Balboa, a Philadelphia club fighter handed an unlikely shot at heavyweight champion Apollo Creed. The setup is almost a fable, but the film understands the ordinary indignities of being underestimated.

John G. Avildsen's film won Best Picture, influencing nearly every boxing drama that followed. Rocky's relationship with Adrian (Talia Shire) matters as much as training. The ending makes a point most imitators missed: earning respect can matter more than winning on the scorecards. Rocky is the definitive fictional boxing underdog, but first place belongs to Ali himself.

No actor has ever reproduced Muhammad Ali quite like Muhammad Ali. Leon Gast's Oscar-winning documentary When We Were Kings takes viewers to Zaire in 1974 for the "Rumble in the Jungle" against George Foreman. The footage reveals a fighter who can command a crowd with a grin, needle his opponent, and make a political statement without waiting for permission.

Amid 1996 movies that still feel untouchable, When We Were Kings stands apart. Gast captures the event's historical significance and the personalities gathered around it. The music gives the occasion a cultural charge, while the boxing remains thrilling even when its outcome is familiar. It's a documentary with a thriller's momentum, powered by Ali himself.

When We Were Kings earns first place because it offers what a dramatization, however accomplished, cannot: the real Ali in all his magnetism and contradictions. Watch it after The Greatest and the astonishing part is how little exaggeration the series needed. Ali really was that much larger than life.

#3431. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3430. Macaulay Culkin Officially Returns as ‘Home Alone’s Kevin McCallister

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Macaulay Culkin gets recognized ten times more between November and January, by his own estimate, something he refers to as having “cornered the fourth quarter market.” Kevin McCallister spent Home Alone trying to get everybody to leave him alone, and now the holidays are when people are most likely to stop Culkin in the street.

Culkin sees it at holiday screenings, too. Adults who grew up watching Kevin take on the Wet Bandits are now bringing kids who have no idea what’s about to happen when Harry grabs that doorknob. Culkin has seen that handoff in his own living room, too. In a new interview with Collider's Hannah Hunt, he expressed that the movie has “taken on its own life,” which goes a long way toward explaining why he’s still game to play Kevin 36 years later.

Macaulay Culkin is officially back as Kevin McCallister for McDonald’s new holiday campaign. The limited-time Home Alone Meal starts rolling out internationally on November 24 and hits participating U.S. restaurants on December 1, while supplies last. Each U.S. meal comes with one of four collectible sock designs inspired by the movie, and the menu runs from a Sausage, Egg & Cheese McGriddles at breakfast to a Big Mac at lunch or dinner.

Little Nero’s may still be the only place Kevin can order a lovely cheese pizza, but McDonald’s is putting that flavor on its fries. The lunch and dinner meals come with Little Nero’s Pizza McShaker Fries, and there’s a Lovely Cheese Pizza Dipping Sauce you can get with McNuggets or McCrispy Strips. The Everything Sundae McFlurry is sold separately and comes with hot fudge, Oreo pieces, and M&M’s. Check out the lineup below. Fans in Los Angeles can also register for the Home Alone Challenge, a pop-up running December 4 and 5 from 5 to 10 p.m. PT. There’s a ball pit, a slingshot challenge, and a free Home Alone Meal for fans who complete the experience.

Culkin’s first thought about bringing Kevin back for McDonald’s was that “it’s about time.” He put the movie and the menu in the same category. You know what the McNuggets are going to taste like, just as you know exactly what’s going to happen when Marv takes his shoes off. You order them and put the movie on anyway. “The actual food and the movie are comfort food, really,” Culkin said. His wife, Brenda Song, was excited about the collaboration, too. “Brenda thinks it’s really cool,” he said. “And that’s really what matters most.”

Culkin had “no notes” when he saw the meal, and he decided to unbox the collectible socks right there on the call. He gave Grimace his due as “the most famous McDonald’s character of all” before holding up a pair with his own face on them. “If you ever wanted to walk on my face,” he joked, “you can just go to McDonald’s, go get yourself some socks.”

As for what Kevin would be like as a grown-up, Culkin figures he’d still get a kick out of “defying authority," which is part of why the movie works so well on kids in the first place. They spend all day being told what they can and can’t do, and here’s somebody their size who gets to tell two grown men exactly where they can step. Culkin thinks the fantasy holds up when you’re old enough to pay for your own pizza, too. “You always have a boss,” he said.

At Culkin’s house, one kid has taken that identification with Kevin a little further. Neither of Culkin’s sons knows their dad played Kevin McCallister, even though they’ve watched Home Alone with him. “They don’t know it’s me,” he told Collider. His oldest, Dakota, has his own explanation. “He thinks he is Kevin.” He looks so much like Culkin did at that age that even a cousin saw the poster while scrolling through a menu and asked why Dakota was in the movie.

The boys ask plenty of other questions while they watch, but Culkin can see Dakota only now starting to put that particular one together. He’s already guessed how the news will break: some kid on the playground, probably named Lenny or Nino, will tell Dakota before he gets the chance. Culkin figures he’ll sit him down afterward and have what he calls a “Beaver Cleaver” moment. Until then, Culkin is happy to let Dakota watch Home Alone and see himself in it, comparing the whole thing to letting his kids believe in Santa Claus:

“You want to keep that magic as long as possible."

For now, there’s still time for another Christmas where Dakota gets to be Kevin and his dad gets to sit beside him and watch. The Home Alone Meal comes to McDonald’s in the U.S. on December 1. The movies are available to stream on Disney+.

#3429. New Apple TV 4K and HomeView now available: Here’s everything you need to know

The new Apple TV 4K and HomeView smart display are officially available. The first pre-orders have arrived for eager shoppers, and you can now also head to your local Apple Store to buy select configurations.

The new HomeView smart display gives you a way to interact with Siri AI, your HomeKit accessories, and more in a 7-inch square display form factor. It’s available in two versions. There’s one with a built-in base, and another that’s designed to be mounted on your wall.

HomeView is powered by an A18 chip and has a built-in 12MP Center Stage camera for FaceTime calls. It’s available in silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray. You can read my full review for all the HomeView details you need.

When buying from Apple for delivery, HomeView in all four colors is backordered to the first week of December. Most Apple Stores, however, seem to have same-day pickup availability today, especially in silver and starlight. It costs $299.

On Amazon, HomeView is available for immediate delivery in Space Gray, Starlight, and Rose Pink. The silver model is backordered until later this month (and on the verge of selling out completely).

Meanwhile, the new Apple TV 4K is also available starting today. It’s powered by the A19 chip, up from the previous model’s A15 Bionic. It also has built-in far-field microphones, so you can now interact with Siri without using the remote.

The new Apple TV also supports Siri AI, enabling things like world knowledge and personal context requests. It’s worth noting that Siri AI is also coming to the second- and third-generation Apple TV 4K models via a software update.

The other flagship feature of the new Apple TV 4K is support for a four-HomePod surround sound system. You need four HomePod (2nd generation) or HomePod mini 2 speakers, arranged in matching pairs at the front and rear of the room.

Read my full review of the new Apple TV 4K for everything you need to know. The big takeaway, though, is that it costs $299, which may be hard for many shoppers to justify.

#3428. ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie

Few films on the 2026 calendar felt like bigger question marks than “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” The prospect of Brad Pitt reprising his Oscar-winning role from “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” in a Netflix pseudo-sequel written by Quentin Tarantino but directed by David Fincher was not on many people’s bingo cards when the project was first announced. The fact that the news originally broke on April Fool’s Day even led some people to wonder if the whole thing was an elaborate joke.

But the crowd who made their way to the TCL Chinese Theater on Monday, November 16 can attest that “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is very much real. The film was introduced by Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos, who joked that he instantly greenlit the film after receiving an 11-word text from Fincher that simply read “Written by Quentin Tarantino. Directed by David Fincher. Starring Brad Pitt.” As Sarandos tells it, he simply responded “Yes.” Related Stories ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Returning to Theaters with a New Rosario Dawson Cameo — and Box Office Records and Oscar Noms in Mind

When the lights went down, the crowd was treated to a rollicking hangout movie filled with elaborate recreations of ’70s Los Angeles, classic rock and soul needle drops, and a meandering plot that blends crime and comedy into one elaborate excuse for Pitt’s Cliff Booth to wander around the city exuding charisma. It wasn’t long before the social media reactions began to flow in, many of which were quite positive.

The online buzz following the premiere praised Pitt’s willingness to do seemingly anything (a few scenes seem destined to go very viral), his romantic chemistry with Elizabeth Debicki, and the film’s unapologetic commitment to capturing both the Los Angeles of yesteryear that Booth inhabited and the style of movie that he loved to watch. And of course, there are plenty “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” Easter Eggs to go around.

“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is set to debut for a two-week exclusive engagement in IMAX Theaters globally on November 25, 2026, before debuting on Netflix on Wednesday, December 23. Keep reading for a roundup of social media reactions following the film’s premiere.

David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is a wild, hilarious hangout movie. #3427. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

#3426. tvOS 27.2.1 launching soon with Siri AI for older Apple TV 4K models

Today the new Apple TV 4K has arrived (order here) with Siri AI as a major tentpole feature. But older Apple TV 4K models are about to get Siri AI too via a tvOS 27.2.1 software update.

Earlier this week, iOS 27.2.1 launched alongside companion updates like macOS 27.2.1, watchOS 27.2.1, and more.

Notably missing was tvOS 27.2.1. But the update’s absence now makes more sense, as Apple has confirmed that tvOS 27.2.1 introduces Siri AI support for select Apple TV 4K models.

Apple’s website has a newly updated support document that lists requirements for Siri AI on Apple TV. It says you need:

tvOS 27.2.1 on Apple TV 4K (2nd generation and later) and a Siri AI-enabled, paired device nearby

Although Apple has not yet specified launch timing for tvOS 27.2.1, it could launch as soon as today, or else early next week.

Because the new Apple TV 4K just now debuted, it’s understandable that Apple wouldn’t want to ship Siri AI for older models before the new one arrived.

As Apple’s website says, you’ll need a 2nd generation Apple TV 4K or later plus another paired Siri AI-enabled device, like a recent iPhone, to get the new Siri experience in tvOS.

To learn more about what Siri AI can do on Apple TV, read our review of the new Apple TV 4K here.

#3425. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 Pro (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3424. ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They?

A grimmer, gloomier “Hunger Games” is on the horizon with “Sunrise on the Reaping,” adapted from Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel about the origin story of the hardened alcoholic Haymitch Abernathy. Here, the teenage version of Woody Harrelson’s character in the original films is played by Australian actor Joseph Zada, the blond, ringletted Adonis who also starred as the moody Cal Trask in the recent “East of Eden” series.

Franchise fans might be riveted by Francis Lawrence’s latest installment — points for consistency, as he’s directed all the films dating back to 2013’s “Catching Fire” — but those audiences not already invested in the dystopian material and tales of tributes will find themselves left out in the cold by an overlong (it’s 158 minutes, so get comfortable), visually soupy, and narratively morose reprisal. But no matter, as this new slice of bankable I.P. is likely to rake in a hysterical amount of money, and perhaps launch Zada’s career as a face of new Hollywood stardom. Related Stories ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

The film is set during the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell. Only 16 years old, Haymitch is thrust into games that are rigged from the start — and whose broadcasting is ultimately edited and deepfaked to look like pro-Capitol propaganda. (The film nudges a little bit toward the ethics of state surveillance and how footage can be manipulated or even fabricated for political ends.) His pastoral, if impoverished, life in District 12 is small but happy, with girlfriend Lenore (Whitney Peak) and a mother and younger brother (Kara Tointon and Smylie Bradwell) with whom he shares close affinity, plus a best friend we’ll eventually find out will become the father of Katniss Everdeen (Lawrence) in the later films.

After a reaping (refresher: that’s when tributes are selected ceremonial-style, here as by a grotesquely pulled-tight-in-the-face Glenn Close as Drusilla Sickle) turns bloody, long-shot Haymitch ends up being selected at only 16. Violence follows him everywhere, as during the subsequent Tribute Parade, tragedy strikes Haymitch’s childhood friend (Molly McCann) during a horse-drawn Tribute chariot ride. Sequences meant to be thrilling often lack connective tissue to the rest of the material, or are devised in such a maelstrom of CGI (as goopy and cacophonous as a Marvel battle) that it’s difficult to feel engaged. It’s also unhelpful that most of the supporting cast is so wildly over the top, especially Capitol residents played by Close and a smarmy and mannered Kieran Culkin. Jesse Plemons as a Hunger Games camera operator brings a shade of moral dimension to the proceedings, but as with his “Digger” role, the actor feels woefully underused. Ralph Fiennes as Capitol president Snow, meanwhile, is given but scraps of material to work with.

The by-the-book script by Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie appears to stick faithfully to Collins’ 2025 novel, with plenty of potential for visual appeal that goes largely unrealized. The Hunger Games arena Haymitch is thrust into is rife with hidden dangers: poisonous streams, a deadly force field, and other trippy flora and fauna that vibe like a dark mirror version of “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory,” but again, “Sunrise on the Reaping” trips up on the CGI fakery.

The movie’s stacked young cast of tributes and mentors (those victors of previous Hunger Games tournaments) includes Mckenna Grace as a District 12 tribute who’s not to be trusted, the endearingly wily Ben Wang (recently excellent in the SXSW film “Brian”), plus a gravely underused Maya Hawke as the winner of the 49th Hunger Games, Kelvin Harrison Jr. as victor of the 34th, and the great Lili Taylor as a legacy tribute played previously by Lynn Cohen (aka Magda on “Sex and the City”) in the second film. These characters mostly exist to introduce themselves to Haymitch, be established as good or evil or helpful or unhelpful, and then be shuffled out of the scene. Elle Fanning is rather amusing, however, as the Capitol stylist Effie Trinket, styled and nearly drowned out by extremely outré fashions. Glenn Close also (with a visage channeling Katherine Helmond as Ida Lowry in “Brazil”) could’ve been used to better effect.

The specter of death looming over the film should not be confused for much in the way of actual depth, and while Zada’s performance is charming enough, his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films. He feels like a cog or a function to get this prequel to line up with the prior films — and isn’t that what he is? Which makes the movie, and ergo probably the book, feel a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series’ lore. When Haymitch comes home from Second Quarter Quell and descends into depression and alcoholism, that’s when the movie gets most interesting. Not a great sign when your film’s tepid coda is also its best moment.

And equally worrying is a series of cameos tacked onto the film’s end that smack of depressing fan service. These movies seem to be mostly critic-proof and hugely appealing to their core audience, but “Sunrise on the Reaping” is a dreary slog, another death-march “They Shoot Horses, Don’t They?” riff with a pretty Gen Z cast, and one that mistakes new layers of darkness (and trauma!) for the sort of profundity that its filmmakers hope will burnish a creatively withering property.

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” opens in theaters on Friday, November 20.

#3423. This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk

If you've seen an uptick in security updates as of late, you're not alone. AI models have become very good at finding new security vulnerabilities throughout 2026. Researchers and hackers alike are increasingly relying on these models in their individual pursuits: Hackers want to find these flaws to exploit them, while researchers want to block hackers from doing so. Microsoft's latest Patch Tuesday update included more than 1,400 patches; meanwhile, Apple's latest security update fixed two iMessage flaws that let both bad actors and innocent parties alike access texts they shouldn't.

Whether you use a Mac or a PC, you probably browse the web with Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser. As it happens, Google's web browsing platform is the latest to receive an important security update—but it's far from the first important Chrome update of the year.

As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Use-after-free vulnerabilities happen when the system frees up a memory location, but a program tries to access it anyway. It's a glitch in programming, but it offers bad actors an opportunity to break into your system. At worst, it allows arbitrary code execution, or, in other words, gives hackers the ability to run their own code in the app or system.

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What's more, this isn't Chrome's first active exploit of the year—this is its eighth. The company is playing catch-up with hackers looking to target users of its browser, which makes sense, seeing as Chrome is by far the world's most popular browser.

If you're using Chrome on your computer, you'll want to update it as soon as possible. Make sure you're running at least versions 157.0.8103.50/.51 on Mac or PC, or 157.0.8103.50 on Linux. To check, click the three dots in the top-right corner of your Chrome window, then go to More > Help > About Google Chrome.

Other Chromium-based browsers may not have the update yet, but they are affected by this flaw. If you use browsers like Microsoft Edge, Opera, or Brave, keep an eye on your updates to install any of the latest patches.

#3422. Robert Pattinson’s Batman Future After James Bond Casting Unveiled In New Report

Following the Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount merger, there are a lot of questions about the future of DC Studios.

James Gunn and Peter Safran are set to leave their positions as co-CEOs, as Jeremy Latcham takes over for them starting on December 1, which has raised a lot of uncertainty about the DC Universe franchise. However, as the world waits to see what happens with the main continuity, one of the Elseworlds properties may now be facing a larger issue in the near future.

It was officially announced on November 16 that Robert Pattinson, who is also currently playing Batman in Matt Reeves' DC franchise, will take on the role of James Bond in the next installment. While the British actor is shooting The Batman - Part II, The Wrap is reporting that "a source with knowledge" of his deal is claiming that due to "the protracted production" of the superhero sequel, it has allowed Pattinson to "slip out from under his contract," which had him signed for a third movie as the Caped Crusader.

It is worth taking into account that The Batman 3 has never been fully greenlit, as it would all depend on how the 2028 sequel does. Skydance has also not commented on the reports surrounding the contract, and how Pattinson's James Bond casting will affect the lead's future with the DC property, as it has not been confirmed if the upcoming comic book entry will be his final one.

Even with him becoming the next 007, that will have Pattinson signed on for a certain number of projects as the iconic spy; it's also crucial to remember that actors do juggle multiple franchises all the time. Given that there are signficant production breaks in between individual films, and depending on how filming schedules are planned, there could be scenarios where he returns for a hypothetical The Batman 3, especially if Reeves' follow-up becomes a commercial success.

The road to The Batman - Part II film has been a long one, as it has been nearly five years since the first movie came out, which grossed $772.7 million at the worldwide box office, as Pattinson brought a younger iteration of the DC legend to life. While the sequel did get greenlit, it wasn't until this year that the follow-up finally began principal photography.

Given the critical success of The Batman universe, which also brought The Penguin spinoff to HBO, it would be shocking if the Skydance regime doesn't at least try to work things out with Pattinson, if the report about his contract is true, to get him back for a trilogy finale. To this point, the actor has not commented on his future as the Dark Knight.

If The Batman - Part II were to end on a cliffhanger that also sets up a third story, it would be even more crucial to make sure that they can at least wrap up the trilogy with Pattinson. Hopefully, as more details emerge about his James Bond gig, it will also clarify what this means for him as Bruce Wayne.

The Batman - Part II is set to arrive in theaters on February 14, 2028.

#3420. 10 HBO Miniseries That Are Perfect From Start to Finish

Justine Kraemer is a Senior List Writer at Collider and a freelance writer based in Ontario, Canada. She is passionate about finding new angles on the latest movies and TV shows. With over five years of industry experience, her goal is to highlight lesser-known and interesting elements of pop culture projects.

HBO has featured some of the greatest miniseries of all time. While the streaming service has no shortage of compelling movies and TV shows for viewers to get attached to, the miniseries stand out. For years, HBO has provided viewers with miniseries that have remained topical and have stood the test of time. While there are many miniseries to choose from, there are several that stand out and can be revisited again and again.

Some HBO miniseries are based on literary works and adapt stories that speak to the human experience. Other series dramatize real events and highlight characters based on real people who had to witness some of the most remarkable moments in history. All of these series feature deeply human stories that provide new perspectives for viewers. The best HBO series are memorable dramas that tackle complex themes and introduce characters who face extraordinary circumstances.

Mare of Easttown is a crime drama that follows Mare Sheehan (Kate Winslet), a weary and emotionally scarred detective in a small Pennsylvania town, as she investigates the murder of a teenage girl while grappling with her own personal traumas. These include the death of her son by suicide and a custody battle for her grandson. Mare of Easttown follows the investigation as it unfolds, and long-buried secrets and tensions in the close-knit community are brought to light.

Mare of Easttown is one of HBO's best miniseries of all time since it captures the atmosphere of a working-class Pennsylvania town with striking authenticity. The characters, locations, and dialogue feel lived-in and genuine, which grounds the story​​​​​. Every character in the series is given a compelling backstory that makes them easy to invest in. While Mare of Easttown is a slow burn, the mystery at the heart of the series is well-crafted, full of twists and emotional stakes.

Olive Kitteridge is based on the 2008 Pulitzer Prize-winning novel of the same name by Elizabeth Strout. The series stars Frances McDormand as the titular character, who's a sharp-tongued, retired schoolteacher who lives in the fictional seaside town of Crosby, Maine. As Olive grapples with her strained marriage, her distant relationship with her son, and her own inner turmoil, the series paints a portrait of a woman who is more than her gruff exterior. The series follows her daily struggles to come to terms with where she is in life.

Olive Kitteridge stands out among HBO's miniseries because of McDormand's haunting and devastating performance. In lesser hands, this character would be far from sympathetic. Instead, McDormand leans into Olive's humanity and shows how emotionally complex she is. Rather than relying on sensationalism or drama, Olive Kitteridge tells a deeply human story about how messy life can be, and what ultimately makes life worth living.

Generation Kill is based on journalist Evan Wright's (Lee Tergesen) experiences being embedded with the Second Platoon of the First Reconnaissance Battalion's Bravo Company during the American invasion of Iraq in 2003. The series follows a group of young Marines as they navigate the chaos, confusion, and contradictions of modern warfare, as they struggle with the tension that exists between their idealism and sense of duty and the brutal reality of combat.

Unlike many war series that dramatize or mythologize combat, Generation Kill presents the Iraq War with documentary-like precision. The series doesn’t rely on clichés or hero archetypes. Instead, it gives viewers a diverse cast of fully realized Marines, some of whom are idealistic, others who are disillusioned, all of whom are flawed. Generation Kill is one of HBO's best miniseries because it asks difficult questions about a war many viewers remember without ever presenting easy answers.

​​​​​​​Watchmen is a sequel to the original 1986 graphic novel by Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons. Like the graphic novel, the series is set in an alternate-history United States where masked vigilantes are treated as outlaws. Watchmen specifically focuses on Angela Abar (Regina King), a masked detective known as Sister Night. The story unravels a complex conspiracy tied to the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre and the legacy of the original Watchmen.

In a media landscape that has no shortage of superhero stories for viewers to choose from, Watchmen stands out as one of the best. The series succeeds in being a spiritual sequel to the graphic novel while creating new stories that new fans can invest in. Watchmen is intricately plotted and full of twists, symbolism, and philosophical depth. Ultimately, Watchmen stands out as one of HBO's best miniseries because it is daring, intelligent, and makes viewers think.

Mildred Pierce is based on James M. Cain’s 1941 novel of the same name. Kate Winslet stars as the series' titular character, a determined, working-class woman in Depression-era Los Angeles who builds a successful restaurant business while grappling with her complex relationship with her daughter Veda (Evan Rachel Wood). Throughout the series, she does her best to gain her daughter's love and respect.

Mildred Pierce stands out as one of HBO's best miniseries of all time because it succeeds as a literary adaptation and a period piece. The series stays true to Cain’s original novel, since it uses a slow and deliberate pace that allows for deeper character exploration. At its core, Mildred Pierce is a devastating portrait of a mother-daughter relationship marked by love, obsession, pride, and betrayal, which is a dynamic many people can relate to.

Tanner '88 is a political mockumentary that originally aired on HBO during the 1988 U.S. presidential campaign. The series follows fictional Democratic candidate Jack Tanner (Michael Murphy) as he runs for president, blending scripted drama with real political events and figures. By inserting its fictional characters into real campaign settings and interactions, Tanner '88 satirizes the political process, media manipulation, and the intricacies of campaigning in America.

Tanner '88 remains one of the best HBO miniseries of all time because it was wildly ahead of its time. The series seamlessly merged fiction with real-life political events, creating a pseudo-documentary style that blurred the line between reality and satire. Tanner '88 offers a biting look at the reality of America's electoral system that remains timeless. The series holds a mirror up to the American electoral process, which remains an object of fascination to those in America and beyond.

The Pacific is a war-drama miniseries that follows the real-life experiences of U.S. Marines during World War II’s Pacific Theater. The series specifically focuses on three main characters, Robert Leckie (James Badge Dale), Eugene Sledge (Joseph Mazzello), and John Basilone (Jon Seda). The Pacific highlights some of the most brutal battles of World War II's Pacific Theater, including Guadalcanal, Peleliu, Iwo Jima, and Okinawa.

The Pacific is one of HBO's best miniseries because it delivers a harrowingly realistic look at some of the most brutal battles of World War II. Unlike typical war dramas that focus only on action, The Pacific deeply explores the psychological toll of combat. The series shows how prolonged exposure to violence and trauma affects anyone who experiences war. In short, The Pacific stands out for its brutal honesty, cinematic scale, and emotional depth.

Chernobyl dramatizes the events surrounding the catastrophic 1986 nuclear disaster at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in Ukraine. The series follows key figures such as scientist Valery Legasov (Jared Harris), government official Boris Shcherbina (Stellan Skarsgård), and fictional composite character Ulana Khomyuk (Emily Watson) as they uncover the truth behind the explosion, battle government denial and secrecy, and risk their lives to prevent further devastation.

Chernobyl succeeds in meticulously reconstructing the events of the 1986 nuclear disaster while balancing dramatic storytelling and factual detail. Rather than sensationalizing this tragedy, the series highlights the systemic failures that led to it and emphasizes the fact that ordinary people had their lives destroyed. Ultimately, Chernobyl plays like a thriller and presents characters who have to fight to survive.

Band of Brothers is a drama that follows the true story of Easy Company, a unit of the 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment of the 101st Airborne Division in World War II. The series follows Easy Company as they experience some of the most pivotal moments of the war, beginning with the D-Day invasion of Normandy, continuing through the Battle of the Bulge, and ending with the capture of Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest. Band of Brothers mainly follows Major Richard "Dick" Winters (Damian Lewis), who does his best to lead his men.

Band of Brothers' attention to detail makes it stand out as one of the best HBO miniseries of all time. The series is more than a war drama. Instead, it's a character study of some of the men who experienced World War II firsthand. Band of Brothers is another example of a series that could have glorified war, but instead provides an honest look at the cost of victory. The series succeeds in highlighting the heroism and sacrifice America's soldiers had to embody to win the war.

Angels in America is a groundbreaking miniseries based on Tony Kushner’s Pulitzer Prize-winning play of the same name. The series is set in mid-1980s New York during the height of the AIDS crisis. Angels in America interweaves the lives of several characters, including Prior Walter (Justin Kirk), a gay man diagnosed with AIDS, and Roy Cohn (Al Pacino), a closeted, powerful lawyer also battling the illness. As their lives unravel, the story blends harsh political and social realities with surreal, fantastical elements.

Angels in America is HBO's greatest miniseries because it's a fearless exploration of the AIDS crisis and the homophobia that enabled it to grow unchecked. The series' unapologetic approach gave visibility and dignity to LGBTQ+ experiences during a time when many were still being ignored and stigmatized. Angels in America uses dream sequences, angels, ghosts, and hallucinations not as gimmicks, but as metaphors for deeper psychological and cultural truths.

#3419. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already put out their plans and even started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this upcoming Black Friday sale a great one. Here is everything you need to know to prepare you for the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. #3416. Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema

A willingness to die for sex is a familiar bargain for queer people. Born in the twentieth century at the wrong place and time? Beware of Nazis, AIDS, and other mortal dangers. Hollywood has at times depicted these threats in ways that emphasize the humanity of LGBTQ+ people, as when Tom Hanks played a lawyer dying of AIDS in “Philadelphia,” during the height of the epidemic in 1993. The industry also has a history of finding ever more creative ways to kill off and scapegoat queer characters, a trope that as recently as 10 years ago seemed to be running amok.

But a more twisted and nervy dance between desire and death has unfolded in this year’s spate of particularly macabre queer films. After years of what felt like permanent advances in rights and representation, LGBTQ+ people have been stung by backlash, including attacks on gender-affirming care, legal threats to marriage equality, and cuts to suicide prevention. Amid a reduced perception of safety, anxieties about the possibilities and consequences of nonnormative desire are spilling out onscreen like so much fake blood. Even so, their formulation is evidence of social and creative progress. Related Stories ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They? ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher Deliver a ‘Pure Riot’ of a Hangout Movie

This alarm has played out, perhaps most obviously, in horror films. In Adrian Chiarella’s “Leviticus” and Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” same-sex attraction engenders extreme and potentially deadly terror, be it from detractors or the people it consumes. Both films explore not the evils of queerness — an argument that belongs to the tradition of queer-coded villains — but the horrors of having one’s desires villainized.

The year’s queer history films also subvert conventional narratives around sexuality and deadly fates. In Andrew Scott’s awards-season vehicle “Elsinore,” Ian Charleson’s dying wish to play Hamlet is one many actors would share; the film doesn’t focus on how or why he has AIDS, but what he wants to do before it kills him. The Spanish epic “La Bola Negra” depicts forbidden romance, but desire isn’t what dooms its multiple generations of queer men. The fact that they’re swept up in the currents of history, just like everyone else, is part of the film’s revolutionary power.

The era for combatting the notion that being gay is a no good, very bad thing in a straightforward way finally seems to have passed. Usually such sermons were preaching to the choir anyway. Gone is the teary earnestness of a conversion therapy drama like “Boy Erased,” from 2018, in which much of the trauma wrought on Lucas Hedges’ character derives from the church but is carried out by earthly messengers. In “Leviticus,” when a healer tries to pray the gay away from a pair of lovesick adolescents, he conjures supernatural and murderous doppelgangers.

After rituals of deliverance are performed over the convulsing bodies of a pair of schoolmates (played by Joe Bird and Stacy Clausen), each one is haunted by an illusion of the other that tries to kill them. The concept of “Leviticus,” named for the Old Testament book that forbids man to lie with man, partly functions as a wry play on the idea that you never get over your first crush. It also takes the fear that so many queer people know well — that what you desire most will be your downfall — to literal and horrifying extremes. Imagining the bigotry of organized religion as a senselessly violent supernatural force is a radical reversal. The boys aren’t the problem; the boogeymen that torment them spring from the so-called good book.

Schoenbrun’s meta queer fantasia “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” likewise performs a canonical revision. The nonbinary killer in the campy franchise within the film were themselves killed and sunk to the bottom of a lake by their comically gender-panicked peers. A victim seeking revenge, the TV-headed slasher is called Little Death, a nod to a French term for orgasm, la petite mort. Hannah Einbinder’s millennial filmmaker is on a quest to reboot the franchise, but more significantly, to achieve her own “little death.” In order to grow more comfortable with sex, and give into her own desires, her fear of intimacy — one that, again, many queer people know well — needs to be killed.

The movie ultimately intertwines fear of death with the fear of intimacy in a way that demonstrates the stakes — how you can feel so afraid of getting close to someone you could just die. But what must be slaughtered in this case is fear itself — so that same-sex desire, which has so often been pathologized and villainized, can flourish. (The trail of straight people extravagantly dispatched along the way, like so many gays before them, is one of the film’s many deranged and delightful flourishes.)

There is a potent realignment evident in the year’s period films as well, which center the desires and fates of queer characters on their own terms, rather than taking their oppression or disease as subjects unto themselves. “Elsinore” leans a bit heavily on obvious sentiment while leaving much of the thematic richness of “Hamlet” on the table. But Charleson’s determination to play the part before he dies is what drives the film, while the indignities of succumbing to AIDS are mostly a secondary plot.

Contrast that with recent period dramas on TV, like “It’s a Sin” (2021) about young people facing the AIDS crisis in London, or “Fellow Travelers” (2023) about the Lavender Scare in the U.S., and focusing on Charleson’s dream itself rather than the injustice of what threatens it marks a distinct shift.

The broad sweep of the canvas in “La Bola Negra” heralds another major turn of the page. The play of the same name by Federico García Lorca that partly inspires the movie, and appears in one of its several timelines, is about a young man denied access to an elite social club because he’s presumed to be gay. But homophobia isn’t the primary struggle (or a harbinger of death) for the film’s other gay characters. It certainly doesn’t help two doe-eyed young men (played by Miguel Bernardeau and Guitarricadelafuente) brought together and kept apart by the Spanish Civil War. But the forbiddenness of their infatuation is just one current swirling around them, the most pressing of which is, well, the Spanish Civil War.

Weaving the fates of queer characters into the broader scope of history, and suggesting a lineage of ancestry and shared desire, as “La Bola Negra” so marvelously does, feels like a kind of imaginative reparations. And it marks a bolder, more robust tactic in humanizing queer lives; the film traces generational ties and uncovers untold histories, rather than contending with acute crises like religious doctrine or deadly disease.

There is a stranger and more expansive creative palette evidenced in these films, one that suggests the unnerving climate for queer people in the real world is only furthering the reaches of the imagination. In carrying forward the legacy of queer cinema, it seems the gays presumed buried by the trope are finally rising up.
