#3415. Why Websites Show the Wrong Server Location When You Use a VPN

There are many reasons why someone might use a VPN, but most often, it’s to conceal your real geographic location or prevent websites from tracking your online activity. It can also be a way to get around location-based restrictions that stop you from accessing certain websites or platforms.

When you connect to a VPN server in the United States, websites are supposed to detect that your online traffic is originating from the U.S. That way, you can access online platforms that use IP filters to block non-U.S. traffic or circumvent regional censorship when travelling outside the U.S. But if you connect to a VPN server in the United States while you’re vacationing in Mexico, and a website thinks your IP address is from Brazil, that might not solve your problem and may even add unnecessary complications.

If you’ve encountered something similar with your VPN provider, there are several fixes you can try. Depending on why your IP location is being misinterpreted, one of these should help you access the internet from the server location of your choice.

IP geolocation isn’t infallible. Websites rely on third-party IP databases to look up your location based on your current IP address. Maxmind, which has one of the largest such databases in existence, claims that its GeoIP products have a 99.8% accuracy. Lesser-known providers with smaller IP databases may be far less accurate.

Websites can also use more than just your IP address to estimate your location. For example, they can send WebRTC requests to your browser or directly query your device’s GPS. Moreover, VPN providers often have physical servers in one country while their IP addresses are registered to another country, and this discrepancy can also create issues. Let’s take a closer look at each of these problems individually, so you can find the fix that works best for you.

WebRTC is an open-source technology that lets your browser reduce latency when engaged in high-bandwidth tasks like streaming or video calls. Based on the IETF standard RFC 8828, it lets a website choose between your VPN server and your real IP address so it can establish the quickest path to transmit large amounts of data and reduce wait times or buffering.

But the catch with WebRTC is that it exposes both your VPN server and ISP-assigned addresses to websites, which can reveal your real IP location and cause websites to reject your VPN server country. Firefox now comes with built-in protections to prevent WebRTC leaks, while Chrome and Edge support third-party extensions like WebRTC Control that you can use to eliminate these issues. To check if your browser is leaking your real IP address during WebRTC requests, you can use a free tool like BrowserLeaks.

Even when a browser isn’t leaking your real IP address, DNS resolvers may fetch inaccurate location information if their nearest servers are too far from your current location. For example, a user in São Paulo may be geolocated to Chile when using Google Public DNS because that’s where Google’s nearest resolvers are located.

If you toggle on DNS leak protection in your VPN app, this will force websites to use your VPN’s resolver to perform DNS lookups. That often solves the problem, but, again, you can confirm the fix worked through a service like BrowserLeaks or IPLeaks.

Websites rely on IP databases like Maxmind, IP2Location, IPinfo, etc. to look up your exact location, but these databases get outdated quickly and need constant updating. Most of these databases also correct errors on request, but that takes some time. Also, each website has its own rules for how often it queries IP databases for updates.

Even when locations are updated in the actual database, a website may be sitting with outdated information unless it actively has refreshed it recently. MaxMind recommends doing this at least twice a week, but that’s ultimately up to the specific website.

VPN providers often rely on virtual servers that use IP addresses registered in a different region than the server’s physical location. For example, ExpressVPN notes that it serves IP addresses in Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela through servers located physically in Brazil.

While this is usually to help with the lack of local infrastructure or strict surveillance laws in the region, many databases and analytics tools will flag the discrepancy for websites, leading to confusion and inconsistency regarding your actual server location. In these cases, your best bet is to switch your VPN server or use a dedicated IP address by signing up for a paid add-on for your VPN.

Before investing in a specific solution, it’s better to do a thorough lookup to make sure why your IP address is pointing to the wrong location and whether a WebRTC or DNS issue, virtual servers, or something else is the cause. Here’s how I’d go about it, step by step:

We’ll start by recording your baseline IP address, country, city, and ASN. With your VPN disconnected, navigate to IPConfig.co on your browser to grab your default IP details. I like this tool because it’s free and uses echoip to pull your location data straight from Maxmind. If you prefer using Terminal instead of your browser, you can also run curl ifconfig.co/json to grab these details in plain text format.

Now connect your VPN server. Then visit IPConfig.co again to note down the changed details.

Make sure the Country and Timezone fields match your current VPN server location. Also make sure the ASN (organization) field does not list your home ISP.

In case these details do not match your VPN server, run a WebRTC leak test and a DNS leak test using BrowserLeaks. If either of these tests doesn’t return your VPN server’s IP address, you’ve found your culprit.

If both the leak tests come back clean but a specific site still gets your location wrong, the issue is likely originating from an outdated database or virtual server.

There’s no surefire way to solve IP location mismatches for good. But if it happens often enough to disrupt your internet use, you can consider switching to a different VPN server and getting a browser add-on that prevents WebRTC leaks. If that doesn’t work, I’d consider buying a dedicated IP address that isn’t based on a virtual server. While many IP databases like MaxMind or IP2Location also have ways to request a location correction, that takes a while to go through and isn’t worth the effort unless it’s a permanent IP address registered through your ISP.

Apple published a new security research post this week detailing Secure Exclaves, a new architecture built to handle what the company calls “ambient sensing.” The latter isn’t anything new. “Hey, Siri” has been using a version of this always-on listening technology for years. The difference now (particularly on newer devices like Apple Watch Series 12 and HomeView) is new features need far more data from your surroundings, and Apple has changed where that data gets processed.

Today, on most Apple hardware, wake-word detections run locally on-device on a smaller, low-power chip. But once it thinks it heard you say “Hey, Siri,” the main operating system gets involved to confirm and wake up the smart assistant for use. There’s nothing necessarily wrong with this process. The split second of audio is all processed locally and not sent to Apple servers.

The problem lies in Apple’s newer features that ask for a lot more from users than a wake word.

Person recognition on HomeView identifies who’s in the room by face and voice, and Siri Recap and Live Rewind need to keep a running sense of what’s been happening around you. That adds up to a constant stream of sensitive camera and mic data, and it needs a more secure way of being processed than anything Apple had before.

Much like the existing Secure Enclaves architecture for authentication, instead of passing operations to the main OS, Secure Exclaves (notice the x) run their own tiny, separate operating system. Raw data goes in and a simple “that’s Arin” or “that’s the wake word” is outputted back to the OS, everything else is thrown away. According to Apple, that data “cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple.”

The changes don’t stop there. In recent SB column, I mentioned how on iPhone, the green dot that appears indicating that the camera or mic is live is all software connected, not like the hardwired LED that exists on the Mac. Now on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, and MacBook Neo, the camera and mic indicators now live inside this new exclave, meaning even a compromised OS shouldn’t be able to hide them for malicious purposes.

It’s apparent Apple is building toward this new level of ambient computing across every type of device when you read technical reports like this. Future AI-first products, like the heavily rumored AirPods Pro with inferred cameras, will most certainly built on this new Secure Exclave architecture.

#3413. Netflix's Epic Sci-Fi Series Is Officially Not Returning In 2026

Netflix's epic science fiction TV series is not going to be returning to the streamer in 2026, and viewers are going to have to wait until 2027 for the next season. We thankfully seem to have moved past the years of Netflix canceling shows at the drop of a hat. Now, if you see a show you like, you don't have to worry it's going to be canceled before it really gets going.

Still, Netflix faces the same production issues as other streaming services. There will always be delays and shows moved from one year to the next. Netflix might have gotten its act together in terms of giving its original series longer leashes, but that doesn't mean you should expect a new season every year.

3 Body Problem is a good example. The hit sci-fi series premiered in 2024, and fans have been waiting for season 2 ever since. Unfortunately, it's not arriving anytime before the end of the year. Based on Liu Cixin's novel series, Remembrance of Earth's Past, 3 Body Problem adapts the first book in the trilogy.

The series brings together a group of scientists, engineers, and thinkers from China and London who are all attempting to make contact with aliens at the height of the Cold War. What they find could alter humanity's future forever. This is the third adaptation of the story, but the first to be made primarily in English.

The series premiered in March 2024 and went on to earn a 78% on Rotten Tomatoes and garnered an Emmy nomination. Two months later, the series was renewed for a second and third season, ostensibly to cover the next two books in the series, but fans are going to have to wait a little longer.

3 Body Problem is set to return for season 2 in January 2027, so those hoping for the next installment of the series before New Year's Eve may be annoyed, but can also be glad the show at least has an official release date, and one that is not all that far away, considering how long they've been waiting.

The series is set to premiere on January 14, 2026, with all eight episodes dropping simultaneously. Artwork for season 2 suggests that the extraterrestrials at the center of the show are making their arrival to Earth. Hopefully, the nearly three-year wait for season 3 doesn't suggest another three-year wait for season 3.

3 Body Problem was a big success for Netflix when it aired. It was nominated for Best Drama at the Emmys, losing to Shōgun, and also nabbed several nominations at the Creative Arts Emmys. It was an ambitious task to take on 3 Body Problem considering its complex story and that it was originally written in Chinese.

It seems to have paid off for Netflix, however, and it's one of the streamer's best sci-fi TV shows. David Benioff, D. B. Weiss, and Alexander Woo managed to take the nerdy, complex story that Woo wrote (he's a former computer engineer) and make it palatable for the masses without dumbing everything down.

The series takes its time setting the stage, and it's only towards the latter half of the season that you begin to understand where the story is going. 3 Body Problem season 2 won't have that problem, and now that the place-setting is done, the series can get right into the thick of things.

#3412. Hackers Now Want Your Browser Sessions More Than Your Passwords, but You Can Stop Them

There’s a very organized dark web supply chain that attackers use to trade in stealer logs. Russian Market has effectively replaced Genesis Market as the new storefront for black hat cybercriminals, although much of the market has also shifted to private channels on Telegram.

According to threat analysts at DarkOwl, approximately 180,000 stealer logs were sold on Russian Market in just the first half of 2025. What's more, Russian Market is a well-designed storefront that users can access even without Onion links or the Tor browser. That means anyone could go there and buy a bunch of stealer logs to start attempting account takeovers at scale.

Meanwhile, Flare Research estimates that this isn’t even close to the actual scale of the threat, because 90% of stealer logs now surface privately on Telegram. There, automated chatbots let scammers shop for stealer logs like it’s Amazon, with options to filter by country, app, and account privilege. Logs sell for anywhere between $5 and $500 a piece, depending on the estimated value of the target accounts.

The easiest way to go about this is to take a look through all your active devices and their locations in your account settings on most websites. If you see a device or location you don’t recognize, you are likely the subject of an ongoing breach. However, keep in mind that this may not always be a reliable method if you use iCloud Private Relay or a VPN. Still, it's generally best practice to log out of all active sessions every once in a while and perform a fresh login to invalidate any unauthorized sessions.

Reset the passwords on your email account, enable two-factor authentication for added protection, and sign out of all sessions before doing a fresh login. Your email inbox is the single point of entry for most attacks because that’s where most websites send their verification codes or magic links.

Sign out of all active sessions on every account that you suspect is compromised. This will log out any attackers who are currently on a hijacked browsing session.

Change your passwords on every platform in order of priority. Start with banking websites, cloud storage providers, and password managers first.

Look through each compromised account’s third-party integrations and app permissions. Revoke access if you can’t recognize an app, or it looks suspicious. Also make sure to rotate any API keys that you’re currently using, since those may have been compromised as well.

But while the initiative has already been open-sourced, no other major online provider has begun offering native support for it as of this article. That means DBSC’s security benefits are limited to Google services like Gmail and Docs, Chrome for Windows, and third-party websites that offer single sign-on (SSO) options for your Google account. We might see a wider rollout in the near future, though.

#3411. Movie Theaters Are Back, but the Rest of Hollywood Seems to Be Crumbling

Movie theater owners have been through hell.

The pandemic forced many of them to shut their doors for months. When they could finally turn their marquees back on, Omicron and other variants made audiences skittish about returning to cinemas. Then the writers’ and actors’ strikes upended production, leaving them with fewer movies to screen. A promised moviegoing revival kept getting delayed or disrupted, often by circumstances outside of the exhibition industry’s control.

At long last, things are finally changing. Domestic ticket sales are up 20 percent year over year, and with potential blockbusters like “Dune: Part Three,” “Avengers: Doomsday,” and “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” on the horizon, analysts expect revenues to easily eclipse $10 billion for the first time since COVID. Grosses in North America currently sit at $8.76 billion through November 15, fueled by franchise fare such as “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “Toy Story 5,” but also by unconventional hits ranging from “Project Hail Mary” and “The Odyssey” to “Obsession” and “You Can See Everything.” Related Stories Desire, Death, and a Breakthrough Year for Queer Cinema ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Review: They Shoot Franchises, Don’t They?

Audiences are showing up for superhero movies and three-hour documentaries about a convicted felon. And media companies, which treated the theatrical business as the sick man of the entertainment industry, are finally seeing the value in cinemas, with the likes of Amazon MGM Studios and Skydance committing to making more movies for the big screen than most major studios did over the last decade. Better yet, younger viewers are driving the comeback, with studies showing that Gen Z members are the most frequent moviegoers.

That’s the good news. Elsewhere, Hollywood seems to be crumbling. Netflix, which has done more to reshape the entertainment industry this century than arguably any other company, is teetering, having jettisoned both chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin in a brutal purge. Ted Sarandos, who is clearly feeling the heat after the company’s stock has fallen 35.6 percent year-to-date, has brought in Peter Rice, a well-regarded former Fox and Disney exec whose calm demeanor and unthreatening good looks are out of c-suite central casting, to steady the ship.

As Hollywood has stumbled around trying to develop a better business model, the solution that many companies have landed on is to get bigger, fast. Thus, Fox sold to Disney, MGM was auctioned off to Amazon, and David Ellison’s Skydance bought Paramount and then quickly merged it with Warner Bros. Others, such as Comcast, spun off assets to make themselves more digestible. Has it worked? That’s the $80 billion question at Skydance, where executives have pledged to make 30 movies a year and turn a combined Paramount+ and HBOMax into a true Netflix challenger. Yet Ellison must pull this off while paying down a massive amount of debt.

So far, their early moves haven’t inspired much confidence. Executives like CBS News chief Bari Weiss have embraced the Silicon Valley ethos of “move fast and break things,” but what they’ve built instead, such as a simulacrum of “60 Minutes,” doesn’t seem better than what they’ve replaced. And if, as a recent Variety story about Skydance’s post-merger strategy suggests, part of their cost savings involves making sure executives don’t send out for “sandwiches and green juices” from Erewhon, they’re in for a world of pain. They can have Jimmy John’s cater lunch, and it won’t make a dent in their debt.

Skydance has already laid off most of Warners’ leadership and offered buyouts to the rank-and-file. Another wave of layoffs is expected at the company any day now. And across town, those types of cuts are the default move, with everyone from Disney and NBCUniversal to Amazon and Sony slashing hundreds of jobs. Are some of these layoffs in anticipation of what a leaner, AI-assisted future might bring? Probably. But with many of these companies’ share prices flatlining or falling, they aren’t being enacted out of foresight or a position of strength.

“I can’t remember a time when things have felt so scary,” an entertainment executive confessed to me recently.

And they’re right. It’s always popular to say the movie business is dying or the television industry is collapsing, and those doomsayers have been proven wrong time and time again. People want to be entertained. It’s just that making money entertaining them has never been harder for Hollywood.

#3409. OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, enabling ‘dot’ agents to make purchases

OpenAI is launching ChatGPT Wallet, which it says is “setting a new bar for secure payments by agents.”

ChatGPT Wallet works with OpenAI’s “dots” agent feature and includes a partnership with American Express, MasterCard, and Visa. Here’s how it works.

OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet is the “first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes.”

“We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users,” OpenAI explains, “so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.”

The feature won’t work with websites that block agents, however, which has increasingly become an issue online.

Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.

After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.

You can read more about ChatGPT Wallet and how it works here.

The company emphasizes that payments are secure, card info isn’t shared with your dot or merchants, and that you’re in control of purchases.

#3407. Aura's Second E-Ink Picture Frame Is Much Improved, and Much Cheaper

Last year, Aura released the Aura Ink, its first digital photo frame using an e-ink display rather than the LCD screens common to the other devices that made them the major player in the market (Aura customers have already uploaded more than one billion photos this year alone). When I reviewed the original 13-inch Aura Ink last year, I recommended it, with a few major reservations. Today, Aura announced its second-generation 10-inch Ink frame, and while I wouldn't exactly say they've solved every one of my issues, the new device is significantly improved—and much cheaper.

Most digital photo frames will remind you of an iPad with a decorative border around it. They're great for displaying hundreds of your photos with vibrant color, but not everyone loves the look, or the fact that these frames always need to be plugged in. An e-ink frame, on the other hand, uses a variant of the sort of low-power screen you'd find in a Kindle Colorsoft—less bright, but more paperlike, and much closer to the look of a traditionally printed photo.The Aura Ink is a great choice if you want a digital frame that looks more like a "real" photo and doesn't need to be plugged in and doesn't light up like a tablet (though it does have a light, it's really to make up for the fact that color e-ink screens don't reflect light very well, and thus can make your pictures look way too dark without an additional boost). You'll still get all the benefits of an LCD frame like the Aura Aspen, including the ability to load photos from anywhere using the versatile Aura app (you can now even text them directly to the frame), but you'll only need to charge it once every few months.

Now for the downsides: Where most digital frames allow you to flick between photos with a swipe, the Aura Ink is much more sluggish—switching from one photo to another takes about 45 seconds. While an LCD can match the colors in your photo exactly, e-ink uses a "dithering algorithm" to blend tiny pixels together to create the illusion of different hues ("millions" of them, according to Aura). In practice, this means up close, your pictures will look rather grainy, and the colors won't be nearly as bright as what you see on your phone screen.

All of that said, the Aura Ink is a great product, provided you know what you're buying, and the new 10-inch model offers some big upgrades over the 13-inch original released in 2025:

Resolution has been bumped up from 150 ppi to 200 ppi, so your images look more detailed and less grainy. (Though the difference is hard to capture in a photo, I can definitely see the improvement when comparing them side-by-side.)

Instead of the six base colors available on the older frame, the 10-inch Aura Ink blends nine different hues to approximate the colors in your images, offering greater color accuracy and improved contrast.

The transition effect when you move between photos has been updated to look more intentional—like waves of color moving across the screen versus a series of increasingly intense flashes.

It's a heck of a lot cheaper: $349, versus $499 for the 13-inch model—though that's still significantly pricier than Aura's most popular offering, the 10.1-inch Aura Carver, which starts around $200 less.

I write a lot about e-ink devices, from e-readers to tablets, and my common refrain, especially with color devices, is that they're great at what they do, but you should understand what they do before you plunk down your money. The Aura Ink will never look as bright and colorful as an LCD frame, and if you want a frame that can switch between images every few minutes or even play video, you'll need to look elsewhere (to maximize battery life, Aura recommends swapping photos on the Aura Ink no more than 12 times per day).

But if you want to display photos that look more like the ones that hung on the walls of your childhood home, in a frame that doesn't need to be plugged in all the time, you'll probably dig it, provided you can stomach the $350 price tag.

#3404. Hunger Games: Every Known Winner (& How They Won)

Spoilers ahead for Sunrise On The Reaping!Katniss Everdeen may be the most famous Hunger Games victor ever, but she's just one of many who have survived the Capitol's competition. Across the franchise, Suzanne Collins has introduced several winners whose stories have helped shed light on Panem's violent history, the evolution of the games, and the Capitol's lasting cruelty towards the Districts.

The original trilogy follows Katniss and her journey, while the prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes expands the story, focusing on District 12 winner Lucy Gray Baird. Then, with the second prequel, Sunrise on the Reaping, the universe expanded even more with the full story of Haymitch's Games, aka the Second Quarter Quell.

In Panem, the annual Hunger Games were first established by the Capitol after the First Rebellion as a way to punish the districts. This way, it serves as a constant reminder of the Capitol's power. Each year, one boy and one girl between the ages of 12 and 18 are selected from each district and forced to fight to the death inside a televised arena. The lone survivor is crowned victor and earns a lifetime of wealth, fame, and status.

Between the books and movie series, Collins has filled in the blanks surrounding the many victors of Panem, revealing how they won and what became of them after leaving the arena. Though 75 Hunger Games took place, only 74 were completed. That said, Katniss' first games featured special circumstances, meaning there were 74 total victors before the games came to an end. Through the movies and the books, a lot can be revealed about the various Hunger Games winners, how they became victorious, and what happened to them afterward.

With Sunrise on the Reaping, there's now even more to explore about the Games and their origin, way before Katniss ever volunteered as tribute.

Years before District 12's Haymitch Abernathy won the games, 16-year-old Lucy Gray Baird took the honor as the victor in the 10th annual event. Lucy Gray was mentored by Coriolanus Snow, the future president of Panem, and their relationship is the focus of the prequel movie The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. The tribute hid for the duration of the games while receiving help from Snow from the outside before poisoning some of the participants. In the movie, she won after being the only tribute not attacked by snakes in the arena.

Lucy Gray Baird is played by Rachel Zegler in the prequel movie. It is revealed that Lucy Gray was purposely reaped for the Hunger Games because of her relationship with Mayor Lipp's daughter's boyfriend. As she makes plans to escape District 12, Snow attempts to kill her, but it is unclear if he succeeded or if she made it to freedom. Though Lucy Gray is different from Katniss in many ways, she shares that heroic rebellious spirit.

The following year after Lucy Gray Baird's victory, another female tribute emerged as the Hunger Games winner. Mags Flanagan became the first victor from District 4, living off of nuts and her survival skills by creating fishhooks. She was also the first victor to move to Victor’s Village before serving as a mentor. During the 75th Hunger Games, Mags volunteered in place of Annie Cresta, but she passed away during the event from an acid fog.

Mags was played by Lynn Cohen in The Hunger Games: Catching Fire. She was the oldest tribute to fight in the 75th Hunger Games which was made up of past victors. Mags was also very close with fellow District 4 winner Finnick Odair who she mentored and practically raised. During the games, she was unable to move quickly and got carried by Finnick until she decided to sacrifice herself to allow the group to continue. Many Hunger Games fans have been hoping for a prequel story about the fan-favorite character.

Beetee and Wiress were two victors from District 3. Beetee was victorious by building an electronic trap in the arena, while Wiress won the Hunger Games by being able to figure out how to hide in her year's mirror arena, navigating light beams to find safety until all the other tributes eliminated each other. Both former victors were chosen for the 75th Hunger Games where they aligned with Katniss. While both assisted with Katniss' survival in the Quarter Quell, Wiress died during the event.

In Catching Fire, Beetee is played by Jeffrey Wright while Wiress is played by Amanda Plummer. While Wiress was killed during the games, Beetee managed to survive and was revealed to be a key ally in the Second Rebellion, helping Katniss destroy the forcefield around the arena so they could escape. He returned in The Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 1 using a wheelchair due to his injuries in the games and remained a big part of the rebellion.

At only 16 years old, Haymitch Abernathy became the second District 12 tribute to win the Hunger Games. Unlike a typical year, the 50th Hunger Games were celebrated as the Second Quarter Quell. This time around, the tributes were doubled. So, now, each district had to send four tributes to compete in the Games.

Haymitch's victory ultimately came down to a confrontation with District 1's last-remaining tribute, Silka. After throwing an axe at Haymitch, the weapon ricocheted off the arena's invisible force field hitting her instead. She accidentally killed herself and Haymitch won.

However, Haymitch's win came at a massive cost. Because he discovered the force field and used it to his advantage, President Snow felt that he'd embarrassed the Capitol. As punishment, all of Haymitch's loved ones were killed, thus sending him into a lifelong alcohol addiction.

Haymitch is played by Woody Harrelson in the original film series and Joseph Zada is taking on the younger version of the character in the Sunrise on the Reaping film adaptation. He becomes an integral part of the Second Rebellion using everything he learned from his Games, and the aftermath, to help Katniss and Peeta destroy the system that ruined his life.

Finnick Odair won the 65th Hunger Games when he was just 14 years old. As a male tribute from District 4, he was mentored by Mags. He was already skilled in fighting but the use of a trident in the arena led to his big win, as did the various gifts sent by sponsors. Like Mags, Finnick participated in the Third Quarter Quell and made an alliance with Katniss.

While Katniss didn't initially want to ally with him, she also didn't know how he had been used by the wealthy members of society of the Capitol or about his relationship with Annie Cresta. The more she learned about Finnick's dark story post-victory, the more she bonded with him.

Finnick is played by Sam Clafin when the character is introduced in Catching Fire. After allying with Katniss and the others in the 75th games, Finnick was rescued and became part of the rebellion. Sadly, Finnick was killed off in The Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 2 during the attack on the Capitol.

Johanna Mason, a tribute from District 7, was the 71st Hunger Games winner. She pretended to be weak so that she wasn't viewed as a threat, but when the opportunity arose, Johanna attacked with fierce intensity. Being from the lumber district, she was skilled at ax-wielding. Johanna was reaped in the Third Quarter Quell since she was the only living female tribute from her district.

Johanna was played by Jenna Malone in the movies. As Katniss was key to the rebellion, Johanna was recruited to help her survive the 75th Games and to facilitate her rescue. While Johanna succeeded in her mission, she was captured along with Peeta. After being tortured by the Capitol, Johanna was freed by the rebel forces and later joined them when she recovered. She managed to survive, lived in what used to be District 13 during the uprising, and presumably was able to return to District 7.

Whereas Peeta Mellark was reaped into the 74th Hunger Games, Katniss Everdeen volunteered in place of her little sister. Both tributes from District 12 survived deep into the games before reuniting. Katniss had her archery skills while Peeta was skilled in camouflage. As the last two tributes, the pair made a suicide pact until the Gamemaker announced that they could share the victory. Katniss and Peeta returned as tributes in the Third Quarter Quell.

Jennifer Lawrence plays Katniss in the movies while Peeta is played by Josh Hutcherson. The fabricated romance between Katniss and Peeta was a popular narrative among the public and a big reason why they survived the games. While the games were used by President Snow to keep the districts in line, Katniss became a symbol within the Games which was ultimately used to bring down Snow and the Capitol.

Woof (unknown games): District 8 male who hid during the entire event. He joined the 75th Hunger Games in his 70s and quickly died.

Seeder (unknown games): District 11 female who outlived opponents by going without food. She was in her 60s during the 75th Hunger Games and died during the Cornucopia fight at the beginning.

Porter Millicent Tripp (38th Hunger Games): District 5 female who won despite a serious spinal cord injury. She was in her mid-50s and avoided the 75th games, but as she is not present among the surviving Hunger Games winners for President Coin's vote of the final Hunger Games, she presumably died during the Second Rebellion.

Chaff (45th Hunger Games): District 11 male who won with his brute power while fighting. He was in his mid-40s when he fought in the 75th Hunger Games. He made it late into the games but was killed by Brutus.

Brutus (unknown games): District 2 male career tribute. He was in his late 40s during the 75th Hunger Games and was killed by Peeta.

Lyme (unknown games): District 2 female career tribute. She was a middle-aged victor by the time the 75th Hunger Games began, and while she was not reaped, she was part of the rebellion afterward.

Blight (unknown games): District 7 male who used an ax to win his event. He was in his 30s during the 75th Hunger Games when he was killed after running into the forcefield.

Cecelia (unknown games): District 8 female that used intelligence and sword fighting. She was a mother in her 30s by the time she was reaped in the 75th Hunger Games where she was killed in the opening massacre at the Cornucopia.

Enobaria (62nd Hunger Games): District 2 female career tribute that had sharpened teeth to rip competitors' throats out. She was in her mid to late teens when she first was reaped and is in her late 20s or early 30s during the 75th Hunger Games. Though she fought against Katniss and her allies in the games, she was rescued by the rebels and joined them.

Gloss (63rd Hunger Games): District 1 male career tribute who had knife-throwing skills and was in his mid to late teens when he won. He returned in his late 20s for the 75th Hunger Games where he was killed by Katniss.

Cashmere (64th Hunger Games): District 1 female career tribute who was also skilled in knife-throwing. She joined the 75th Hunger Games in her late 20s and was killed by Johanna.

Augustus Baun (67th Hunger Games): District 1 male career tribute. He was not reaped in the 75th Hunger Games but died sometime during the Second Rebellion.

Annie Cresta (70th Hunger Games): District 4 female who won due to her swimming skills. She was in her early 20s when the 75th Hunger Games took place but was spared when Mags volunteered as tribute. She later married Finnick and had his child after he was killed.

Out of all the Hunger Games winners that are known in the movies and books, it is clear one district rises above the others. As the entire list of winners is not known, judging by the information known, it appears that District 2 has the most Hunger Games victors with five in total.

That isn't surprising given that they produce "Career Tributes" along with District 1 which has three victors and District 3, which has two winners. District 12 has the most prominent victors with Katniss, Peeta, Haymitch, and Lucy Gray making up its four winners. As for the rest, District 4 has three while Districts 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11 have two each.

Although not all 74 winners are mentioned or known to readers and viewers throughout the series, there are some intriguing facts about certain winners that help them stand out. As noted, District 2 having the most winners is important, as are the prominent winners from District 12.

Gloss and Cashmere won in consecutive years and were both from District 1, which is the only time that a District had repeat winners in back-to-back years (though District 12 was likely to do so in the 75th Games). Gloss and Cashmere are also the only sibling winners in Hunger Games history. District 12 also had the distinction of having three previous winners still living by the end of the war in Katniss, Peeta, and Haymitch, which was incredibly rare since the Capitol made sure living winners were executed during the events of the Second Rebellion.

With The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping, as well as other lines about unnamed victors in the Hunger Games novels, it's evident that Suzanne Collins has plenty more Hunger Games history to explore.

The Hunger Games is a multi-movie franchise starring Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss Everdeen. The films are based on the young adult dystopian book series by author Suzanne Collins. The first film was released in 2012, followed by Catching Fire in 2013, Mockingjay Part 1 in 2014, and Mockingjay Part 2 in 2015. In 2023, the fifth film in the series was released, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.

#3402. ‘The Rings of Power’ Is Officially Being Review-Bombed on Rotten Tomatoes

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. He also writes obsessively about the box office, charting the many hits and misses that are released weekly, and how their commercial performance shapes public perception. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole new world of cinema.

There's a chasm between critics and audiences that occasionally becomes wider and more noticeable. For instance, several of Dwayne Johnson's recent movies — Red One, Black Adam, and even the Moana live-action remake — have all earned solid audience scores on Rotten Tomatoes despite having been poorly reviewed. The reverse of this phenomenon is equally prevalent. Just as a star can get their army of fans to rally behind a critically panned film, fans can also organize a mob to take down any film or show that goes against their values and beliefs.

This act of targeted hate designed to affect a film or show's popularity rating on an aggregator website has come to be known as review bombing. Typically, such campaigns are orchestrated by disgruntled fans who object to the most basic progressive ideas, such as inclusivity and diversity. This is one of the reasons why titles that have been most affected by review-bombing tend to feature actors or filmmakers from minority groups. Take, for example, Star Wars: Episode VIII — The Last Jedi, the series The Acolyte, and HBO's The Last of Us.

One of the biggest examples of audiences outright rejecting a major new project and making their dislike felt online is The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power. The mega-budget streaming series recently returned with a third season on Prime Video, and while the reviews have been mostly solid, the fan reaction has been predictably unpleasant.

The Rings of Power premiered in 2022 amid reports that Prime Video invested $250 million before the show's release and committed $1 billion over five seasons. The first season of the show clocked 150 million views, according to Amazon, but reports suggested that the series struggled to retain audiences for the duration of its eight-episode run. The second season saw similar issues. The third season is getting an unusual rollout, beginning with four episodes out of the gate, with two more the next week and the final two the week after that.

The Rings of Power holds an overall 83% critics' score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, but its audience score is languishing at 53%. The first season was most affected, with a 38% audience score based on more than 25,000 ratings. The third season, on the other hand, holds a 68% audience score. Viewers have been comparing the show to Peter Jackson's landmark film series, while also questioning some of the creative decisions and casting choices. You can watch The Rings of Power on Prime Video and make up your own mind. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3401. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3399. Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving

iOS 27 gave Apple Maps a handful of new features, and my favorite is one that keeps offering fresh updates every week: Local Lists.

Apple Maps has long offered a ‘Guides’ feature where you can browse curated collections of places worth checking out. Sometimes they’re created by Apple’s editorial team, other times by celebrities or in conjunction with current events.

But in iOS 27, there’s a new feature—Local Lists—that’s sort of an extension of Guides, but it gets updated weekly with the latest trending places.

Here’s how Apple describes it, via Apple Newsroom:

You can browse all available lists by opening a Trending Restaurants list then tapping where you see the Apple logo and ‘Local Lists’ near the text that says when it was last updated.

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

#3395. NBC’s Blue Bloods For Adults Replacement Reverses The Original Reagan Family Curse

Warning! Spoilers for Line of Fire season 1, episode 8, "Besieged."

Family has always been central to the success of television's best police procedurals, and NBC's Line of Fire is putting a devastating twist on the formula that made Blue Bloods so beloved. Although both series revolve around families dedicated to law enforcement, the Hollingsworth family are facing a predicament that completely reverses one of the Reagan family's greatest tragedies.

Throughout Blue Bloods, the Reagan family remained united by their shared grief over Joe Reagan, whose death before the series began left an irreplaceable hole in their family. Despite their disagreements, the Reagans consistently demonstrated that family came first, making their inability to fully reunite particularly heartbreaking.

However, Line of Fire presents a much darker possibility for its central family. After spending years believing their son and brother, Jack, was dead, the Hollingsworths are gradually approaching a reunion that could permanently destroy their already fragile relationships. Rather than offering the closure they desperately need, Jack's return threatens to expose devastating secrets.

Where the Reagans would have welcomed the opportunity to have Joe back, the Hollingsworths might be better off without Jack. This reversal highlights how Line of Fire is transforming the familiar family procedural into something considerably more complicated.

The Hollingsworth family has spent much of Line of Fire season 1 struggling with the consequences of Mike and Jane's secrets. Their decision to conceal the truth about Jack (Charlie Barnett) from their children has already created significant tension, particularly as the family attempts to rebuild relationships damaged by years of deception. Unfortunately, the latest developments in the investigation threaten to undo whatever progress they've made.

After initially believing Jack was dead, Jane now has reason to believe her son is alive. Under ordinary circumstances, discovering that a child thought to be dead has survived would be a cause for celebration. However, the troubling circumstances surrounding this revelation make Jack's potential return considerably more complicated. His connection to the ongoing murder investigation raises serious questions about what he's been doing and how his actions could implicate the rest of the family.

More importantly, Jane must decide what to do with this information. Will she immediately tell Mike that Jack is alive, or will she keep the discovery to herself until she understands the extent of his involvement? Given everything the Hollingsworths have already endured, withholding the truth from her husband could create another devastating fracture in their relationship.

Of course, Jane might have understandable reasons for keeping quiet. Jack's possible involvement in the murders means his survival isn't necessarily the happy ending she and Mike might have envisioned. Sharing the discovery could force them to confront the possibility that their son has become someone they no longer recognize. Nevertheless, another secret would only perpetuate the behavior that has already threatened to tear their family apart.

The situation becomes even more concerning when considering what the Hollingsworth children are already experiencing. Clare's ordeal with Logan has left her struggling to trust her own judgment, while Russ is still navigating questions about his identity and place within the family. Meanwhile, Micah is attempting to establish confidence in his professional abilities and determine where his career is headed. Discovering that their parents have concealed yet another life-changing truth could destabilize all three siblings when they desperately need stability. Rather than bringing the Hollingsworths closer together, Jack's return could deepen the insecurities and fractures that have already defined their relationships throughout season 1.

For the Hollingsworths, the real danger isn't simply that Jack is alive, but that the truth about his survival could expose everything they've worked to keep hidden.

Unlike the Hollingsworths, the Reagan family never had the opportunity to reunite with their lost loved one in Blue Bloods. Joe Reagan's death before the events of the series left an undeniable void in the family, particularly for his father, Frank, and brothers, Danny and Jamie. Although Joe was never physically present during the show's run, his memory remained an important part of the Reagans' identity.

The introduction of Joe Hill, Joe Reagan's previously unknown son, offered the family an unexpected connection to the man they had lost. However, even as he gradually found his place among the Reagans, the younger Joe's presence couldn't undo the tragedy of his father's death. The family could grow, but it could never truly be whole again.

Nevertheless, the Reagans' shared grief helped reinforce the loyalty and commitment that defined their relationships throughout Blue Bloods. Their family Sunday dinners became a reminder that, despite their disagreements and personal struggles, they could always depend on one another.

That is what makes the Hollingsworth family's predicament such a fascinating reversal. While the Reagans would have welcomed Joe's return, Jane and Mike have reason to fear what Jack's survival could mean for their children. Their family isn't facing the impossibility of reunion, but the possibility that reunion could expose betrayals too devastating to overcome.

Ultimately, Line of Fire transforms one of Blue Bloods' most heartbreaking family tragedies into a very different kind of threat, demonstrating that bringing a family back together doesn't necessarily mean making it whole.

Line of Fire airs Mondays at 10 p.m. EDT on NBC.

#3394. This tiny iOS 27 camera feature really makes a huge difference

When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control.

But a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app. If you aren’t already using customizable controls, I highly recommend doing so …

Developers know that a big reason for using third-party camera apps is being able to use them in much the same way you would a standalone camera. A key part of this is having easy access to manual control over things like aperture (on the iPhone 18 Pro), shutter speed, white balance, and choosing between manual and auto focus. Those settings are right there on the main screen of almost all third-party apps.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, the same set of controls are also available in Apple’s stock camera app. By default, these are tucked inside a menu, requiring an initial tap to open it. As we noted back in September, however, iOS 27 brings customizable controls to the camera app.

Simply open the menu and tap the Edit button (top-left when holding the phone vertically) and you can add any of the controls to the main screen. This makes them available in a single tap.

Aperture, shutter speed, and white balance as these are the three main manual controls I use. Exposure compensation, because sometimes the only reason I want to take manual control is to increase or decrease the exposure, and that provides a faster way of doing so (quicker than the alternative drag up/down within the photo, in my experience). Finally, I have one-tap access to the histogram to help in setting exposure.

It’s a similar story in video mode. I again have aperture and white balance along with exposure compensation and the histogram. But here I add instant access to frame-rate and focus modes (as I’m more likely to switch focus mode when shooting video).

Of course, third-party apps still have an important role, but this one change has made a big difference to me when using the stock camera app for both photos and video.

Do you make use of this feature yourself? If so, please share the details in the comments.

When one of the densest sci-fi shows ever made arrived on Netflix in March 2024, it made one thing abundantly clear: humanity is absolutely screwed if aliens ever decide to pay us a visit. #3391. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

#3388. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

Siri AI in iOS 27 brings major upgrades by providing world knowledge, personal context features, and being more conversational than ever. But one previously announced Siri improvement—an expanded set of actions for Apple apps—didn’t make the cut in iOS 27.0.

Now in iOS 27.3, though, Apple is rolling out its first set of new app actions for Siri AI.

Siri AI has new capabilities across apps like Calendar, Files, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It’s a big step toward making voice-driven computing more powerful on Apple platforms, and I’ve had fun experimenting with everything new Siri can do.

Apple Health gets a big overhaul in iOS 27.3, with a fresh design and new features that utilize Apple Intelligence for more personalized health insights. Per Apple:

A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.

"iOS 27.3 adds three new features I've used almost every day", "Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving". What's with these terrible clickbait titles lately? Did we go back to 2014?

Siri Recap functions like an outsourced short-term memory reserve. The data it collects is saved inside the Siri app in a new Recaps tab, where it lives for seven days and is then deleted—unless you manually save a specific recap.

So far in the beta, I’ve found the summaries Siri generates to strike a good balance of being helpful but not too invasive. It reminds me of key details, but there’s nothing I’ve seen that feels overly sensitive or personalized. That may change over time the more I use it, but so far I think this could prove a really valuable feature.

#3385. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.
