#3348. Indie App Spotlight: ‘Milton’ lets you turn your old iPad into a home dashboard

Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

Apple finally released its new HomeView this week, a smart display that serves at the center of your home. What if you don’t want to buy a new product though? Milton is an app for older iPads running iPadOS 17 and later that can serve a similar purpose.

Milton offers a customizable dashboard that allows you to put your most important tiles front and center. It can show your calendar, chores, shopping lists, weather, the clock, a photo frame, a to do list, and so much more. Everything you include will show on the family iPad, but it can also sync to iPhones if you want to check something remotely.

There’s one neat feature that’ll be fun for families: a points system. If your kids complete chores, they can be awarded points and as a parent you can set goals for what kids can earn with enough points. This system can be used to encourage kids to complete chores or follow routines. Parents can also sign off on the chores to ensure kids aren’t just tapping the complete button.

It also serves as a nice recipe guide. If you take photos of cookbooks, Milton can parse through what you captured and provide a step by step guide for cooking. If you don’t have certain ingredients, it can quickly be added to your shoping list.

This only scratches the surface of what Milton can do. You can read their website for the rest.

Here’s why Josh, the developer, decided to build Milton:

I’m a software engineer, and my partner is an oncology pharmacist. She wanted one place that kept our household organised: the calendar, the chores, the shopping, what’s for dinner. Skylight is expensive, and the iPad apps that do this charge a subscription every year. We wanted something that fit our lives, connected us as the Apple family we already are, and didn’t cost families a fortune.

Like most families, we had an old iPad lying around. We put it in a case with a magnet, stuck it to the fridge, and that became Milton.

Milton provides a very generous free offering on the App Store. The core organizer features are all available out of the box, but if you want to add more people to the app, sync across devices, or share the app with other family members (for their personal devices), you’ll need to purchase Milton Individual for $4.99 (one time purchase) or Milton Family for $14.99. Milton Family automatically shares with your iCloud family sharing group.

#3346. Forensic Experts Suggest Jeffrey Epstein Was Killed, Despite Suicide Ruling

The debate over whether Jeffrey Epstein was killed or committed suicide in jail will seemingly never die ... with a new opinion now surfacing from forensic experts who say the late pedophile was likely the victim of a homicide.

The trio of forensic experts -- Dr. Michael Freeman, Professor Anders Eriksson, and Researcher Itiel Dror -- spent months reviewing autopsy records and photos while producing a biomedical reconstruction of the case. Based on that information, the experts came to the conclusion that Epstein was likely attacked and killed by another person.

However, the New York City Medical Examiner's Office says it stands by its original ruling that Epstein died by suicide. Several federal investigations have also found that Epstein hanged himself in his jail cell in the New York City Metropolitan Correctional Center on August 2019 while he was awaiting trial on child sex trafficking charges.

The 3 forensic experts issued their findings Monday in London with the help of Epstein's brother, who provided them with photos and files pertaining to the case.

As you know, the Epstein case has taken on a life of its own ever since his death, with many believing Epstein was murdered to protect rich and powerful people to whom Epstein offered his alleged child sex trafficking services. Epstein was well known for hanging out with the so-called elite.

In 2020, Epstein's brother hired famed forensic pathologist Dr. Michael Baden to investigate Epstein's death -- and Baden concluded, based on the evidence he reviewed, that Epstein was probably murdered.

#3344. Beats 360 vs Studio Pro: Here’s which Beats headphones you should buy

In September, Apple introduced the new Beats 360 headphones, the first overears from Beats since the Beats Studio Pro in 2023. That said, the older Beats Studio Pro still remain on sale at a lower price point – so it begs the question, which Beats headphones are more worthwhile?

One of the biggest differences between the two will be the price. The Beats Studio Pro, since they’re older, are regularly available on discount. Currently, you can pick up Beats Studio Pro for $199-249 on Amazon, compared to Beats 360, which aren’t discounted from their $349 launch pricing.

Despite being older and cheaper, the Beats Studio Pro have a couple advantages over the Beats 360. On top of the fact that they’re $100-150 cheaper, you may very well still want to consider them.

The biggest advantages, in my view, have to do with the form factor. The Beats Studio Pro can fold down into a much more compact size, whereas Beats 360 don’t fold at all. This means it’s easier to carry around the Beats Studio Pro.

Beats Studio Pro also offer a headphone jack, whereas Beats 360 don’t have any sort of wired audio at all, even over USB-C. This means Beats Studio Pro are easier to use in environments where bluetooth audio isn’t convenient, such as with a game console or on an airplane.

One of my favorite things about the Beats 360 is that they offer UltraPlush cushions you can swap into, but those cost extra. Beats Studio Pro by default come with UltraPlush cushions, so you can have a more comfortable experience out of the box.

Of course, Beats 360 are newer, so by default they do a number of things better. That includes:

Out of everything on this list, I’d say clearer transparency, stronger noise cancellation, and automatic device switching make the biggest difference. In my testing, its hard to hear with the transparency mode on the Beats Studio Pro, so I end up taking the headphones off to have conversation. With Beats 360, that isn’t the case.

As for noise cancellation and automatic device switching, I feel that if you’re buying Beats for the sake of having Apple headphones, you should buy the ones that offer true automatic device switching – and those are the Beats 360. Noise cancellation is more of a personal preference, but if you value having the best noise cancellation, the Beats 360 are noticeably better.

Lastly, the Beats 360 do have the customizable design going for them. While customization is more aesthetically pleasing, it also has an advantage longer term – when the earcups start wearing down over the years, you can quickly replace them on the Beats 360.

While it’s hard to overlook the fact that Beats Studio Pro come in at a much lower price point, I’d generally say that if you want a great pair of headphones that offer an Apple experience, you probably shouldn’t buy the Beats Studio Pro. The Beats Studio Pro are a fine pair of headphones for the price, but you certainly aren’t getting all of the same ecosystem creature comforts that Beats 360 offer.

That said, Beats 360 simply do not offer a headphone jack or a foldable design, and if those things matter to you, then Beats Studio Pro might still be the way to go. Beats Studio Pro also offer a ton of different color options that aren’t available on Beats 360, while costing $150 less.

They also support wired audio via 3.5mm or USB-C.

The headphones last around 50 hours per charge (about 10 hours longer than their predecessor), and 10 minutes of charging gives you around five hours of playback, with a full recharge taking approximately two hours. In its review, PCMag describes the sound as “sculpted with accentuated bass and highs."

Although they lack ANC and adjustable EQ, these headphones still have plenty of extra features for Apple users, and those shortcomings are much easier to forgive at almost 66% off. For $69, the Beats Solo 4 headphones are a compact and well-equipped option for casual listening, with long battery life and that classic Beats aesthetic.

#3337. Jacquees' DUI Arrest Body Cam Shows Singer Passed Out in Cop Car

Jacquees ended up in handcuffs after allegedly passing out behind the wheel of his Jeep in Florida ... and new body cam footage shows how the R&B singer's September arrest unfolded.

Video obtained by TMZ shows cops and firefighters surrounding Jacquees' white Jeep Gladiator in Hollywood, Florida, before the singer is seen lying on a stretcher inside an ambulance, where officers and paramedics attend to him.

Jacquees is later seen sitting up inside the ambulance ... but he appears to doze off again in the back of a police cruiser, then later while lying on a bench at the jail.

Police say they smelled alcohol on the singer ... and things allegedly turned physical when he became combative with first responders, with authorities claiming he struck an officer's arm while they were attempting to restrain him.

Jacquees was arrested on charges of DUI, battery on an officer, firefighter, or EMT, and resisting an officer without violence.

The singer later denied the allegations while leaving jail ... telling reporters the accusations against him were false.

#3335. Gracie Abrams: ‘I Was Thrown Into the Deepest End Possible’

A t present, Gracie Abrams is trying to give herself a little grace. “I’m very interested in softness these days,” she says, wearing a serene expression and a top that looks like a cirrus cloud.

She’s sitting onstage at New York’s famed Cherry Lane Theatre. Outside, it’s a soft October night. Inside, an audience of 150 is assembled for another edition of The Rolling Stone Residency, which involves a live edition of the Rolling Stone Interview followed by a stripped-down concert. Events have not gone as planned — Abrams was meant to perform with longtime collaborator Aaron Dessner of the National. “He was supposed to be here and is so sick,” Abrams tells the crowd. “So everything that I’m playing tonight is improvised arrangements of the songs” — arrangements she came up with that day. “It’s a funny little challenge,” she says, laughing. Another chance to give herself grace, to treat herself softly.

The past few months, Abrams admits, have sometimes made that difficult. In July, she released her third studio album, Daughter From Hell, her most ambitious and musically varied offering to date — a reflection on the perspective that comes from entering adulthood, and an artifact of the time of life when one develops that perspective. The day of the album’s release, she flew to Berlin to begin filming her first feature film, Please, the latest movie from Babygirl director Halina Reijn. The anticipation leading up to these milestones had worsened the panic attacks Abrams has been having since she was a kid. Stepping outside herself, and into a role she could inhabit, had provided a welcome relief — and, ironically, helped her return to a calmer, softer version of herself.

At the Cherry Lane Theatre, her calm and grace pay off: The six-song set she plays, stripped down to just her voice and a piano is hauntingly beautiful, with plenty of playful banter between Abrams and fans, one of whom came in from Alaska for the event. Before the set, in a wide-ranging conversation mixed with humor and candor, Abrams discusses the moment of life she’s in right now, her experience filming Please, her dream collaborations, and what’s still keeping her up at night. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

The last time we talked, Daughter From Hell was coming out in two or three hours, and you were like, “I’m going to watch the last 20 minutes of Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf, turn off all devices, and be asleep before midnight.” Did that actually happen?That did happen! I didn’t lie.

How do you do that? I imagine the anticipation is pretty strong at that moment in time.In my experience thus far releasing something out into the world, it feels real when we’re on tour. When we are together is when it [feels] kind of legitimate. So I get the anticipatory adrenaline around shows, but [otherwise] I feel like I can retreat and still find peace.

So you woke up the next morning, and the album had come out. Do you go online then? Well, my relationship with the internet has changed. I was lucky that the day the album came out, I went to Berlin and we started shooting this crazy project. It really was like [being in] a fully different universe the next day. I feel like I’ve not been in the regular, present-day world for the past three and a half months, really, so my attention wasn’t online much. I would check in every once in a while. My mom would text me screenshots of stuff, and I’d be like, “Thanks, mom,” or I’d be like, “Don’t send me that. That hurts.” [Laughs.]

You have a beautiful song about your mom on this album. Does she have people over for dinner and be like, “Oh, I’m just gonna put on this little ditty?”No, no, no! Jesus. [Laughs.] No, she’s not like that. I love her so much, and she’s deeply supportive, but it would shock me to the core if I were to ever walk into the house and hear her playing the song. Do your parents play your albums at home, though?I don’t know. I don’t live there anymore, so I hope they’re listening to something else. But maybe?

Have you heard the album playing out in the world? I was in the car today, and “Minibar” was on the radio, and I was like, “What?” Of course, it feels good, it feels lovely, but mostly it makes me feel like I am sick in the head because it feels like a hallucination. There’s nothing normal about it. It’s not casual, I would say. It’s very trippy.

“I like touring because I’m unavailable and with people who have taken the music and made it theirs.”

It still doesn’t feel normal.No. If you’re not personally choosing to hear your own voice, and all of a sudden it’s happening —

It feels like an affront?Well, maybe. I haven’t unpacked this. I haven’t unpacked the psychology behind why it feels so weird.

We’re gonna get into psychology. Don’t worry. Great, can’t wait. We’re set up for it. I feel like I should be lying back.

I know. We need a sofa here, clearly. Yeah!

So you literally left the day the album came out to go make a movie with the amazing Halina Reijn. Can you talk about getting the role? Well, Halina is a genius. She’s one of my favorite people to be around, and I fell in love with her work. I loved Bodies, Bodies, Bodies. I just thought it was so fun and epic, and made me laugh so hard. And then Babygirl, obviously, blew my mind. She and I have a mutual friend, and three years ago we were set up on a date, basically, like, “I think you guys would like each other and should know each other.”

Were you going to maybe write music for her? Or was it more of a friend date?To me, it was. To me, I was just like, “I’m in love with you.” But I think she had some question marks around music for Babygirl at the time. Anyway, she let me watch it early, and I was like, “Ah!” But I met her, and it ended up just being one of those you-feel-like-you’ve-known-the-person-forever kind of a thing. And she’s a witch. Like, she’s really a witch.

I feel like you are too, though.Thank you. But she really is. Anyway, right around this time last year, she texted me and said, “I wrote a script. Do you want to read it?” I thought she was just letting me read it. Like, I didn’t gather from anything that she said that she was implying that she would then like me to audition for it. But I read it immediately, and again, it just kind of blew my mind. Really blew my mind. And then she asked if I would audition for it, and then that was a whole long, amazing process where my expectations were completely nonexistent. It just was, for me, this really sick opportunity to spend another hour in her company.

Her energy is so infectious and wild and really singular. And as I grow up and meet women who are farther along in life than I am and are so smart, I just want to spend time around them. So for me, this experience of auditioning was just a really cool gift.

And she didn’t tell you that as she was writing the script, she was envisioning you? She did not tell me that, no.

Would that have made you more nervous or less nervous? Well, I just think probably I would have read it with a different lens initially — through the lens of just deafening fear.

And it would have been weirder if you didn’t get the part.Yeah, imagine! Well, I was imagining that! I can’t believe we did it, and I just can’t believe it was documented.

It is, I believe, on film. Yeah. Watch out!

So you show up in Berlin. Were you very quickly on set? It was two days later.

Wow. I don’t know what I’m allowed to talk about, but I feel like my entry point for this was just my experience touring, where it’s a group project. Everyone who’s there has to be there in order for the thing to work, and that requires a lot of trust and mutual respect. I mean, what a humbling thing to do. You come from a Hollywood family. You know what this is to some extent, but you’ve never done it. What is going through your head? Yeah, I knew that you go to set and you do something. [Laughs.] You can understand something in theory, but I [was thrown into] the deepest end possible. And, again, just a true credit to everyone there who for some reason trusted me to do it and taught me everything.

How Method did you go?[Laughs.] Zero. I mean, definitely zero percent. I was not taking her home with me. But the reason that I fell in love with the character so much was because of how human she felt on the page. I was just trying to be as present as possible with it.

“Getting offline has felt so healthy for me.”

Did it feel pretty innate once you got going?God, I don’t know. I don’t know yet how to talk about it because we wrapped three weeks ago, and it feels very fresh. And also, I don’t feel like I’ve remotely earned the right to speak about what it feels like to do these things. I’m green, and I’m grateful, and it’s still raw. But it felt really thrilling to have this kind of crazy environment, this universe that Halina dreamt up to try lots of different crazy versions of existing, and to do it with people who are so brilliant, who I got to watch. That was just entertaining on its own. I was like, “Whoa, you’re so talented!” all the time.

And I was so afraid leading up [to it]. This whole summer, with the album coming out and knowing that this [movie] was coming, as everything was inching closer, I was not really taking great care of myself for a good chunk of time, and it was catching up with me. I had had panic attacks in my childhood, but nothing close [to what] I started having. Like, you go to the hospital because you’re sure you’re dying, and then it’s like, “Oh, my God, how did I convince myself [of that]?” And then it makes you feel kind of powerful because you’re like, “I tricked myself into thinking [that].”

“Look at what my brain can do.” Yeah, yeah. So that was heavy and not cool. And then I did do some stuff to help myself out. I felt like that helped prep me to get there and not be drowning in fear, and then it felt weirdly more relaxing than a lot of other parts of my life have felt over the past few years — I think because it wasn’t about, like, “Hi, my name is Gracie, and this is a story about my personal life, and I’m gonna go promote it.” That concept feels more and more complicated as I age.

As a sort of famously introverted person who has made a career baring your soul in music, was it a relief to be able to hide behind a character a little bit?I think it was a relief to spend three months not thinking about myself and about presentation. It’s not a normal thing. I think that’s why so many people who get into public-facing careers — even if it’s in a lane that is based in true love and passion for the thing that they do — there’s something that is very insidious and twisted about the selling something, the perception thing.

The marketing of a human being.Yeah, it’s just not nice. So that’s why I like touring: because I’m unavailable and with people who have taken the music and made it theirs. That tie is super powerful to me.

Did your amazingly talented partner, Paul Mescal, give you any acting advice?I mean, [he was] just the most brilliant sounding board. Just any- and everything that went through my head, per usual, I’m just like, “What about this? Answer me that.” Any time I personally get to better understand the inner life of anyone that I love by doing something myself, it’s cool. I like to have a truer understanding of that.

You have talked before about how writing music brings up unexpected emotions that you then have to confront and deal with, which you do in part, I suppose, by writing the music. But I’m wondering, with Daughter From Hell, what came up that is an issue that, outside of the music, you have been thinking about and working through.Just the strangeness and beauty of aging and seeing your parents as people that are doing all of this for the first time themselves too, and having a newfound softness and this internal switch from this constant urge to move far away, get far away. This switch flips, and all of a sudden, I’m on the phone to my mom six times a day. I just want to absorb as much of her wisdom as possible. I think it was nice to articulate that.

What is the existential crisis of the moment for you right now? Like, what’s keeping you up at night? Oh, Jesus! Oh, God! I mean, there’s so much. Where do you even truly begin with the state of the world right now? I think bird’s-eye view, looking down on the crises, the amount of pain and suffering and targeted, inflicted harm upon so many people — so many people — right now the way that we treat each other outside of these institutions that are completely, horribly corrupt and sinister.I feel like it’s one of the reasons that getting offline has felt so healthy for me. It’s just so normal to be so hateful, casually, and that feels unfortunate, because I think we benefit from having curiosity and compassion towards one another … And it’s weird, too, because I feel hyper-aware of what my bubble is. For the past five years being on tour, for example, that feels like an exception. It’s so beautiful on tour. It’s these spaces filled with people that are curious and compassionate and soft toward themselves and one another, at least in the room on that night. And then you end tour and you kind of reemerge into the world, and it just feels so awful. So I admire our audiences because they feel like the resistance or something.

I was gonna ask what you do for self-care these days, but you actually kind of just answered it,To not be online?

Yeah, and to be in a room where people have gathered and chosen to come together and listen to music and celebrate that. Is there something else? Like, what is your home life like right now? Well, it’s very small. All of our friends live kind of within 10 minutes of us, and it feels like a really tiny, tight-knit village. I walk a lot at the park. We watch a lot of documentaries. I think there’s something socially that’s happened to me in the past couple years where I really like to hang out. I used to really not.

Yes, it’s pretty fun, actually. It’s so nice.

What does that mean, though? What does hanging out look like? If friends are coming over and we are drinking wine or something, it’s very fun — it’s fun sober too — to do a blind-contour drawing. People always really like them and find them impressive, but they’re the opposite of impressive. I think people like to see themselves reflected back on paper or something. So anyway: writing, walking, sleeping.

What in the culture has its hook in you right now? What are you listening to? What are you reading? I’m listening to a lot of Mick Flannery at the moment. There’s this song called “Baby Talk.” I was shown this song last week, and I’ve been obsessed with it. What did I just finish? You know when you get asked a question, [and] you’re like, “I’ve never had a single experience or thought in my life.” I’ve been writing a lot of music, to be honest.

I mean, you’re always kind of writing a lot of music. Sort of, but when the album came out, I was in the middle of something completely different that really had a death grip on me. I wrote one song while I was in Berlin that was so sad and so upsetting. Honestly, it’s so upsetting. You would hate it. [Laughs.]

You’ve had a few weeks off. Have you made it up to Aaron Dessner’s studio at Long Pond? No. I’ve just been sleeping, dude. I’m literally so tired.

Do you have plans to go?I don’t right now have any plans. But, I mean, I can’t ever stay away for too long.

“It’s fun to make new arrangements of old songs and see how they are in conversation with one another.”

When I interviewed Aaron for [your cover] story, he said that when you go to Long Pond, you basically don’t leave. But I was wondering, when you do leave, what do you do? What is life like up there for you? What is there to do? Well, I think once I drove from the city to Long Pond, and that’s the one time I had a car there.

So you’re there because you’re stuck.Literally stuck. Happily stuck, though. But, yeah, Aaron is my chaperone whenever we go into town. I can only get there if he drives me, because we’re quite middle-of-nowhere vibes. But the thing is, when we do leave, we just leave and do the same thing that we do at the house. Which is, like, drink. [Laughs.]

I thought you were gonna say work on music, but no. No. Just drink.

Both of you, together, have done collaborations with some amazing artists like Noah Kahan, Justin Vernon, Taylor Swift. Is there someone you haven’t collaborated with yet that you have in your sights?Yeah, of course. I mean, I just want to sit in a room and watch people write. Adrianne Lenker, I would love to watch write. Hayley Williams, I would love to watch write. My algorithm is just Hayley Williams. It’s just videos of her onstage. Who else? Remi [Wolf]. Remi’s new album is so genius, and I love her so much. I just want to watch people write. I love doing stuff together in a room. That makes me happy.

Speaking of that, let’s talk about the Look at My Life Tour, which is coming up in December. I feel like I’ve been under a rock in the sense that ahead of the album release, we kind of front-loaded a couple things, because I was about to be off the grid for three months. Now, I feel the funny lag period between release and then being like, “Wait, I’m here. We’re doing it now.”

But you’re going into lots of rehearsals for the tour.Yeah, we ran through the full set list yesterday for the first time, which was really fun. It felt really good.

Is there a song you’re particularly excited about playing live? Well, it’s kind of sweet at this point having the amount of music that I’ve made out in the world. You have to make choices about what you’re including and what you’re not including.

It must be kind of cool to reach that point. Yeah, it’s fun to make new arrangements of old songs and see how they are in conversation with one another. I started having this weird fantasy yesterday mid-rehearsal: There’s a song from Good Riddance and a song from Secret of Us and a song from Daughter From Hell that all feel like a little triangle, like they’re so related, and then I had this fantasy, like, “I kind of want to do some kind of weird Frankenstein version of an album of songs that all feel really connected, and kind of reproduce them.”

But what song am I excited to perform? I love doing all of them. “Hit the Wall” I really love and am excited to play. “Death Wish” is one of my favorite songs to play.

“If I get overwhelmed or frustrated or scared, I like to talk to myself with softness. Something about acknowledging it makes it just continue to flow down the river.”

Is there a song that you’re like, “Oh, no, I have to play this.”I just don’t play them anymore! [Laughs.] No, I think I’ve been gone long enough that every sour emotion that I harbored has kind of dissipated, and now I’m feeling normal.

Do you feel like a different person coming off tour than you were when you started the tour? Yeah, like broken? No, I’m just kidding! Yes, of course. For sure. There’s so much that you absorb getting to do [a tour]. The energy of the crowds is so pure that I feel like the Grinch where his heart grows 10 sizes. That’s how ending a tour makes me feel.

I know lyrics can feel like time capsules. Is there a particular lyric you have where, when you sing it, it continues to really resonate in the moment every time?Oh, yeah, “I Told You Things.” Because of the weight of the relationship that that song is about, how lit on fire I felt writing that song, how in the trenches I felt, I think there’s something that will be permanently visceral for me. I think also it’s amplified by the crowd screaming it back. It’s like they’re enabling me. I’m like, “Straight to the vein.”

Last question: Do you have a mantra or a piece of guidance or advice that you hold close? Let it be soft.

What does that mean?To me it means that it’s OK to allow everything to exist at the same time. It doesn’t need to be my life experience that if I get scared or overwhelmed or frustrated with myself, that I’m attacking myself for those things. If I get overwhelmed or frustrated or scared, I like to now talk to myself with softness. There’s something about acknowledging it that makes it just continue to flow down the river.

#3332. These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Soundbars From Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Upgrading your TV's sound doesn't necessarily mean spending a fortune on a full home theater setup, especially with early Black Friday deals bringing substantial discounts on soundbars and audio systems from Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG. Sony has some of the biggest price cuts, with savings of up to 32% across select Bravia Theater models, including more than $700 off its premium Theater Trio system.

Samsung's Dolby Atmos soundbars are also discounted by as much as $400, while Bose and LG have more affordable options for anyone looking to improve dialogue clarity, add some bass, or enjoy surround sound without a complicated setup. Whether you're shopping for a compact speaker for a bedroom TV or a more immersive system for movie nights, here are the deals worth considering.

For anyone building a premium home theater around a large TV, the Sony Bravia Theater Trio is down to $1,498 from $2,199.99, saving you $701.99, or roughly 32%. Unlike a conventional soundbar, the Trio uses three separate front speakers for the left, center, and right channels, helping spread dialogue and effects across a wider soundstage. You can read PCMag’s “excellent” review for more details.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 7 is down to $718 from $869 for anyone who wants a single soundbar under the TV. Its nine speakers include upward- and side-firing drivers that widen the soundstage and give Dolby Atmos some height, but there’s no subwoofer, so the now $898 Bar 7 with a wireless sub bundle (down from $1,099.99) might be the better pick for deeper bass.

Moving down Sony's lineup, the Bravia Theater Bar 6 is $548, down from $699.99, and pairs a 3.1.2-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer and upward-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos height effects. Spending $100 more gets you the Bravia Theater System 6, now $648 from $799.99, which adds rear speakers in a 5.1-channel setup for movies and games where sound moves behind you.

For a more affordable upgrade, the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is down to $278 from $349.99, saving you nearly $72. It's a 3.1-channel system with a dedicated center speaker and wireless subwoofer, so dialogue should come through more clearly while music and movie effects get some additional low-end presence.

Sony’s older systems are discounted too, including the HT-S400 at $258, down from $299, which pairs a 2.1-channel soundbar and wireless subwoofer with S-Force Pro Front Surround to widen the sound for everyday TV, sports, and casual movies. The HT-S40R is arguably the better deal at the same $258, down from $329.99, since it adds two rear speakers for a full 5.1-channel setup, though neither model supports Dolby Atmos.

For smaller rooms or for anyone who mainly wants dialogue to come across more clearly, Bose has two compact soundbars on sale: The newer Bose TV Speaker (2nd Gen) is down to $239 from $299, with an updated acoustic design that Bose says improves clarity and overall sound performance. Meanwhile, the original Bose TV Speaker is $199, down from $279, and offers a similarly compact design with a dedicated dialogue mode and adjustable bass.

Samsung’s HW-Q800H is down to $697.99 from $1,097.99, a $400 cut on a 5.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar with a wireless subwoofer. Its side- and upward-firing speakers help place effects around and above you, while a dedicated center channel keeps dialogue clear during busy action scenes.

For something that takes up less space, the Samsung HW-S60D is $277.99, down from $399.99, and fits seven speakers, including side-firing drivers, into a compact 5.0-channel soundbar. It also supports Dolby Atmos, Adaptive Sound, and a voice enhancement mode, along with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, and Chromecast for music streaming. That said, it has no upward-firing speakers or subwoofer, so its height effects and bass won’t match that of the Q800H.

If you're looking for a complete surround sound system without spending several hundred dollars, the LG S6FTR is down to $249.99 from $399.99, saving you $150, or roughly 38%. It's a 5.1-channel home theater package with a soundbar, subwoofer, and dedicated rear speakers. That makes it particularly appealing for action movies and games, where directional sound adds to the experience.

The LG S40TR is another affordable option for anyone who wants rear speakers included in the box. It's currently $199.99, down from $279.99, and offers a 4.1-channel arrangement with a wireless subwoofer and two rear speakers. This should give movie soundtracks a greater sense of direction than a basic soundbar, while the subwoofer handles the lower frequencies that smaller TV speakers often struggle to reproduce.

At just under $187, the S60T is the least expensive system in this roundup, pairing a 3.1-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer for clearer dialogue and fuller sound than your TV’s speakers. That said, it lacks rear speakers and Dolby Atmos height channels, so it’s better suited to someone who wants a simple, affordable upgrade without filling the room with additional hardware.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3331. Sen. Josh Hawley Says Outages Feel Like Possible Coordinated Cyberattack

Sen. Josh Hawley isn't buying the idea that America's recent wave of massive outages is just one big coincidence ... and he's worried the country could be dealing with a coordinated cyberattack!!!

Charlie caught up with the Senator from Missouri in D.C. Tuesday ... and he admitted he's just as concerned as everyone else after a string of disruptions involving the FAA, banks, Microsoft Outlook and United Airlines.

"You can't tell me it's a coincidence," Hawley told us ... saying his first thought was that the country was under a cyberattack. He added, "Maybe I'm wrong. I hope I'm wrong."

And he's not exactly sold on the explanation for Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop ... questioning how a single router in Arkansas could bring air travel across the country to a screeching halt.

Hawley says the bigger problem is lawmakers haven't been briefed on what's happening ... leaving him with no more answers than the average American scrolling through the news.

For context, the FAA says it has found no evidence of a cyberattack, while JPMorgan Chase blamed Monday's banking disruption on a software bug.

Still, Hawley wants a full investigation and believes President Trump should be pressing his cabinet secretaries for answers.

The senator warned the uncertainty could lead to something even uglier ... people afraid to fly or a run on banks as Americans worry about accessing their own money.

But before anyone starts building a bunker, Hawley pumped the brakes ... telling us there's no reason to stockpile supplies or cause a panic just yet.

His bottom line? Americans deserve answers ... before fear takes over.

#3330. Microsoft Officially Apologized for Yesterday's Outages

If you were having trouble accessing certain services like Microsoft Teams or Outlook, you were not alone. Early Thursday afternoon, many of Microsoft's biggest apps and services were experiencing downtime. According to Downdetector, which tracks user reports of issues with websites and platforms, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Teams, and OneDrive were all experiencing issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft has restored service to many users, and has officially apologized for the outages.

When I first published this article on Thursday, I couldn't even load Microsoft 365's status page. (I've reported on many service outages, but I can't recall a time when a service's status page was also down.) Even as of Friday afternoon, the page still says "Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise)," and Microsoft says the following services may be affected: Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 admin center, Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center, Microsoft 365 Education, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft Power Apps, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft To Do, Power BI, SharePoint Online, Universal Print, and Windows 365.

Looking specifically at Outlook, Microsoft's email service had hundreds of thousands of user reports Thursday afternoon, signaling a major issue somewhere in Microsoft's pipeline. The reports did "slow down" throughout the day, but Downdetector still showed over 50,000 reports coming in every 15 minutes when I checked Thursday afternoon.

While the root cause of the issue was a mystery throughout Thursday's outage, Microsoft confirmed the problem in an apology on Friday. According to the company, "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI [or] agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions."

Microsoft says it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption to its customers and partners. The company says the fix rolled out slower than some might expect, since it wanted to restore service gradually to evaluate stability at each stage. It also says it will release a full post-incident report once it completes a review.

During the outage, the company had confirmed that some of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load, which it said was likely contributing to the issues. Microsoft then said it was pausing all deployments and moving traffic from affected infrastructure, and that it found that a number of its servers were unexpectedly unavailable after failing health checks. The company then thought a specific component responsible for processing server health may be the reason the system is failing health checks. Microsoft said an alternative service health check method successfully restarted some of the affected servers. The company was then actively restarting and validating affected servers to bring them back to service.

#3329. MacBook Neo 2: Here’s everything we know so far

Apple released the all-new MacBook Neo earlier this year, and it’s been a resounding success by all indications. Here’s everything we know so far about what’s next for Apple’s most affordable laptop …

The current MacBook Neo is powered by the A18 Pro chip, which is the same chip used in the iPhone 16 Pro. As reported by Bloomberg, Apple is working on a next-generation MacBook Neo powered by the A19 Pro chip.

In terms of performance, the A19 Pro is about 10-15% faster than the A18 Pro in single-core and multi-core CPU tests. The jump in GPU performance is even bigger, with benchmarks showing an up to 40% boost for the A19 Pro. This is because every GPU core in the A19 Pro has Neural Accelerators built in.

The A19 Pro chip is also used in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone Air.

According to reporter Tim Culpan, Apple will likely use a “binned” version of the A19 Pro chip in the MacBook Neo. While the A19 Pro chip in the iPhone 17 Pro has a 6-core GPU, the MacBook Neo version of the chip will likely have a 5-core GPU.

One of the compromises of the MacBook Neo is that it has 8GB of RAM. The rest of Apple’s Mac lineup nowadays starts with 16GB of RAM.

The next-generation MacBook Neo won’t jump all the way to 16GB of RAM. Instead, it’s expected to offer 12GB of RAM thanks to the aforementioned A19 Pro.

As I wrote in my review, I don’t think it’s a huge limitation that the MacBook Neo has just 8GB of RAM. Still, an increase for the next-generation model is a great improvement.

The combination of the A19 Pro chip and 12GB of RAM upgrades should also unlock support for Apple’s more powerful on-device AI model announced at WWDC. This model enables a more accurate dictation experience and new options for customizing the Siri voice.

The current MacBook Neo doesn’t support this feature because of its A18 Pro chip and 8GB of RAM.

The MacBook Neo is available in an array of fun colors, including citrus, blush, indigo, and silver. Bloomberg reports that Apple’s plan is to “periodically” update the MacBook Neo with new colors.

There aren’t any details on which colors the next-generation MacBook Neo will be available in.

Apple released the current MacBook Neo in March. Tim Culpan reports that the A19 Pro version of the machine is slated for a release sometime in 2027.

What changes do you want Apple to make with the second-generation MacBook Neo? Are you a MacBook Neo user? Let us know down in the comments.

#3328. Techno Innovator Juan Atkins Will Be Honored With a 12-Hour Celebration of Life in Detroit

The family of late techno legend Juan Atkins will celebrate his life and legacy at a special event in Detroit this Sunday, Nov. 22.

The public event will take place at the Lincoln Factory and run for 12 hours, starting at 2 p.m. and ending at 2 a.m. Fans will be able to RSVP to attend via electronic music website Resident Advisor. Full details about the event haven’t been revealed yet, including who might speak or perform. A statement shared on social media read, “The gathering will bring together family, friends, fellow artists and fans to honor his music and his influence. All are welcome. Please celebrate his life and work with us.”

Atkins died on Nov. 1 after being found unresponsive in a hotel room in Mexico City the day before. He was 64. An official cause of death has not yet been revealed, though Atkins had reportedly been battling health issues related to diabetes in recent years.

Born in Detroit, and raised in nearby Belleville, Michigan, Atkins played a pivotal role in the creation of Detroit techno, fusing elements of early Chicago house with the electronic music being made by groups like Kraftwerk and Yellow Magic Orchestra. Atkins worked closely with his longtime friends and collaborators, Kevin Saunders and Derrick May; the trio met in high school and eventually came to be known as the “Belleville Three.”  Trending Stories Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years Jennifer Lopez Teases New Music on ‘Fallon’: ‘This Does Feel Like a Happy Era’ Cynthia Erivo, Travis Barker Honor Phil Collins With Big Vocals, Big Drums at Rock Hall Ceremony Miley Cyrus Shares Sweet Memory of Godmother Dolly Parton as They Earn a Grammy Nod Together

Atkins began has career as a DJ before forming the group Cybotron, which released one influential album, Enter, in 1983. He went on to found his own label, Metroplex, and, under the moniker Model 500, released the seminal early Detroit techno classic, “No UFO’s,” in 1985. Atkins continued to record as Model 500 over the next several decades, though occasionally used other aliases and his own name.

“A great DJ is a leader. A mediocre DJ is a follower,” Atkins told Rolling Stone in 2024. “That’s what I try in DJ’ing and making music and presenting music. The public attention span is pretty short, and people are always interested in what’s next. Not so much what happened yesterday. Not so much what’s happening right now. But what’s next?”

#3327. 10 Books Like ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering new depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

The story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

If Feyre’s grit and determination are your favorite aspect of ACOTAR, Julie Kagawa’s Iron Fey series (starting with The Iron King) will be your next obsession. Meghan Chase has never felt ‘normal’ in her life, and she’s been haunted by her father’s disappearance since she was a child. When her brother also vanishes, she goes on a quest for answers, learns that she’s actually the daughter of a faerie king, and finds herself in a magical world that blurs in elements of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Meghan is determined to save her brother (and herself), but a certain ice-cold fae prince captures her attention, even though he’s as dangerous as he is beautiful.

If you’re looking for some serious romance in your fantasy, Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Blood and Ash series is a must. Poppy was chosen at birth to be the kingdom’s Maiden, isolated and untouched in order to be ready for her Ascension to ensure the land is protected from the evil force that took her family. But it’s a lonely existence—until Hawke is assigned as her sworn protector. Golden-eyed and beautiful, Hawke offers Poppy the connection she’s craved. When chaos erupts around her, Hawke takes the opportunity to spirit Poppy away. But Hawke has a secret, and Poppy is soon in danger of losing both her heart and the favor of the gods themselves.

If you love how A Court of Thorns and Roses takes the “enemies-to-lovers” trope and builds it into a deep, complex mesh of emotions and plot twists, you’ll love Shelby Mahurin’s Serpent & Dove series. When witch Louise le Blanc flees her coven, she takes shelter in the city of Cesarine, where magic is forbidden, and witches are unceremoniously hunted and burned. Louise’s life gets infinitely more complicated, dangerous, and steamy when she’s trapped into an unwanted marriage with Reid Diggory—who happens to be a huntsman of the Church, charged with tracking down and eliminating witches. And then Louise starts to realize that Reid is actually pretty darn hot.

If you’re looking for a romantasy that’s broadly similar to ACOTAR while being its own thing, read A.K. Mulford’s The Five Crowns of Okrith series, starting with The High Mountain Court. Remy is a red witch, which means she’s in hiding and ready to make a run for it if the fae get near. So when a group of fae shows up at her tavern, she makes for the exit—only to be captured by Prince Hale of the Eastern Court. Instead of striking her down, however, Hale asks Remy for help—he needs to locate two ancient magical artifacts created by red witches, and he needs her red magic to find them. Hale promises to set her free and even reunite her with the red witches still living. More importantly, Remy finds Hale irresistible and has a primal urge to stay with him, no matter what the cost.

Looking for a romantasy with a slightly different vibe from ACOTAR? Variety is the spice of life, after all—and The Fourth Wing delivers. Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean Series made a huge splash when it debuted, and for good reason—it has everything, from a capable, intelligent heroine thrust into a dangerous scenario (in this case, a dragon rider academy where failure can be deadly) and forced to navigate alliances, conspiracies, and her own heart, which is pushing her towards a romance that might be as dangerous as the dragons themselves.

Love the moral complexity of ACOTAR, where everyone has at least a touch of darkness? Check out The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black. When Jude was a child, the father of her half-sister, the faerie Madoc, murdered her parents and took her back to the Faerie world with him. Raised as part of the gentry, Jude lives in a world where her mortal nature is hated and despised, but she battles for her place at court anyway while struggling with her love-hate relationship with her adoptive father and a growing bond with the titular prince, a relationship that is strictly forbidden. Jude is a fierce and extremely morally gray character, and one that fans of Feyre will adore.

Looking for more smart women at the center of beautifully-rendered fantasy stories? You’ll love Princess Lucero-Elisa de Riqueza of Orovalle, star of this series-starter by Rae Carson. Elisa was chosen for “Service” as a baby, when a godstone was placed in her navel by the gods, signaling that she was destined for greatness. But as a young woman, Elisa is self-hating and miserable. She’s never done anything even remotely great, and spends her time isolated, overweight, and reading military strategy books. One day she’s shocked to discover she’s been married off to the king of a distant land on the brink of war—and suddenly all that rage and book learning becomes invaluable as she struggles to survive an unfamiliar court and help her new homeland survive a dangerous onslaught.

If you loved Feyre’s journey as she discovered unknown reservoirs of power and courage inside herself, you should read Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse novels, starting with Shadow and Bone. As a child, Alina was tested by the Grisha and found to possess no magical ability. As an adult, she serves as a cartographer in the army. Charged with guiding the Darkling—the most powerful of the Grisha—across the dangerous and terrifying Shadow Fold, Alina is unexpectedly revealed to have incredible powers and is packed off to train with the Grisha. There, she must determine who her friends and enemies are, even while falling under the spell of the charismatic Darkling.

Emilia di Carlo and her sister Vittoria are very different—Emilia is bookish and shy, Vittoria outgoing and brash—but they share a secret: They’re both streghe, and have spent their lives learning to use magic. In this version of Italy, the Malvagi (the seven princes of Hell) haven’t been seen in a long time, but a terrifying accident summons the Prince of Wrath and leaves three witches dead, including Vittoria. Emilia swears to use her power to avenge her sister, but when her revenge is delayed and she’s forced to work with Wrath, unwanted feelings begin to tick up the spice level to an uncomfortable degree.

#3324. The Lost Michael Jackson Tapes

T he track begins with funky guitar-strumming set to a rock & roll backbeat; 30 seconds in, a group of singers sweetly harmonizes about peace in the valley. Then a lone voice emerges, sharp and clear: “You should see what a lovely, lovely world this would be/Everyone has to live together.” It’s a soulful cover of the Rascals’ 1968 hit “People Got to Be Free,” tastefully done, but one element stands out: that solo voice, which sounds oddly familiar, especially when he hits the high notes. Is that…?

You’ve probably never heard this track, or six others believed to have been recorded at Crystal Sound Recording Studios in Los Angeles in 1976. Almost no one has. They were never released as singles or on rarities albums. They never even made it into bootleggers’ hands. But the lead voice sounds unmistakably like Michael Jackson, and the backup singers sound like his brothers, Jackie, Marlon, Tito, and Randy, just a few years removed from their immortal string of Jackson 5 hits at Motown.

According to Susan Michelson and Alex Cyrell, a husband-and-wife duo of veteran producers who shared the seven tracks with Rolling Stone, these recordings were made during a mysterious blip in the Jacksons’ career. They seem to capture Michael, then 17, in a transition between his brassy Motown voice and his “Billie Jean” sneer, scatting and ad-libbing through “Sweet Music,” the pleading ballad “Blues Away” (which later appeared in a different version on an official album), the wah-wah guitar-heavy rocker “Disco Kids,” a bluesy version of Boz Scaggs’ yet-to-be-released “We’re All Alone,” the pillow-talking disco love song “Goodness Knows,” and the midtempo piano boogie “Gimme What I Need,” as well as “People Got to Be Free.”

Richard Lecocq, a Paris-based Jackson biographer who co-wrote Michael Jackson: All the Songs: The Story Behind Every Track, which covers more than 200 releases, seems shocked to learn the songs exist. “I would definitely be interested in hearing this,” he says.  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Even veteran L.A. musicians listed on studio documents as having played these sessions seem a bit confused: “In 1976? Oh, Lord,” says veteran bassist Nate Watts, who acknowledges he remembers only the barest details. Before he died in April, drummer James Gadson recalled in an interview: “I probably did the sessions. But I don’t know what happened to them.”

Could it be? Are these unreleased, unheralded, almost completely unknown tracks actually lost recordings featuring the King of Pop? The Jacksons’ history has been studied and retold and examined and analyzed for decades — so if the tracks are real, what do they portend for our understanding of that history? And why is this the first time anyone is hearing about these songs?

IN 1976, MICHAEL JACKSON was stuck between two phases of his superstar career. He and his brothers had just finished their run as the Jackson 5, the bubblegum-soul kids behind Motown smashes like “ABC,” “I Want You Back,” “I’ll Be There,” and “The Love You Save.” Their manager, family patriarch Joseph Jackson, wanted his sons to write and produce more of their music, giving them a lucrative share of the publishing royalties — good timing, it would turn out, since Michael was growing into a gifted songwriter who within a few years would come up with classics like “Don’t Stop ’Til You Get Enough” and “Billie Jean.” So in March of 1976, the Jackson 5 left Motown.

Because Motown owned the name “Jackson 5,” the brothers would now be known as the Jacksons. The newly renamed group signed to Epic Records, then a division of the powerful CBS Records. Future success did not seem guaranteed. The brothers’ most recent Top 10 hit had been 1974’s “Dancing Machine,” and executives were skeptical the family group could pull off the rare trick of growing into adult hitmakers.  Related Content Big Oil, Climate Change, and a ‘Smoking Gun’ Looze Cannon Was Rapping Before You Met ‘Big Michael’ Stevie Wonder's Eviction Lawsuit Escalates as Rent-Free Resident Demands Repairs to Walls and Plumbing Paris Jackson Calls Estate Executor’s $109 Million Fee Request ‘Offensive,’ Seeks Reduction

Walter Yetnikoff, CBS’ fiery president, took in a 1975 Jacksons concert at the Westbury Music Fair on Long Island, New York, and found it “less than spectacular,” as he recalled in his autobiography. Yetnikoff was especially unimpressed when Michael stepped into the spotlight and sang his Motown ballad “Ben.” But he let two more-enthusiastic underlings, Epic promotions men Ron Alexenburg and Steve Popovich, talk him into signing the group. Sure, Michael had sung about a dead rat, Popovich told Yetnikoff. But, he added, “‘Ben’ was a smash. We’ll make money on this group, believe me.”

The Jacksons were determined to prove they weren’t a washed-up boy band, and Alexenburg and Popovich did all they could to help. To make the group’s first album, Alexenburg reached out to producers Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff. As heads of Philadelphia International Records, they’d turned unknowns like Harold Melvin and the Blue Notes and the O’Jays into stars. Huff wrote the music, Gamble wrote the lyrics, and they pioneered a lush and orchestral soul style that proved to be the bridge from Motown to the disco era.

Michael, Jackie, Tito, Marlon, and Randy (who briefly replaced Motown loyalist Jermaine during this period) worked with Gamble and Huff to make The Jacksons, a slickly produced, gently funky album that largely concerns itself with dancing and having a good time, especially on its biggest hit, “Enjoy Yourself.” It’s perhaps most notable for the vocal whoops and Oh, yeah’s that were to become Michael’s signature.

“We clicked with them immediately. They got us right away,” Jackie Jackson recalls of Gamble and Huff. “It pretty much changed our sound from a young sound to an older adult sound.” The Jacksons went gold and hit the Top 10 of Billboard’s Soul chart.

But there may have been an evolutionary step before this album that Jacksons historians haven’t been aware of: those mysterious Crystal Sound sessions earlier in 1976. According to several sources, the producer behind those sessions was Bobby Taylor, a singer who had played a crucial role in the Jacksons’ story. After the brothers opened for his R&B band, the Vancouvers, in 1968, he was so impressed that he mentioned the family group to Berry Gordy Jr., the powerful head of Motown Records. Taylor’s discovery — which Motown falsely attributed to Diana Ross — led to the Jackson 5’s audition and eventually to classic hits like “ABC” and “I Want You Back.”

Before he died in 2017, Taylor discussed the Crystal Sound recordings in a phone interview from his home in Hong Kong. He had trouble remembering details, and may have confused the Crystal Sound sessions with Jackson 5 songs he’d produced years earlier for Motown. “The sessions went great,” he said. “Everything I gave [Michael] to sing, he could sing it right back. That’s how I told him to do everything.”

Joe Jackson commissioned the sessions and brought in Taylor as the main producer, according to Susan Michelson and Alex Cyrell, the husband-and-wife duo who joined the project at Taylor’s invitation. Epic’s Popovich, Cyrell says, was “deeply and closely involved with production and approval, attending sessions, choosing songs (the “People Got to Be Free” cover was his idea), overseeing budgets, and meeting over meals with the three producers. Cyrell and Michelson add that Epic paid for the sessions — claims backed up by pay stubs, invoices, and studio receipts they’ve kept for decades and shared with Rolling Stone.

Cyrell and Michelson met in New York in 1974. Michelson, who’d been a vocal major at Boston University, had just returned from London, where she worked as a backup singer at the legendary Olympic Studios; Cyrell was a drummer who’d played in the house band at a resort in the Catskill Mountains, at one point backing the great soul singer Jackie Wilson. At the time he met Michelson, he was producing an album for the bubblegum-pop label Buddha Records. After meeting at Cyrell’s SoHo loft, they soon started dating. They married six years later and have a daughter, now in her thirties. “I had this feeling of familiarity: ‘Oh, no, I’m getting into a relationship again,’” Michelson recalls. “I didn’t know I was going to spend 50 years with this guy.”

Cyrell met Alice Cooper’s manager Shep Gordon just as the shock-rocker’s career was taking off, and soon Cyrell and Michelson became pals with Cooper himself. By 1976, in fact, they were living in Cooper’s guest house “at the top of Beverly Hills,” according to Michelson, because a fire had recently damaged his main house.

Around then, Cyrell and Michelson started becoming friends with Taylor, who invited them into the Jacksons project. The Jacksons themselves socialized at Cooper’s property: “Randy and Jackie would come up all the time,” Michelson says. Occasionally, the young producers visited the Jacksons at their family home in Encino, California, where matriarch Katherine Jackson cooked dinner and they encountered the family’s Dobermans.

Crystal Sound’s late owner, a classically trained pianist named Andrew Berliner, had designed and built the studio with a huge central console. It was a busy studio back then, near the intersection of Santa Monica Boulevard and Vine Street in Hollywood. While Taylor, Cyrell, and Michelson say they ran the Jacksons’ sessions by day, Stevie Wonder was working all night at Crystal on his masterpiece Songs in the Key of Life.

Cyrell and Michelson sharply remember the sessions. They say the Jackson brothers, several of whom were still teenagers, arrived with a tutor, Rose Fine, who supervised them by day. Also present: nine-year-old Janet Jackson, who, at one point, sang on studio recordings, possibly for the first time in her career. “If we wanted to work late, I will admit, we all pretended the kids went home,” Michelson says. “But they didn’t, and they came back to the studio and worked with us more into the evening.” Cyrell calls the sessions “intimate,” and adds: “Bobby told me that Michael would often say to him, ‘Hey, Bobby, stop cussing so much!’ There was almost a paternal aspect.”

In June 1976, Taylor sent a memo to Epic executives along with six hastily mixed tracks, including “Disco Kids” and “Goodness Knows”: “They are VERY ROUGH COPIES, intended only to give you a good, general idea of what is on the tracks,” he wrote.

The tracks in Cyrell and Michelson’s possession — seven overall, with the addition later of “People Got to Be Free” — are what Cyrell calls the “verified complete final mix” sent to Epic’s Popovich after the Crystal sessions. Because they were never released, Popovich kept them in his private archive; after his death, his son, Steve Popovich Jr., shared them privately with Cyrell and Michelson.

Cyrell is proud of the recordings, which he calls “finished product. It’s not Michael doodling in the studio.” (Although: Michael may have been literally doodling at times. Michelson recalls Jackson requesting a pencil during the session, and shows me a scribble of a face she says Jackson produced during breaks from recording.)

Many musicians and engineers who worked at Crystal in 1976 recall interacting with the Jacksons. “I saw them a lot,” says John Fischbach, a producer who worked on Songs in the Key of Life. “I remember the sessions were with Bobby, but I was so busy with Stevie that I can’t tell you anything other than that.” Watts, the bassist who provided the funk on Wonder’s “I Wish,” “Sir Duke,” and other Songs In the Key of Life classics, says he also backed the Jacksons at Crystal.

Bob Manchurian arranged dozens of big 1970s recordings, by artists from the Supremes to Patti LaBelle. He’s 92, so it makes sense that he wouldn’t recall every detail from every session he worked on. But he remembers one thing about Michael Jackson and his siblings, for whom he arranged several tracks at Crystal in 1976. “They liked my beard. They gave me a comb for my beard,” he says, by phone from his home near Atlanta. “They used to mess with me. Michael used to say, ‘Let’s get it out of the way.’”

In addition to the seven unreleased tracks featuring Michael and his brothers, siblings Randy and Janet dueted on four sprightly tracks of their own: “Rock You to Your Socks,” “The Two of Us,” “You’re My Everything,” and “Sugar Candy Kisses.” Watts remembers this part of the Jacksons experience in particular: “We were coming in at night. I remember that day because [sister] La Toya came, too, and Joe was there.” (Janet Jackson did not respond to requests for comment.)

Over Zoom, guitarist Jay Graydon immediately recognizes his playing at the beginning of “Rock You to Your Socks.” He expresses incredulity that the songs were never released. “Record companies make money selling product. Why would they not sell product?” he asks.

One possible answer: The sessions never took place, as Alexenburg, who signed the Jacksons as an Epic senior vice president, insisted in a 2017 interview: “I wouldn’t have allowed it,” he said then. “There’s so much going around about Michael that’s not true — ’76 had one producer, Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff. That was it.”

But today, he amends this assessment: “We signed them in 1976. They certainly were recording only for Epic, and I don’t know about anything that was earlier recorded independently. I certainly would have been told. I never heard anything.”

At least one of the Jacksons remembers the Crystal Sound sessions. “It’s very vague. A lot was taking place. So many songs,” Jackie Jackson, who continues to tour internationally with the Jacksons, told Rolling Stone in 2017. “I remember Crystal Sound. We made a lot of music there. I recognize the names. I remember ‘Goodness Knows.’”

Given the meticulousness of Michael Jackson and Jackson 5 fans, and their intense social media presence, would Rolling Stone be making a mistake to publish a report about this “lost” album? “No, you’re not,” he responded. “I know the titles of those songs. I really know those songs. I remember those songs. I just can’t think of the melody of how it went.”

On all seven of the tracks, the Jackson brothers sound sharp, particularly Jackie in his high pitch. Michael stretches out Hey’s, Oh’s, and Yeah’s and hits impossibly high notes. “When you get it all together/You still gotta be a man,” he sings on the ballad “Gimme What I Need.” “It’s all a will-o-the-wisp/Try to catch it if you can.”

At times, he is a mannered member of the Jacksons’ ensemble, but frequently he’s determined to show what he can do with his maturing voice. On “Sweet Music,” which anticipates the later Jacksons hit “Blame It on the Boogie,” he wrings out the emotion on the word “rhyme” and throws in a Yeah! at the end; on “People Got to Be Free,” he growls “Tell me why” in a way that recalls his famous Shamone! in “Bad” and “Man in the Mirror” more than a decade later.

These songs showcase a voice a hair deeper than we’d just heard on “Dancing Machine,” with more willingness, and perhaps more permission, to air out the growing complexities of his singing. “Michael’s voice is pristine. Seventeen years old, just before he turned 18,” says James Whitney, a veteran Los Angeles songwriter who contributed “Disco Kids,” “Goodness Knows,” and “Sweet Music” to the 1976 sessions. “Very expressive.”

Matt Forger, an engineer on several of Jackson’s classic solo albums in the Eighties, listened to the tracks and responded to questions over email. “Sounds like Michael to me. Sounds like that era as well,” he wrote. “MJ’s voice has a younger character and the music is not as sophisticated as later albums by the Jacksons.”

Given the detailed memories of Cyrell and Michelson and the financial records and documentation they provide, plus the more foggy recollections of veteran musicians who played on many recordings every day, we can say with confidence that these Jacksons sessions took place at Crystal Sound in 1976. Neither Sony Music Entertainment, which bought Epic in 1987 and therefore owns the recordings, nor Jackson’s estate have denied their existence. So the recordings are almost certainly real.

But this only raises one more question: Why haven’t the songs been released?

BACK IN 1976, THERE may have been business reasons for CBS to sit on the Crystal tracks: Some who worked on the recordings vaguely recall a dispute over publishing between Epic executives and Joe Jackson. (A representative for Joe Jackson, who died in 2018, said in 2017 that he didn’t remember anything about that period; other than Jackie Jackson, none of the Jacksons responded to interview requests.)

Plus, while Popovich and Alexenburg worked closely together at Epic, they may have been pushing the Jacksons in separate directions. Alexenburg favored Gamble and Huff. He says the Crystal sessions “were never mentioned to me by Joe Jackson, his awful father, or Michael, or Richard Arons, who was the lawyer.”

It is possible that Popovich acted independently — without informing Alexenburg — when he set up the Crystal sessions with Taylor. By 1977, Popovich may have become distracted. He abandoned his $100,000-per-year salary at Epic, moved home to Cleveland, and used seed money from Epic to form an indie label called Cleveland International. You may have heard of its first signing: Meat Loaf. With Popovich gone, the Jacksons’ Crystal recordings lost their champion.

Why Sony continues to keep the tracks unheard remains a mystery. “I’ve had the opportunity and pleasure to listen to these songs over the years, and they’re brilliant,” says Popovich’s son, Steve Popovich Jr., a Nashville music-company consultant. “I don’t understand why they’ve never been released.”

Representatives for the label, which owns the recordings, declined to comment for this story, as did reps for Michael Jackson’s estate. Presumably, Michael Jackson’s estate, Tito Jackson’s estate, Randy Jackson, Jackie Jackson,  and Marlon Jackson, as the performers on the tracks, would have to agree to any release, but neither Sony nor reps for the Jacksons would discuss the details of their record contracts at the time.  Popovich gave a video interview shortly before his 2011 death acknowledging the Crystal sessions and recalling meeting Michael Jackson at his home studio in Encino around the same time. “It’s wonderful to listen to today, and how far the whole Jackson empire progressed since that time,” Popovich said in the video.

Since Michael Jackson’s death in 2009, Sony, with the cooperation of Jackson’s estate, has rolled out multiple reissues and compilation albums, including a 25th-anniversary version of Bad and a 40th-anniversary version of Thriller. The first of these was 2010’s heavily hyped Michael, which initially contained three tracks later removed after fans derided them and claimed they belonged to a soundalike imposter. (One fan filed a lawsuit against Sony and Jackson’s estate in 2014; eight years later, Sony pulled the tracks from the album and settled the suit.)

Sony’s posthumous releases have largely ignored the Jackson siblings, despite their big-selling albums in the Seventies and Eighties. “When you think of it, none of the albums have been properly reissued, [like] Destiny or Triumph,” Lecocq, the biographer, notes.

Cyrell and Michelson have been sitting on the mixes for decades. They hardly share them with anybody, partly because they don’t want Sony to sue them for releasing tracks to which, the couple acknowledge, they do not own the rights; and partly because they want to be responsible partners in case they have to collaborate with the label on future reissues.

In the 50 years since the Jacksons sessions, Cyrell and Michelson have been what they call “serial entrepreneurs,” creating DIY businesses like Future Primitive Designs, which sold musical-instrument miniatures, and OmniMount Systems Inc., a way of attaching loudspeakers and other heavy objects to walls. Michelson managed the late Dick Wagner, Cooper’s guitarist, and edited his 2012 memoir, Not Only Women Bleed: Vignettes From the Heart of a Rock Musician. Cyrell published Creativ, a glossy magazine. The pair continued to play sporadically on album releases.

Michelson corresponded with Popovich before his death. Later, Cyrell met with John Doelp, a former Sony exec who oversaw Michael Jackson reissues for years. In 2010, Cyrell wrote Doelp a detailed memo about the tracks, noting, “I can and will help you with names, writers, performers and other valuable retrospectives surrounding this great music.” Cyrell says the exec was “really excited” about the tracks, but that Doelp took several year to locate the original session tapes in Sony’s vaults. Cyrell and Doelp met to review and compare both sets of tracks at Sony’s Los Angeles offices in 2014. Afterward, according to Cyrell, Doelp said he didn’t know when the tracks would be released and the conversations between the two trailed off. (Doelp, who no longer works at Sony, did not respond to requests for comment.)

Three years after that, Whitney, the L.A. songwriter, communicated with Doelp, too. He recalls that Doelp had never heard of the recordings and said he had to look for them — but after four months of email exchanges, he says, Doelp and other Sony execs stopped responding. “I got to Columbia/Epic and they said, ‘We found it — and everybody’s out in the hall dancing to it right now!’” Whitney recalls. “Then they called me and said, ‘We can’t release it yet.’”

Whitney is frustrated. “It would be the lost album,” he says by phone. “I said, ‘I’ve got to finally tell somebody.’ I haven’t talked to anyone about it. It’s been 50 years! I feel like I’ve been sitting on an egg.” Trending Stories The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For Sade Are Not Attending Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years Pink Floyd’s Roger Waters Files for Divorce From Fourth Wife Kamilah Chavis After 5 Years of Marriage

Sitting at a dining-room table overlooking a pool and palm trees in Paradise Valley, Arizona, Cyrell and Michelson rock out to the Jacksons tracks almost nobody has ever heard. When teenage Michael ad-libs “All right-ah” in his inimitable voice, on “We’re All Alone,” they point and mouth the words. The songs prompt their memories of the Jacksons’ work at Crystal. “I never saw any dispute or any discomfort with each other,” Michelson says. “Michael was very into it. He’d sit really close to me, almost leaning into me, and talk right into my ear very softly. He liked most of the time to face away from the control-room window.”

After all this time, why alert the world to sessions that took place 50 years ago? Mostly, Cyrell and Michelson say, they’re tired of keeping the secret and want Sony to release the tracks, already. “Look, I’ve got a lot going on in my life. This isn’t ‘the moment I’ve been waiting for,’” Cyrell says. “But it’s crazy this stuff is being held back.”
